Collectors on the forums generally rank early deep-groove Prestige originals with RVG stamps above the 1970s reprocessed-stereo and most later reissues for tonal immediacy, though surface noise and mastering roughness (a known Van Gelder trait of the era) are common complaints. Within the Soultrane fidelity hierarchy, this mono deep-groove first-pressing sits at the top alongside other early-stamper copies, ahead of the 1960s stereo "reprocessed" Prestige pressings (which are electronically rechanneled and generally disfavored), the OJC reissues mastered from later-generation tapes, and modern audiophile cuts such as the Analogue Productions 180g mono edition, which improves surface quality and quiet but is sourced from tape generations further from Van Gelder's original lacquer.

albums.albumStory: Standard Coltrane assembles material Coltrane recorded for Prestige on July 11, 1958, during the extraordinarily prolific stretch when he was still a member of the Miles Davis Sextet while also fulfilling his own contract for Bob Weinstock's label. Paired here with trumpeter Wilbur Harden and the Red Garland-Paul Chambers-Jimmy Cobb rhythm section borrowed from the Davis band, Coltrane turns his attention to four well-worn popular standards and show tunes rather than originals, using the familiar changes as a canvas for the harmonic density and long, searching lines that critics of the day were already calling 'sheets of sound.' The album captures Coltrane mid-transformation: still rooted in the hard-bop vocabulary he shared with Davis and Garland, but visibly reaching past it toward the more exploratory language he would soon develop on his own Atlantic and Impulse! dates. Ballads like 'Don't Take Your Love From Me' and the lesser-known 'Invitation' show a surprisingly tender, vocal quality to his tone alongside the harmonic reharmonization for which he was becoming known. Coming from a period when Prestige was releasing Coltrane material steadily to keep pace with his growing reputation, the record is historically valuable less as a planned artistic statement than as a document of a major stylist's rapid evolution, capturing him at a moment critics were already debating in terms as polarized as 'anti-jazz' and visionary. It remains a minor but respected entry in the Coltrane discography, valued by collectors and historians for the quality of the playing and for Harden's comparatively rare presence on record with him.

Collectors on the forums generally rate the original Prestige mono Van Gelder pressings of this era as the most natural-sounding version of Coltrane's Prestige work, ahead of the contemporaneous 'true stereo' PRST pressings which can sound thinner, and well ahead of the OJC reissue cuts of the 1980s-90s which use later-generation masters. The 2003 Analogue Productions 45 RPM two-LP reissue, mastered by Kevin Gray/Doug Sax from the analog tapes and pressed at RTI, is the modern audiophile benchmark for surface noise and top-end extraction but trades some of the original mono's tonal density for stereo separation and is a different listening experience rather than a strict upgrade. This deep-groove Prestige mono first pressing sits at or near the top of the album's practical fidelity hierarchy for collectors who prize the original mono Van Gelder sound.

albums.title: The Other Village Vanguard Tapes
albums.musicians: John Coltrane (soprano and tenor saxophone, all tracks), Eric Dolphy (alto saxophone, bass clarinet on A-1, A-2, B-1, C-1, D-1), McCoy Tyner (piano on A-2, B-1, C-1, D-1), Jimmy Garrison (bass on B-1, C-1), Reggie Workman (bass on A-1, A-2, C-1, C-2, D-1), Elvin Jones (drums, all tracks), Garvin Bushell (oboe, contrabassoon on C-1, D-1), Ahmed Abdul-Malik (oud on C-1)

albums.albumStory: These are unreleased sides from the same November 1961 Village Vanguard engagement that produced Impulse!'s original Live at the Village Vanguard LP, capturing Coltrane's classic quartet expanded by Eric Dolphy on alto and bass clarinet, plus guest bassist Ahmed Abdul-Malik on oud and Garvin Bushell on oboe and contrabassoon on the more exploratory tracks. The residency found Coltrane pushing hardest into modal and near-free territory, stretching "Chasin' the Trane," "Spiritual," and "India" into side-length improvisations built on drones and modal vamps rather than conventional chord changes. Dolphy's astringent, angular alto and bass-clarinet lines drew some of the era's most hostile critical response - Down Beat's infamous "anti-jazz" branding stems largely from this run - even as the music now stands as a pivotal bridge between Coltrane's hard-bop roots and the fully open improvisation of his mid-1960s work. "Untitled Original" and the alternate "Greensleeves" and "Spiritual" takes offer additional glimpses of the group testing different lengths and shapes on the same tunes across the week. Compiled and issued by ABC/Impulse in 1977 from tape vaults, the set filled a major gap in the Coltrane discography and let listeners hear how far this quintet pushed the Vanguard material beyond what fit on the 1962 single LP. It remains essential listening for tracing Coltrane and Dolphy's brief, incendiary collaboration and the roots of Coltrane's later modal and free explorations.

The label is flat-edged, without a deep groove, consistent with the late-1970s ABC Impulse! rainbow era (roughly 1974-1979), before the MCA/Impulse! buyout switched to the black MCA-era labels seen on the 1980 AS-9325/2-4137 and MCA2-4137 reissues. The spine carries the catalogue number AS-9325 while the labels carry AS-9325/2, placing this copy within the 1977 US pressing of this catalogue number. Several runout-stamp variants exist under this catalogue number; this copy's four runouts do not fully match any one of them stamp-for-stamp, each missing a circled stamper digit found on the others. All variants share this same rainbow-target flat label, catalogue number and 1977 US pressing, so this is read as an unlisted stamper sub-run within the same first US edition rather than a later or different pressing; the exact stamper generation is not identified.

Collectors on the forums rate the ABC Impulse rainbow-label era as competent but unglamorous mastering compared to the Van Gelder-cut original Impulse! Later reissues - the 1980 MCA2-4137 gatefold and the 1987 Japanese (55XD-590/1) and European (254 639-2) remastered CDs - offer cleaner, quieter surfaces but are digitally sourced and generally regarded as tonally flatter than this vinyl cut. albums.albumStory: Recorded across three sessions at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio in late 1961 and 1962, Ballads found John Coltrane's classic quartet - McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones - stepping back from the harmonic density of his contemporaneous live work to interpret eight standards with unusual tenderness and restraint. The project reportedly grew out of producer Bob Thiele's and Coltrane's own wish to answer critics who had branded his sound harsh or "anti-jazz," and to show the lyrical side of a saxophonist then better known for extended, searching improvisation. Coltrane plays close to the melody throughout, his tone warm and unhurried, while Tyner's comping and Jones's brushwork give the record a chamber-like intimacy rare in the quartet's catalog. Arriving between the more exploratory Coltrane and Duke Ellington and John Coltrane and Johnny Hartman sessions, Ballads sits at a pivotal, transitional point in Coltrane's early-1960s Impulse! period, bridging his hard-bop roots and the modal and spiritual directions to come. It has long been regarded by critics and fans alike as one of the most accessible and emotionally direct entries in his discography, frequently recommended as a starting point for listeners new to Coltrane, and it remains a benchmark recording in the jazz ballad tradition.

albums.title: Coltrane
albums.musicians: John Coltrane (tenor sax), McCoy Tyner (piano), Jimmy Garrison (bass), Elvin Jones (drums), Roy Haynes (drums, "Out of This World")
sides:
1. Out Of This World (H. Arlen-J. Mercer) (14:02)
2. Soul Eyes (Mal Waldron) (5:22)

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio across sessions in April and June 1962, Coltrane arrived as the saxophonist's regular working quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones was solidifying into one of jazz's defining bands, with Roy Haynes sitting in on drums for the epic reworking of "Out of This World." The album balances Coltrane originals like the modal showcase "Miles' Mode" and the African-inflected "Tunji" against standards and show tunes - "Soul Eyes," "The Inch Worm" and the Harold Arlen/Johnny Mercer title that opens the record - stretched into extended, sheets-of-sound explorations. It sits at a pivotal point in Coltrane's Impulse! years, bridging the harmonic density of his Atlantic period with the freer, more modal and spiritually searching music that would culminate in A Love Supreme two years later. The record is widely regarded by critics and historians as an important transitional statement, showing Coltrane's quartet mastering long-form modal improvisation while still rooted in the American songbook. It remains a touchstone of his catalog and a favorite among listeners tracing the evolution of his sound through the early-to-mid 1960s.
albums.lpNotes: Mono repress (c.1965-66) - ABC-Paramount Impulse! label with -A/-B suffix; matrix A-21-A/-B LW, Van Gelder stamped.

Impulse mono labels carry this ABC-Paramount wording from 1963 through 1966/67, before the label was reset to read "ABC RECORDS INC, New York, N.Y. 10019" for 1967-68. This copy's ABC-Paramount wording together with the -A/-B side suffix places it as a mid-1960s (c.1965-66) mono repress, later than the original 1962 Am-Par first pressing, which prints "Am-Par Record Corp." with no -A/-B suffix, and earlier than the 1967 ABC Records relabelling. Deep groove is not evident on this pressing.
albums.fidelity: Van Gelder's original tape and lacquer work underlies this pressing, and the LW-stamped, Van Gelder-etched runout matches the marks found on the earliest Am-Par lacquers, indicating no remastering occurred for this later label run. Collectors on the forums generally rate any Van Gelder-stamped mono Impulse pressing of this title well above the later ABC/MCA reissues and well above the 1997 Ron McMaster remaster. Within the album's own fidelity hierarchy this ABC-Paramount-label repress sits just below a true first-pressing Am-Par copy (same stampers, later label print only) and above the 1967 ABC Records repress, the 1970s ABC Impulse reissues, and the digitally sourced later reissues; it also predates and generally outranks the mono-to-stereo era's rechanneled pressings.

The runout (A21-A/A21-B LW, Van Gelder stamped) carries the same etched "LW" and stamped Van Gelder marks as the original lacquers, indicating the same stampers/mother continued to be used for this later label run.

albums.title: Evenings at the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy
albums.countryOfOrigin: US release, manufactured in Mexico (Vantiva, Guadalajara - stated on companies list and shrink-wrap text)
albums.producer: Ken Druker (Producer), Ravi Coltrane (Executive Producer), Richard Alderson (Recording Engineer), Kevin Reeves (Mastering, East Iris Studios)
albums.musicians: John Coltrane (tenor saxophone, soprano saxophone), Eric Dolphy (alto saxophone, bass clarinet), McCoy Tyner (piano), Reggie Workman (bass), Art Davis (bass), Elvin Jones (drums)
sides: 1. My Favorite Things (15:45)

1. When Lights Are Low (15:10)
2. Impressions (10:00)
1. Greensleeves (16:15)
1. Africa (22:41)
albums.albumStory: In August 1961 John Coltrane brought his working quartet, newly expanded with Eric Dolphy and a rotating pair of bassists (Reggie Workman and Art Davis), into the Village Gate in Greenwich Village for a short club engagement that was captured on tape by the venue rather than for commercial release. Coltrane was at a pivotal juncture, having just left Atlantic for Impulse! and begun stretching the modal vocabulary of "My Favorite Things" and "Impressions" into longer, more exploratory group improvisations, with Dolphy's astringent alto and bass clarinet pushing the music further outside straight-ahead harmony. The material captured here overlaps with the more celebrated Village Vanguard sessions from the same period and documents the same restless creative partnership, including extended readings of "Greensleeves" and the African-derived vamp "Africa" that anticipate Coltrane's turn toward modal and world-music-inflected large-ensemble writing on Africa/Brass and Impressions. Dolphy's tenure with Coltrane, controversial with critics at the time who found his playing "anti-jazz," is now regarded as one of the most fruitful and adventurous pairings in early-1960s jazz. The recordings sat unheard for decades in the New York Public Library's Music & Recorded Sound Division before being restored and assembled into a single narrative program, giving listeners a fuller picture of this quintet's nightly working method than the studio albums of the period could. As a document it deepens the record of Coltrane's transition from the classic quartet sound toward the harmonically freer, modally expansive music of his mid-1960s work, and it stands as important late testimony to Dolphy's brief but influential association with him before Dolphy's death in 1964.
albums.lpNotes: 2023 Impulse!/UMe reissue (mono, gatefold, B0037785-01) - modern grey/orange i! label, flat (no deep groove), Vantiva Mexico pressing; not a vintage pressing of any kind.
albums.labelNotes: The label is the current Impulse! "i!" grey-and-orange design with a black-and-white bar carrying repeated i! logos around the rim and "impulse!" text alternating orientation - this is the 2020s reissue-era Impulse! design used across the UMe/Verve Label Group catalog, not the vintage orange-and-black "waterfall" AS/A-9xxx label of the 1960s-70s pressings. No deep groove ring, ear logo, or vintage rim text is present on any side, consistent with a flat modern label stock - flat label. This design and the B0037785-01 catalogue prefix place the copy squarely within the 2023 Impulse!/UMe reissue program, not any vintage Village Gate-era pressing (the recordings themselves are from 1961 but were first compiled and issued complete only in this 2023 release).
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Kevin Reeves at East Iris Studios from tapes restored via the New York Public Library's Music & Recorded Sound Division, this is a modern digital-sourced restoration rather than an analog cut from an original 1961 master tape chain, since the material was never mixed or mastered at the time. Pressing is by Vantiva (formerly Technicolor/MPO) at its Guadalajara, Mexico plant, generally regarded by collectors as a competent modern pressing though not in the audiophile tier of Pallas or Optimal. As there is no vintage pressing of this specific unreleased material to compare against, this gatefold mono edition is effectively the primary/reference pressing for the album, sitting alongside the contemporaneous non-gatefold orange-vinyl edition and Japanese SHM-SACD/vinyl variants as the only fidelity options currently in circulation.
albums.generalNotes: This is the 2023 Impulse!/UMe gatefold mono reissue of previously unreleased 1961 Village Gate recordings. The modern i! label design (no deep groove, no vintage rim text) and the B0037785-01 matrix prefix with stamped Vantiva Guadalajara pressing codes confirm a current-era pressing rather than any period issue. Side C and D runouts carry matrix numbers matching the catalogue's official listing; Sides A and B show different trailing stamped digits, described in the release's own notes as separately stamped pressing-run identifiers (distinct from the etched catalogue/matrix numbers), so this remains the same catalogue variant, just a different pressing run/date stamp.

albums.title: Tenor Conclave
albums.musicians: John Coltrane (tenor sax), Zoot Sims (tenor sax), Al Cohn (tenor sax), Hank Mobley (tenor sax), Red Garland (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Art Taylor (drums)
sides:
1. Tenor Conclave
2. Just You, Just Me

1. Bob's Boys
2. How Deep Is the Ocean
albums.albumStory: Recorded September 7, 1956 at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack studio, Tenor Conclave is one of the classic Prestige 'battle of the tenors' summit sessions that producer Bob Weinstock built his catalogue on, pitting four contrasting saxophone voices - John Coltrane, Hank Mobley, Zoot Sims and Al Cohn - over the same two standards and two originals so listeners could compare styles directly. At the time Coltrane was still a sideman in the Miles Davis Quintet and not yet the leader he would soon become, making this one of several mid-1950s Prestige dates that captured him developing his harmonically dense 'sheets of sound' language alongside more mainstream swing-rooted players like Sims and Cohn. Mobley, fresh off his own hard-bop dates and contributing the two originals 'Tenor Conclave' and 'Bob's Boys', anchors the session's compositional identity, while Red Garland, Paul Chambers and Art Taylor - Coltrane's Miles Davis Quintet rhythm-section colleagues - provide a tight, blues-inflected pulse throughout. The record is prized by hard-bop collectors as a document of the era's informal jam-session ethos, where individuality of phrasing mattered more than novelty of material, and it remains a touchstone for studying how differently schooled tenor players (bebop-inflected Coltrane and Mobley versus swing-lineage Sims and Cohn) could co-exist within a single blowing date. It has held a steady place in Coltrane discography surveys and hard-bop reissue programs as an accessible, high-quality example of the mid-1950s tenor-battle format.
albums.lpNotes: 1962 mono reissue (Bergenfield yellow/black fireworks label, PRLP 7249) - deep groove both sides, RVG stamp, Abbey (AB) pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The label on this copy is the yellow-and-black 'fireworks' Prestige design with the swirl-and-splatter pattern in the rim, 'PRESTIGE' in a curved black-outlined box at top, and the address 'PRESTIGE RECORDS, INC., 203 SOUTH WASHINGTON AVE., BERGENFIELD, N.J.' printed above the title - the Bergenfield fireworks mono label used from 1958 to 1964, replacing the earlier 446 W. 50th St., NYC address used on the 1957 first pressing of this recording (then catalogued PRLP 7074). Deep groove is present on both sides. The catalogue number on the label, PRLP 7249, matches Prestige's 1962 renumbering/reissue of this 1956 session in mono, not the original 1957 LP 7074 issue; the runout etchings (PRLP-7249-A/B, RVG stamp, 'AB' Abbey Manufacturing plant code) are consistent with the Abbey-pressed Bergenfield-era Prestige mono run. This is a mono Bergenfield-label pressing of the 1962 PRLP 7249 reissue, one step below the 1957 PRLP 7074 first pressing in the hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Original recording and lacquer cut by Rudy Van Gelder at his Hackensack studio; this 1962 Bergenfield mono pressing uses the same Van Gelder-cut lacquer lineage as the 1957 original but is a later stamper generation, pressed by Abbey Record Manufacturing. Collectors on the forums generally regard early Van Gelder-stamped Prestige mono pressings (both 7074 and its 7249 renumbered mono reissue) as sonically close and clearly preferable to the 1962 'Remastered for Stereo' PRST-7249 rechannel, which is not a true stereo recording. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy this pressing ranks below the 1957 PRLP 7074 true first pressing but above the stereo reissue, later Fantasy/OJC pressings, and CD reissues; the 2013/2022 Analogue Productions APRJ 7074 mono LP is the modern audiophile benchmark for the title.
albums.generalNotes: This copy is the 1962 Prestige mono reissue under the renumbered catalogue PRLP 7249, not the original 1957 PRLP 7074 issue. The Bergenfield, N.J. address on the yellow/black fireworks label dates production to the 1958-64 window, consistent with the 1962 reissue date. Deep groove on both sides and RVG runout stamps with Abbey Manufacturing's 'AB' plant code mark this as an Abbey-pressed Bergenfield-era mono pressing rather than the earliest 446 W. 50th St. NYC first pressing.

albums.albumStory: Don't Sleep In The Subway was recorded across three August 1967 sessions in New York for Verve, pairing the Ellington orchestra's peerless alto voice with a large studio big band arranged and conducted by pianist Jimmy Jones. Producer Esmond Edwards built the set around a mix of a then-current pop hit (the Tony Hatch/Jackie Trent title tune, a Petula Clark smash) and standards alongside several Hodges originals, a commercial strategy typical of Verve's late-1960s jazz-with-strings-and-brass releases aimed at a broader listening audience. Hodges, already one of the most celebrated alto stylists in jazz through his decades with Duke Ellington and his own small-group Verve dates of the 1950s-60s, brings his instantly identifiable, vocal-like tone and gliding legato phrasing to material well outside the hard-bop mainstream. The supporting cast - Snooky Young, Frank Wess, Jimmy Hamilton, Hank Jones, Milt Hinton and Grady Tate among them - reflects the top-tier New York studio talent Verve could call on for these sessions. Critical reception was mixed-to-positive: Allmusic's retrospective view judged the orchestrations uneven while singling out Hodges himself as consistently sharp, a fair summary of how the album is remembered - a minor, late-period showcase valued chiefly for Hodges's own playing rather than for the material or arrangements.

This grey Big-V design with MGM ownership text is Verve's standard 1963-67 house style under MGM Records' stewardship, placing this pressing squarely in the album's first US stereo release window (1967). A US mono edition (V-8726) and a promo yellow-label DJ pressing were issued from the same session alongside this stereo commercial copy; no different label artwork is claimed for any of them, as this stereo grey label is the only design associated with this copy.
albums.fidelity: This is an analog-era Verve/MGM stereo cut from the 1967 National Recording Studios sessions, mastered and pressed under MGM Records' in-house operation rather than by an audiophile specialist; there is no known audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Speakers Corner, etc.) of this title to rank it against. Collector commentary on this relatively minor, late-1960s big-band Hodges date is sparse on the forums, with little dedicated discussion of mastering quality; general consensus on late-60s MGM/Verve pressings is that they are solidly but not exceptionally engineered compared to the label's earlier Norman Granz-era jazz dates. Within the album's own pressing history, this original US stereo edition is the primary sonic reference point, ahead of later international pressings (UK, Canada, Germany, Spain) which derive from the same or dubbed masters with variable plant quality.

albums.albumStory: Recorded for Norman Granz's Norgran label in the early 1950s, this album finds Johnny Hodges - the alto saxophonist Duke Ellington called "Rabbit" and whose lush, vibrato-laden tone was one of the defining voices of the Ellington orchestra for over two decades - stepping out from the big band to revisit Ellington and Ellington-associated repertoire in small-group settings. Hodges had left Ellington's employ in 1951 to lead his own combo, and this session gathers several fellow Ellingtonians (Lawrence Brown, Emmett Berry) alongside guest tenor stars Ben Webster, Flip Phillips and Al Sears to reinterpret staples like "Sophisticated Lady," "Solitude," "Come Sunday" and "I Got It Bad and That Ain't Good." The program blends Ellington-Strayhorn ballads with the loping swing Hodges made his trademark, and "Come Sunday" in particular carries over some of the prayerful character of its origin in Ellington's "Black, Brown and Beige" suite. As one of Hodges's most celebrated Norgran dates, the album is prized by collectors and historians as a showcase both for his own singular alto voice and for the guest tenor men, with Flip Phillips's ballad turn on "I Got It Bad" often singled out as a departure from his usual up-tempo image. It stands among the definitive small-group Ellington-repertoire albums of the 1950s and a key document of Hodges's post-Ellington freelance period, cementing his reputation as jazz's foremost interpreter of the alto sax ballad style.
albums.lpNotes: Original first pressing (mono, 1954) - Norgran yellow trumpeter deep-groove label, MGN-1004-A/B matrix.
albums.labelNotes: The label on both sides is the yellow Norgran "trumpeter" design with black print - a stylised trumpet player logo left of the spindle, the album title and artist name to the right, catalogue number MGN-1004-A/B, and "Jazz At The Philharmonic, Inc. - Made In U.S.A." around the rim - with a visible deep groove ring. Norgran was Norman Granz's label from 1953-57 before its catalogue was folded into Verve; this yellow-label deep-groove pressing with the trumpeter graphic is the label design used for Norgran's original 1954 issues, before the same title was reissued under a new Norgran number (MG N-1092) and later moved to Verve as "In A Mellow Tone" (MGV-8180). The deep groove and this label design place the copy squarely in the first Norgran pressing run rather than any of the later Norgran or Verve reissues.
albums.fidelity: This is an early-1950s Norman Granz small-group jazz production, mastered for the original Norgran lacquers rather than any later remaster; specific mastering engineer credits are not documented for this release. Original deep-groove Norgran pressings are generally rated favorably for warmth and presence relative to the later Verve reissue, though surface noise and equipment of the era limit ultimate fidelity compared to modern remasters. No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Classic Records, etc.) of this title is known to exist, so this original 1954 Norgran pressing represents the top of this title's practical fidelity hierarchy, ahead of the 1957 Verve MGV-8180 reissue and any later stereo-era or South African pressings.

albums.albumStory: This LP pairs two documents of the postwar country-blues tradition, undocumented in most standard references, united by their connection - real or claimed - to Robert Johnson. Johnny Shines, who actually travelled and played with Johnson across the Depression-era South, went on to build his own international career from the 1960s onward, becoming one of the most compelling links between prewar Delta style and the electric blues that followed; his side here was drawn from a 1978 festival performance in the Netherlands, delivered solo and largely in his own idiom rather than as pure Johnson repertoire. Blind Will Dukes is an undocumented, obscure figure outside this release, a Detroit guitarist who claimed to have been shown Johnson's style firsthand and whose entire discography effectively begins and ends with the informal 1975 field session heard on side two, built heavily around Johnson standards alongside a handful of originals. The pairing captures both the mainstream survival of Delta blues through a well-documented elder statesman and the raw, largely undocumented margins of the tradition through a performer almost no one else recorded. For collectors of vernacular blues the album's importance rests less on studio polish than on rarity and testimony: it is one of the only recorded windows onto Dukes at all, framed alongside Shines at a mature, confident stage of his live career. Critically the album has been valued chiefly as a folklore document rather than a front-rank artistic statement, prized by specialists in the genre for what it preserves rather than for chart or crossover impact.
albums.lpNotes: 1984 UK first pressing on JSP Records - pink/white split label, 112 Sunny Gardens Road address, catalogue JSP 1079.
albums.labelNotes: The label is a flat (non-deep-groove) pink-and-white split design with a boxed JSP Records logo at centre-right, the JSP 1079 catalogue number and artist/title credit on the white half, and the 112 Sunny Gardens Road, London NW4 address printed on the pink half - the standard house style JSP used for its early-to-mid 1980s blues reissue and compilation series. This address and logo place the pressing squarely in JSP's first decade of operation (the label was founded in 1978), and the design is the only one documented for this catalogue number, so it also represents the sole first pressing of the title rather than a later re-set label sharing the same address.
albums.fidelity: Side one was cut from a 1978 festival tape of Johnny Shines performing solo, and side two from a 1975 informal field session with Blind Will Dukes, so both sources are modest, semi-professional recordings rather than studio masters. The cutting and pressing were handled through a UK jobbing facility, consistent with JSP's small-label reissue and compilation output of the period, and playback quality is generally regarded by specialist collectors as functional rather than audiophile. Recorded over two January 1955 sessions in New York, the album pairs the two trombonists' contrasting tones - Johnson's crisp, bop-schooled precision against Winding's warmer, more legato attack - across a set of standards and originals contributed by both leaders. The rhythm section is unusually deep for a working group, drawing on bassists Milt Hinton and Wendell Marshall alongside pianist Dick Katz and drummer Al Harewood, giving the frontline a supple, swinging cushion. albums.albumStory: The Köln Concert captures a solo piano performance Keith Jarrett gave at the Cologne Opera House on January 24, 1975, an evening that nearly did not happen: he arrived exhausted after a long drive, and the venue's staff provided the wrong instrument, a small, out-of-tune rehearsal Bösendorfer with sticking keys. Rather than cancel, Jarrett improvised the entire concert around the instrument's limitations, leaning into its bass register and repetitive vamping figures to compensate for its thin upper end. Producer Manfred Eicher, who convinced Jarrett to go on despite his reservations, recorded the performance for ECM, and it was released later that year as a completely improvised, wholly spontaneous double album with no pre-composed material. The record became the best-selling solo piano album and the best-selling ECM release in history, introducing a mass audience to long-form free improvisation and cementing Jarrett's reputation as the preeminent solo improviser of his generation. Critically it is regarded as a landmark of the ECM aesthetic and of 1970s jazz more broadly, prized for its lyrical, folk- and gospel-inflected melodic invention sustained over sidelong stretches. Its legacy endures both as a commercial phenomenon and as a touchstone for improvised solo performance across jazz and beyond.

Later audiophile reissues (e.g. 180g Made in Germany pressings) exist and are sometimes preferred for surface noise, but collectors still rank the original-era German pressings, including this later-1970s variant, above generic later reissues and well above the CD for warmth and tape-like presence. Within the ECM pressing family this copy sits in the middle of the fidelity hierarchy: below the true 1975 first pressing, but above later reissues and the digital editions.

albums.albumStory: Recorded live at the Cologne Opera House on 24 January 1975, The Köln Concert captured Keith Jarrett's completely improvised solo piano performance, played on an undersized, out-of-tune rehearsal instrument substituted at the last minute after the concert grand promised by the venue was unavailable. Jarrett, exhausted and reportedly ready to cancel, was persuaded by an eighteen-year-old promoter to go on anyway, and the resulting concert became a landmark of spontaneous composition, blending gospel, folk, minimalist vamps and classical figuration into long continuous arcs. It arrived at a pivotal moment in Jarrett's career, following his American and European quartet work, and established him as the pre-eminent solo improviser in jazz. Produced by Manfred Eicher, it became ECM's best-selling release and remains the best-selling solo piano album and one of the best-selling jazz albums in history. Critics praised its lyrical, meditative sweep, and it is widely credited with bringing improvised piano music to a mainstream listening audience well beyond the jazz world. Its influence persists in the solo-piano concert tradition and in the broader crossover appeal of instrumental music.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in 1966 for Verve under producer Creed Taylor, A Generation Ago Today finds guitarist Kenny Burrell paying tribute to the swing era, reworking tunes closely associated with Benny Goodman and the Charlie Christian small-group sessions of the late 1930s. Burrell, one of the definitive post-bop jazz guitarists of the era known for his work with Blue Note and his own sideman dates for Miles Davis and John Coltrane, here reaches back to the music that shaped his own playing, framing Christian's pioneering electric-guitar vocabulary within a modern small-group setting. The presence of alto saxophonist Phil Woods lends a bop-inflected voice to swing-era staples like 'Stompin' at the Savoy' and 'Rose Room,' while the closing quartet track 'Wholly Cats' strips the band down for a leaner, more intimate look at the repertoire. The album sits in the middle of Burrell's prolific Verve period, when he moved fluidly between mainstream jazz dates and more commercial crossover sessions, and it stands as one of his more overtly historical, backward-glancing statements. Contemporary and later critical assessment has generally treated it as a solid, respectful genre exercise rather than a landmark, valued chiefly for Burrell's fluent, blues-rooted guitar lines and the quality of his supporting cast. It remains a minor but appealing entry in the guitarist's substantial 1960s discography, of most interest to collectors tracing his stylistic range across the decade.

albums.albumStory: Recorded for Blue Note at Manhattan Towers on May 14, 1958, Blue Lights was one of two LPs drawn from a single marathon blowing session led by guitarist Kenny Burrell, then just twenty-seven but already established as one of the era's most fluent and lyrical hard-bop guitarists. Producer Alfred Lion assembled an all-star sextet-plus-rhythm lineup - trumpeter Louis Smith, tenor men Junior Cook and Tina Brooks, pianists Duke Jordan and Bobby Timmons, bassist Sam Jones and drummer Art Blakey - and let the group stretch out on standards and blues heads in the loose, informal spirit that defined many of Blue Note's late-1950s sessions. Burrell's warm, economical playing anchors the date, most memorably on the relaxed, blues-drenched opener "Yes Baby" and the atmospheric reading of "Autumn in New York." The session captures Tina Brooks and Junior Cook, both still emerging tenor voices, alongside a characteristically driving Art Blakey and the contrasting piano styles of Jordan and Timmons. Blue Lights helped cement Burrell's standing as a leader beyond his prolific work as a Blue Note session guitarist, and it remains a favorite among hard-bop collectors for its music and for its striking cover, illustrated in its earliest form by a young, pre-fame Andy Warhol working for Blue Note's art department under Reid Miles.

albums.albumStory: Both Feet On The Ground was cut in February 1973 at Village Recorders in Los Angeles during Kenny Burrell's Fantasy Records period, after he had left the Verve/CTI orbit and settled on the West Coast label for a run of early-1970s sessions that leaned into contemporary soul-jazz textures. Benny Golson supplied most of the arrangements, dressing Burrell's cool, blues-rooted guitar in flute, piccolo and electric-piano colors that reflect the era's crossover instincts without abandoning a jazz core. The program mixes originals like the title track and 'Listen to the Dawn' with covers of Billie Holiday's 'Good Morning, Heartache' and the bossa-tinged 'Nana' and 'All Mine (Minha)', and brings in Brazilian percussionist Moacir Santos as a guest colorist. By this point Burrell was a two-decades-plus veteran whose guitar sound had already defined a generation of hard-bop and soul-jazz sessions for Blue Note and Prestige, and this album shows him adapting that voice to the fusion-leaning jazz marketplace of the early '70s rather than chasing rock guitar trends outright. It was received as a solid, if not landmark, entry in his catalog - valued more by collectors of his Fantasy-era work and by soul-jazz/rare-groove diggers than by mainstream jazz critics - and it remains a minor but distinctive chapter bridging his hard-bop legacy and the smoother fusion direction jazz guitar took later in the decade.

albums.labelNotes: The label is the tan/gold Fantasy 'FJ' swirl-logo design with a salmon-pink cross-band, used on Fantasy's Berkeley-era jazz catalogue through the mid-1970s; this is the same base design used on the standard stock stereo pressing of F 9427, but here it is over-stamped 'F 9427-DJ' with 'DJ Copy - Not For Sale' printed beneath the catalogue number, marking it as a radio/promotional service copy rather than the commercial stock pressing. Fantasy issued this design continuously from the label's 1971-72 Berkeley move (after the earlier 'stereo' rainbow-swirl design) through the mid-1970s, so the artwork alone does not separate promo from stock pressings made in the same 1973 window - only the printed DJ text and the runout suffixes do. This copy's DJ overprint places it in the small promotional-pressing run issued alongside the regular 1973 stereo release, made from the same 1973 lacquers rather than a later re-pressing.
albums.fidelity: Recorded by Baker Bigsby at Village Recorders and remixed by Jim Stern at Fantasy Studios, Berkeley, this is a well-produced but not audiophile-grade early-70s jazz-funk date; Fantasy's Berkeley/RCA-adjacent pressing plants of the period are generally solid but unremarkable sonically. There is no dedicated audiophile reissue (no Mobile Fidelity, Analogue Productions, Speakers Corner, or Blue Note-style Tone Poet edition) of this title, and it receives little discussion among collectors on the forums beyond passing mentions in Burrell discography threads. As an original-era US pressing (DJ promo, same 1973 lacquers/mastering as the stock release aside from an earlier side-A stamper), this copy sits at the top of the title's practical fidelity hierarchy alongside the standard 1973 US stereo pressing, well above the mid-70s reissue and the Japanese LFP-88128 pressing.
albums.generalNotes: This is a 1973 Fantasy F 9427 DJ/promotional pressing, not the ordinary stock copy: the label is over-stamped 'F 9427-DJ' with 'DJ Copy - Not For Sale' beneath the catalogue number. The standard stock stereo pressing carries a side-A runout of F-9427-ARE1, while this copy's side-A runout reads F9427-A-1 - an earlier-suffix lacquer that points to Fantasy's separate US promo variant. Side B (F9427-B-RE1) matches the RE1 remix stamper on both the promo and standard release, so the same 1973 remix lacquer was used for side B across variants while side A on this copy carries an earlier cut.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in 1956 across several dates - two studio sessions at Van Gelder's Hackensack studio and a live date at Café Bohemia - this was guitarist Kenny Burrell's second Blue Note leader album, first issued as BLP 1523 'Introducing Kenny Burrell' and reissued the following year under the self-titled BLP 1543 with the now-famous Andy Warhol cover illustration, one of only three Blue Note jackets Warhol contributed. Burrell, a Detroit-trained bebopper who would soon become one of the defining guitar voices of soul-jazz, moves fluidly here between small combos featuring Kenny Dorham, J.R. Monterose, Frank Foster, Tommy Flanagan and Oscar Pettiford, and a Latin-tinged opener with Candido on congas. The material mixes standards (Get Happy, But Not For Me, How About You) with originals and lesser-known vehicles (Cheeta, Phinupi), giving a picture of a versatile young guitarist already assured in multiple settings. Critically the record is viewed as transitional and somewhat episodic - drawn from disparate sessions rather than a single unified date - but it remains valued for strong individual performances, particularly Foster's tenor work and the interplay on the Café Bohemia track, and for its place at the start of Burrell's decades-long, influential run as a leader and first-call sideman.
albums.lpNotes: 2022 Blue Note Tone Poet Series mono reissue (BLP 1543) - all-analog, Kevin Gray/Cohearent Audio mastering, produced by Joe Harley, pressed at RTI; labels carry a documented factory misprint of the earlier catalogue number BLP 1523.
albums.labelNotes: The label on this copy is a modern replica of the original Lexington Avenue design: white field, blue rim reading BLUE (left) / NOTE (bottom), the '33 1/3 MICROGROOVE LONG PLAYING' arc, and hand-lettered script reading 'BLUE NOTE RECORDS 767 LEXINGTON AVE NYC' - the same wording used on Blue Note's original 1956-59 New York address labels. However fine print along the rim ('UMG Recordings, Inc., 1750 N. Vine Street, Hollywood, CA 90028', barcode B0033486-01A) and the small credit 'A Blue Note Records release; Originally released in 1957' identify it unmistakably as a 2022 manufacture, not a vintage pressing. Notably the label prints catalogue number 'BLP 1523' (the number of the earlier, differently-titled 'Introducing Kenny Burrell'), a documented factory error carried over from source material - the jacket correctly reads BLP 1543. This retro-address label design is a modern homage; it does not indicate an original Lexington-era manufacture, which would show period-correct paper stock, a flat or deep-groove pressing, and RVG/ear stamps in the deadwax rather than the etched code seen here.
albums.fidelity: This Tone Poet edition was mastered all-analog from the original tapes by Kevin Gray at Cohearent Audio and pressed on 180g vinyl at RTI, a combination collectors on the forums consistently rate as quiet, dynamic and among the best-sounding modern jazz vinyl available. It sits well above the many thin 1970s-90s Blue Note/Liberty/Capitol reissues and above standard modern Blue Note '75th/80th Anniversary' pressings, and is regarded as the practical sonic equal of a clean original for most listeners, since very few playable original Lexington-label copies survive in top condition. It ranks below only a truly premium original NY/Lexington first pressing with Van Gelder stamp and Plastylite ear in exceptional condition, and stands alongside other Tone Poet and Music Matters titles as the modern gold standard for this catalogue.
albums.generalNotes: This is the 2022 Blue Note Tone Poet Series mono reissue of BLP 1543 'Kenny Burrell,' not a vintage pressing. Etched runouts B0033486-01-A2/B2 with KCCCA codes, all-analog Kevin Gray mastering credited on the jacket, and Joe Harley's production credit (the Tone Poet series producer) confirm the modern edition; RTI pressed the vinyl. The labels reproduce the vintage Lexington Ave address text but misprint the catalogue number as BLP 1523 (the earlier 'Introducing Kenny Burrell' issue) - a known, documented error for this specific reissue, with the jacket correctly showing BLP 1543.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in a single session at Van Gelder Studio on January 8, 1963, Midnight Blue found guitarist Kenny Burrell paring his working group down to a spare, blues-drenched quintet, deliberately omitting piano so his own chording could carry the harmony. Burrell had already built a reputation as one of the most versatile guitarists in jazz, equally comfortable in bebop, soul-jazz and blues settings, and this date leaned hard into the blues and Latin-tinged grooves that were then reshaping Blue Note's commercial sound. Tenor saxophonist Stanley Turrentine's warm, vocalized tone became the record's second voice, while Ray Barretto's conga added a subtle Afro-Cuban lift that distinguished tracks like Chittlins Con Carne and Wavy Gravy from straight 12-bar blues. The album's unhurried, late-night mood and its emphasis on feel over flash made it an immediate favorite with listeners beyond the jazz-specialist audience, and it remains Burrell's most enduring and best-selling Blue Note session. Critics have long cited it as a high-water mark of early-1960s soul jazz, prized for its economy, groove and the chemistry between Burrell and Turrentine. It cemented Burrell's standing as a leader in his own right after years as an in-demand sideman, and its title track and Chittlins Con Carne have become minor blues-guitar standards. The record's blend of blues authenticity and jazz sophistication continues to be cited as a touchstone of the genre.
albums.lpNotes: 2nd press (mono, c.1966) - Blue Note NY USA label WITHOUT deep groove; Van Gelder stamp + Plastylite ear retained in runout.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show the classic white/blue Blue Note design with a single "BLUE NOTE" wordmark split vertically, "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC." arcing above "NEW YORK, USA" beneath the 33 1/3 MICROGROOVE LONG PLAYING legend - the same New York-address design used on the true 1963 first pressing. This copy does not show deep groove on either side, which rules out the earliest (1963) pressing run and instead places it as a 1966 reissue that kept the same New York labels and the Van Gelder/Plastylite-ear stamps in the dead wax but was pressed after Plastylite's deep-groove stamper rings had been retired (deep groove disappeared industry-wide, and at Blue Note specifically, by the mid-1960s). Because the label wording and address here still read "NEW YORK, USA" with no "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" text, this predates the post-1966 Liberty-era relabeling, placing it as a transitional, non-deep-groove NY pressing - the second rung in the BLP 4123 pressing hierarchy, below the deep-groove original but above the later United Artists/Liberty and 1970s reissues.
albums.fidelity: The Van Gelder-cut lacquers and Plastylite pressing are unchanged from the original configuration, so this non-deep-groove NY pressing sounds essentially identical to the 1963 first press, differing only in the cosmetic loss of the deep-groove ring from the stamper/press setup rather than any change in mastering. Collectors on the forums generally rate all Van Gelder/ear-stamped mono Blue Notes of this era as sonically superior to the later Liberty/United Artists reissues and to the stereo remix, prizing the punch and warmth of the mono cut. Within the fidelity hierarchy for BLP 4123, this pressing ranks just behind the deep-groove 1963 original (which commands a premium mainly for collectability, not audible superiority) and above the post-1966 Liberty-era and 1970s United Artists reissues, and well above the 1985 digital remaster; modern audiophile cuts (Music Matters, Analogue Productions) use fresh transfers and outclass all vintage mono pressings sonically but trade the vintage-mono character for higher fidelity and are generally stereo, not mono.
albums.generalNotes: This is not the true 1963 first pressing: there is no deep groove on either side, ruling out the earliest deep-groove NY USA stamper run. The label design is otherwise identical to the original - full "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC. NEW YORK, USA" address, no Liberty-era text - and the runouts still carry the Van Gelder hand-etch and Plastylite ear, consistent with a c.1966 non-deep-groove reissue on the same New York labels, made before the label wording changed under Liberty ownership. That places this copy as a second-pressing variant: later than the 1963 deep-groove original but earlier than the Liberty/United Artists label changes that followed. Released May 1963; this pressing dates to the mid-1960s reprint run.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in September 1967 at Chess's Ter Mar Studios in Chicago, Ode to 52nd Street paired guitarist Kenny Burrell - on loan from Verve - with the ambitious arranging of Richard Evans, Cadet's in-house writer-producer who was pushing the label's jazz artists toward larger orchestral canvases in the late 1960s. The centerpiece is the four-part 'Suite for Guitar and Orchestra,' a through-composed work that let Burrell stretch beyond the blues-drenched hard-bop persona he'd built at Blue Note and Prestige into something closer to a concerto, alternating his lyrical, unhurried guitar lines against string and horn charts. The second side balances that ambition with more digestible material: two Evans/Burrell originals, a reading of Dizzy Gillespie's 'Con Alma,' Evans's own Latin-tinged 'Soulero,' and a moody instrumental take on 'Wild Is the Wind.' Burrell, already one of the most versatile and in-demand guitarists of his generation - equally at home behind vocalists, in organ trios, or fronting his own dates - used the album to reassert his standing as what one contemporary account of the sessions called 'the whole player,' a musician as comfortable with formal, orchestrated writing as with straight-ahead swing. The record sits alongside his more celebrated Blue Note and Verve work as a lesser-known but distinctive entry in his catalog, valued by collectors for its adventurous suite and Evans's inventive charts. It never achieved the canonical status of Burrell's Midnight Blue or Guitar Forms, but it remains an interesting document of a guitarist testing orchestral jazz at the height of his career, and of Cadet/Chess's late-'60s push into more ambitious jazz production.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (stereo, 1967) - US Cadet LPS-798, Chess Producing Corp. manufacture, spiral-flower Cadet label.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show the classic late-1960s Cadet design: a blue-to-white vertical gradient field, the pink-to-cream 'CADET' wordmark at top, and the circular spiral/pinwheel 'flower' device at right - the standard Cadet house label used for Chess-group jazz product from roughly 1966 through the early 1970s, with 'MFG. BY CHESS PRODUCING CORP., CHICAGO, IL 60616' printed around the rim. This label design and address place it as a first-issue Cadet stereo pressing, with no later Cadet label style used. The rim text and Chess Producing Corp. manufacturing credit place this squarely in the original 1967 pressing run before Cadet's catalog was reissued under Chess/GRP/Chessmates branding in later decades.
albums.fidelity: This is a Chess/Cadet in-house Chicago production (Ter Mar Studios, engineer Doug Brand), not a Van Gelder or RVG-style audiophile cut, and there is no known audiophile reissue (Tone Poet/Music Matters/Speakers Corner) of this specific title. Collectors on the forums generally rate the Chess/Cadet Chicago pressings of this era as solid but unspectacular, full-bodied but occasionally a touch bright on orchestral material. Within this title's own reissue history (Spain 1983, Japan 1997/2021 remasters, 1998 GRP CD/LP reissue), the 1967 US Cadet stereo original is considered the most authentic-sounding vinyl source, ahead of the later reprocessed reissues and well ahead of the digital-sourced GRP CD reissue.
albums.generalNotes: 1967 Cadet LPS-798 stereo, the original US first-pressing configuration of this master. Label design, Chess Producing Corp. manufacturing credit, and matrix prefixes (UR4S-369x-1) align with the earliest stereo variant of this master. The runout is stamped LPS-798, not LPS-797, matching the catalogue number printed on the labels.

albums.albumStory: Recorded April 4-5, 1966 at RCA Victor's New York studios, The Tender Gender arrived immediately after Burrell's ambitious solo-guitar showcase Guitar Forms and just before the holiday-themed Have Yourself a Soulful Little Christmas, part of his prolific mid-1960s run for Chess's Cadet jazz imprint under producer Esmond Edwards. Burrell leads a compact working quartet - pianist Richard Wyands, bassist Martin Rivera and drummer Oliver Jackson - a stripped-down format that puts his blues-rooted, vocal-toned guitar at the center of a relaxed, after-hours program mixing five originals with standards like "People" and Erroll Garner's "La Petite Mambo." The record is often praised as quite possibly one of Burrell's best albums of the 1960s, with a tight, well-focused rhythm section behind his playing, and his chord-melody work on "People" singled out as tender and lush - the intimate, melodic character that has kept the album a favorite among soul-jazz guitar collectors even though Burrell's Cadet output remains less celebrated than his Blue Note and Prestige work of the same decade.
albums.lpNotes: Original 1966 mono pressing - Cadet LP-772, first-issue blue-fade label, matrix XCTV121427/121428 -1A runouts.
albums.labelNotes: This copy's labels are the blue-fading-to-white Cadet design with the pinwheel/shell logo at 3 o'clock, black "CADET" credit lettering, and the printed "MONOPHONIC / Side 1 (2)" text - the first Cadet label design used from 1965-1970 across the jazz series LPS-758 to LPS-848, which this LP-772 falls squarely inside. Cadet had only just been renamed from Argo in 1965 to avoid confusion with the UK Argo label, so this design marks the label's earliest jazz-series pressings rather than any later GRT/All Platinum era redesign (orange/blue horse-head labels from 1971 on). The printed matrix on the label (#14816 / #14817, prefix XCTV) and the etched runout (XCTV121427-1A / XCTV121428-1A) identify this as an original mono pressing rather than the RCA Indianapolis-pressed stereo variant, which carries a different RCA master-number runout format (TR4S-...).
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Bob Simpson and Ray Hall at RCA Victor's New York studios and mastered for Cadet's standard commercial run rather than any audiophile process; the stereo Indianapolis pressing has been described as a decent mix with a little too much reverb on guitar, a characteristic likely shared with this mono cut from the same session tapes. No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Speakers Corner, etc.) of The Tender Gender exists beyond the Japanese Baybridge and Cadet BT-5095 reissues, which are conventional commercial pressings, not audiophile cuts. As an original-era mono pressing sourced directly from the 1966 master rather than a later reissue, this copy ranks at the top of the title's available fidelity options by default, though the mix itself (rather than mastering craft) is the more commonly noted sonic issue among listeners.
albums.generalNotes: This copy is the original 1966 US mono pressing on Cadet LP-772, identified by the blue-fading Cadet pinwheel label printed "MONOPHONIC" and the etched XCTV121427-1A/XCTV121428-1A runouts, distinct from the RCA Indianapolis-pressed stereo variant (TR4S- master numbers with an "I" stamp). No club, promo or later reissue markings are present. Recorded April 4-5, 1966 at RCA Victor's New York studios and produced by Esmond Edwards, this pressing sits at the top of the title's mono pressing hierarchy.

albums.albumStory: Bluesey Burrell was recorded on September 14, 1962 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio, one of a run of relaxed, blues-and-ballad-centered sessions Prestige cut for its mood-music Moodsville imprint. Guitarist Kenny Burrell, already established as one of the most lyrical and blues-steeped voices on the instrument, is paired here with tenor giant Coleman Hawkins, the father of the jazz tenor saxophone, for four of the seven tracks, while the remaining pieces feature Burrell's quartet alone with pianist Tommy Flanagan, bassist Major Holley, drummer Eddie Locke and conguero Ray Barretto. The program mixes standards ("I Thought About You," "Out of This World," "Guilty") with a Latin-tinged original, "Tres Talbras," and two Burrell-penned blues, reflecting the loose, unhurried, late-afternoon session described in the original liner notes by Robert Levin. The record arrived at a productive moment for Burrell, sandwiched between other Prestige/Moodsville dates and just months before his best-known Blue Note album, Midnight Blue; it captures him at his most relaxed and unhurried, favoring warm tone and economical phrasing over technical display. Hawkins, for his part, was enjoying a late-career renaissance in the early 1960s, and his appearances here are treated by critics as a highlight, his still-vital, breathy authority anchoring the more uptempo cuts. Though a modest, low-key release even by Moodsville's mood-music standards, the album has endured as a favorite among deep soul-jazz collectors for its unpretentious blues feeling and the rare studio pairing of Burrell and Hawkins, and it was praised on release, drawing a four-star review in Down Beat.
albums.lpNotes: 1963 mono first-issue pressing - deep-groove green Moodsville label, MVLP 29, etched Van Gelder mono runouts.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the standard green Moodsville design with silver print, MOODSVILLE banner, the 203 S. Washington Ave., Bergenfield, N.J. address, and "HIGH FIDELITY" band at the base, consistent with Moodsville's 1961-64 label design. This copy carries the label catalogue number MVLP 29 (mono) rather than MVST 29, and the vinyl is deep-groove on both sides, distinguishing it from the flat, no-deep-groove mono pressing of the same label misprint. The label's track A4 is printed "MONTUNO BLUES," a Moodsville-era typo also seen on the non-deep-groove mono pressing and carried through into the 2016 Analogue Productions reissue, so the misspelling alone does not separate pressings - it is the physical deep groove that dates this copy to Moodsville's earliest (1961-63) mono manufacturing run, before the deep-groove feature was phased out industry-wide by the mid-1960s.
albums.fidelity: Rudy Van Gelder recorded and cut this session himself; the mono lacquer carries his signature warm, present, slightly forward jazz sound typical of his early-60s Prestige/Moodsville dates, and the deep-groove pressing here represents Moodsville's earliest and most direct cut from that master. Collectors on the forums generally rate these original mono Van Gelder Moodsville/Prestige pressings above the contemporaneous stereo counterpart for tonal cohesion, since the mono mix avoids the hard-panned, less-musical channel separation of the stereo and later stereo-sourced reissues. Within the album's full fidelity hierarchy this original mono Van Gelder pressing sits at or near the top alongside the stereo original, well above the 1968 Prestige PRST 7578 reissue and the OJC/RVG CD remasters, and is generally considered a different but comparably desirable listening experience to the audiophile Analogue Productions 45 RPM and SACD editions (2016/2019), which are sourced from the stereo master and prized for extreme quietness and separation rather than mono cohesion.
albums.generalNotes: This is the mono Moodsville pressing (label reads MVLP 29, not the stereo MVST 29), with etched "MVLP#29A/B VAN GELDER" runouts and a stamped Van Gelder mark. The deep-groove vinyl places it with the earliest mono manufacturing of this release rather than the later, flat-label mono repress, supporting an early-1963 manufacturing date. The label's "Montuno Blues" misspelling (corrected to "Montono Blues" on the jacket) is a known Moodsville-era printing error and does not itself distinguish pressings, so the deep groove is the decisive tell here.

albums.albumStory: Country Soul (1962) came early in King Curtis's tenure at Capitol Records, a stop between his celebrated 1950s session work (Coasters, Chuck Willis, Clyde McPhatter) and the R&B chart breakthroughs he'd achieve later at Atco with 'Soul Serenade' and 'Memphis Soul Stew'. The concept - a saxophonist steeped in R&B and rock and roll tackling honky-tonk and Western standards like 'Your Cheatin' Heart,' 'Tennessee Waltz,' and 'Tumbling Tumbleweeds' alongside instrumental staples 'Raunchy' and 'High Noon' - reflected a period fascination among R&B artists with crossing genre lines for a broader pop audience. King Curtis, born Curtis Ousley in Fort Worth, Texas, had already built a reputation as one of the most influential saxophonists in rock and roll and R&B, having supplied the famous solo on the Coasters' 'Yakety Yak' and countless other hits as a first-call New York session man. His Capitol albums of this era, including Country Soul, were commercially modest compared to his 1960s Atco work but showcase his facility for melodic, blues-drenched improvisation applied to unlikely repertoire. The liner notes, contributed by NBA star Wilt Chamberlain (a Small's Paradise regular who knew Curtis from the Harlem club scene), speak to Curtis's reputation as a versatile, soulful bandstand performer capable of moving effortlessly between jazz, R&B, and pop idioms. While Country Soul itself remains a minor, largely overlooked entry in Curtis's discography, it illustrates the breadth of his musical curiosity in the years just before he became one of the most in-demand saxophonists in soul and rock, later backing Aretha Franklin, Sam Cooke, and the Rolling Stones' touring/session circles. Critically, the album is chiefly of interest to Curtis completists and country-soul crossover collectors rather than being considered a landmark in his catalog.

albums.albumStory: Everybody's Talkin' is a posthumous compilation assembled by Atco/Atlantic following King Curtis's murder in August 1971, gathering studio odds and ends, cover versions, and instrumental sides recorded during his final years as house bandleader and A&R man for Aretha Franklin and the Atlantic soul roster. Curtis, born Curtis Ousley, was one of soul music's defining tenor saxophonists, whose honking, vocal-toned solos powered hits from The Coasters to Aretha Franklin and whose own instrumental hits like "Soul Serenade" and "Memphis Soul Stew" made him a star in his own right. The tracks here find him reworking contemporary pop and soul staples - King Floyd's "Groove Me," Sly Stone's "You're The One," Stephen Stills's "Love The One You're With," Tim Hardin's "If I Were A Carpenter," and the Nilsson-popularized title cut - alongside originals like "Central Park" and "Wet Funk," backed by his working band the Kingpins and the Memphis Horns. The album captures the tail end of a career that helped define the Muscle Shoals/Atlantic soul-instrumental sound, bridging 1950s R&B saxophone tradition with early-1970s funk. Critically it was received as a minor, somewhat scattershot posthumous cash-in compared to his tighter late-60s/early-70s studio LPs, but it remains valued by collectors and soul-jazz enthusiasts for its stellar session personnel and Curtis's typically muscular, soulful playing. Its lasting legacy is less as a landmark statement than as a coda to one of the era's most influential session and bandleader careers, cut short at just 37.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis was already the era's most in-demand R&B saxophonist, a session ace behind the Coasters, the Shirelles and countless Atlantic dates, when ATCO captured him fronting his own road band for a live date at Small's Paradise, the storied Harlem nightclub. The set tours the mid-1960s soul-instrumental landscape - Curtis's own gritty originals like "Preach" and "Soul Theme" sit alongside covers of the day's dance and pop hits, Rufus Thomas's "Philly Dog," the Holland-Dozier-Holland-penned "Road Runner," Henry Mancini's "Peter Gunn," and a bristling reading of Bob Dylan's "Blowin' In The Wind." His touring band - Cornell Dupree on guitar, Melvin Lastie on cornet, Willie Bridges on baritone, Charles Rainey on bass and Ray Lucas on drums - was a tight, funky unit that would go on to seed the first-call New York soul-session scene of the following decade. The album stands as one of the era's definitive documents of black nightclub showmanship, capturing the call-and-response energy, honking solos and dance-floor immediacy that made Curtis's live shows legendary among musicians and audiences alike. It cemented his reputation as a bridge figure between jazz, R&B and soul, and its loose, horn-driven grooves have been cited by generations of soul and funk revivalists as a touchstone of instrumental soul. Critically it has endured as a high point in Curtis's discography, valued as much for atmosphere and band chemistry as for individual solos.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis, the Fort Worth-born tenor saxophonist who had already made his mark as a session player on hits like 'Yakety Yak,' built 'Soul Serenade' around his gift for turning familiar instrumental staples into greasy, danceable big-beat workouts. Rather than an album of new compositions, the set is a covers showcase - taking chart-proven instrumentals like 'Tequila,' 'Night Train,' 'Honky Tonk,' 'Java,' and 'Watermelon Man' and running them through Curtis's driving, vocalized tenor sound backed by a tight studio rhythm section. The title track, 'Soul Serenade,' co-written by Curtis with Luther Dixon, became one of his signature compositions and a much-covered soul standard in its own right. The album arrived at a pivotal moment in Curtis's career, as he was transitioning from jazz and R&B session work toward the funkier, dance-oriented instrumental sound that would define his mid-1960s Capitol output before his later, more celebrated Atlantic years fronting the Kingpins. Within the saxophone-instrumental genre that flourished on jukeboxes and in dance halls through the early-to-mid 1960s, Curtis was among its most reliable hitmakers, and this collection captures him at the height of that commercial run. It remains valued less as an artistic statement than as a solid, swinging document of the era's instrumental dance-music trend and of Curtis's own irresistible tone.

albums.albumStory: King Curtis, born Curtis Ousley in Fort Worth, Texas, was one of the defining tenor saxophonists of R&B and early soul, celebrated for his "yakety" honking style heard on hits by the Coasters and countless New York session dates of the late 1950s. The tracks gathered here - "Soul Twist," "Big Dipper," "Camp Meetin'," "What'd I Say," and companions - stem from his early-1960s instrumental sax-combo recordings for Bobby Robinson's Harlem-based Enjoy/Tru-Sound labels, cut in the wake of his Prestige jazz dates and just before his mid-1960s Capitol and Atco/Atlantic years. "Soul Twist" itself was a genuine national hit, riding the twist-dance craze to the top of the R&B charts in 1962 and becoming one of Curtis's signature instrumentals. These sides capture Curtis at a pivotal, transitional moment - moving from raw honking rock and roll saxophone toward the funkier, groove-driven instrumental soul he would perfect later in the decade - and they helped cement the tenor sax as a lead voice in soul music rather than a mere backing texture. The music's blend of gospel-tinged organ grooves, twist-era backbeats, and Curtis's blistering solos made it a favorite on jukeboxes and in dance clubs, and it remains prized by soul and R&B collectors as some of Curtis's most purely danceable, unpretentious work. Critically, Curtis's catalog from this era is regarded as foundational to instrumental soul-jazz, bridging 1950s rock and roll sax and the Memphis/Muscle Shoals soul sound he would later champion as a bandleader and session ace for Aretha Franklin and others.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York on April 25, 1961 for Prestige's short-lived Tru-Sound subsidiary, this LP is the only album on which King Curtis, otherwise renowned as the era's premier R&B/soul tenor and soprano saxophonist, stepped forward as a lead vocalist. Curtis had grown up steeped in Texas church singing and the sound of blues shouters, and here he applies that grounding to a program of blues and lightly gospel-tinged standards, backed by a compact combo (guitar, piano, bass, drums) and a female vocal trio for gospel-styled call-and-response. He also plays alto sax and, unusually for him, guitar on several tracks rather than his customary tenor. The album arrived amid Curtis's peak years as New York's most in-demand session saxophonist, and stands as a curious, personal side-project rather than a genre-defining statement, valued by collectors chiefly for its rarity and for the glimpse it offers of Curtis outside his usual studio-cat role. Contemporary reviews, including a favorable notice in Down Beat, treated it as a surprisingly assured blues-singing debut. It remains a minor but historically interesting entry in Curtis's catalog, illuminating the breadth of a musician far better known for his instrumental hits and his later work with Aretha Franklin and the Coasters.

albums.albumStory: La Dispute is a Grand Rapids, Michigan post-hardcore band known for pairing intense spoken-word vocals with dense, literary lyricism across albums like Wildlife and Rooms of the House. Tiny Dots grew out of a 2015 documentary of the same name that chronicled the band's process and touring life; Side A of this record is the instrumental score the band composed for that film, while Side B captures a stripped-down, seated live performance filmed in Kingston, UK in May 2014, drawing mostly on material from Rooms of the House. Rather than a conventional studio album, Tiny Dots functions as an archival bridge release between Rooms of the House (2014) and the band's later Panorama (2019), showing an unusually intimate, largely wordless and acoustic side of a band typically defined by cathartic vocal delivery. It offered longtime fans a rare instrumental and stripped-back counterpoint to the band's studio catalog and reinforced La Dispute's reputation within post-hardcore and emo circles for ambitious, format-defying releases tied to visual/multimedia projects.

albums.albumStory: Black Acid Soul is the 2021 debut album by Lady Blackbird, the reborn persona of Los Angeles singer Marley Munroe, who had spent years as a journeyman vocalist under other names before producer Chris Seefried helped her recast herself in the image of the great jazz-soul divas. Recorded largely live at Sunset Sound's Studio B in Hollywood, the album strips soul, jazz and blues to voice, piano, double bass and brushed percussion, putting Munroe's huge, scarred, Nina Simone-evoking voice front and center. The set is built on daring reinterpretations: Simone's civil-rights anthem "Blackbird" opens the record as a statement of identity, Irma Thomas's "Ruler Of My Heart" becomes a slow-burn showcase, and Tim Hardin's "It'll Never Happen Again" closes the cycle with devastating restraint, alongside originals like the title track co-written with Seefried. Trombone Shorty drops in a trumpet cameo on the gospel-inflected "Nobody's Sweetheart," underscoring the album's New Orleans soul undercurrent. Critics on both sides of the Atlantic hailed it as one of the standout vocal debuts of the year, with particular praise for Munroe's ability to sound simultaneously ancient and new, and it established Lady Blackbird as a major festival and jazz-club draw. The record taps directly into the lineage of Simone, Billie Holiday and Esther Phillips while remaining unmistakably contemporary in its stark, minimalist production.

GEMA/BIEM" with LC19813, 538711481 and 4050538711486 printed around the perimeter, with no deep groove - consistent with a modern European pressing plant (Optimal Media GmbH). Foundation Music Productions licensed the album to BMG Rights Management (UK) in 2021, and this configuration is the wide-retail trade pressing carrying a printed catalogue number in the runout, distinguishing it from the FMP 008 etched-matrix runout found on the 500-copy Bandcamp/Rough Trade colour-vinyl exclusives. albums.fidelity: Mastered by Bernie Grundman at Bernie Grundman Mastering, Hollywood, from Seth Atkins Horan's mixes - a high-end credit for a modern indie release, and the spare voice-and-piano production plays to Grundman's strengths in warmth and midrange clarity. All 2021 vinyl variants, black and colored alike, derive from this same Grundman master, so sonics are equivalent across the family; the runout's "ST" lacquer-cut stamp is consistent with the standard black-vinyl issue. The caveat is pressing consistency: user reports across nearly every variant of this title cite surface noise, pops and occasional warps from the European (Optimal Media) plant, making individual copy quality the variable rather than the cut. The 2022 2xLP Deluxe adds remixes but uses the same core mastering, and no audiophile-tier reissue (Analogue Productions, MoFi, etc.) exists as of this writing - the Grundman-mastered LP is the top vinyl tier available.

albums.title: Cornbread
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Jackie McLean (alto sax), Hank Mobley (tenor sax), Herbie Hancock (piano), Larry Ridley (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)

albums.albumStory: Cornbread was recorded by trumpeter Lee Morgan on September 8, 1965, for Blue Note, reuniting him with fellow Jazz Messengers-connected players Jackie McLean and Hank Mobley alongside a young Herbie Hancock, bassist Larry Ridley, and drummer Billy Higgins. Arriving in the wake of Morgan's crossover hit "The Sidewinder," the album found him balancing the same soulful, boogaloo-tinged accessibility with the harder-edged, more harmonically adventurous hard bop he had built his reputation on since his teenage years with Dizzy Gillespie and later Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. The title track and "Our Man Higgins" showcase the blues-drenched, two-tenor-plus-alto frontline interplay, while "Ceora" became one of Morgan's most enduring compositions, a lyrical Latin-tinged ballad that has since become a jazz standard covered widely by other artists. "Ill Wind," the sole standard, gives space to McLean's astringent alto voice against the rhythm section, and "Most Like Lee" closes the set with a churning minor blues. Morgan, one of the defining post-bop trumpet voices of his era, was at a creative peak in the mid-1960s, and Cornbread is frequently ranked among his strongest and most fully realized Blue Note dates from that period. Despite its quality, the album was held back from release until 1967, arriving after several other Morgan Blue Note titles had already reached the public. Critics and collectors have long regarded Cornbread as an underappreciated gem in Morgan's catalog, prized for its cohesive band chemistry and the compositional strength of "Ceora" in particular.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1967) - Blue Note "New York, USA" label, no Liberty credit; Van Gelder stamp in deadwax; promo "Audition Copy" stamp on jacket.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the plain white-top/blue-bottom Blue Note design reading only "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC \u2022 NEW YORK USA" with no "47 West 63rd St" street address and, critically, no "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" text. Blue Note dropped its West 63rd Street address in the early-to-mid 1960s in favor of the plain "New York, USA" credit, and this design continued to be used for a period even after Liberty Records acquired the label in 1965, before Liberty's corporate credit was added to the perimeter text later in the pressing run. Cornbread was recorded in September 1965 but not released until 1967, so this "New York, USA"-only label without the Liberty line places this copy at the very front of the BLP 4222 pressing run - the true first-pressing label for this title. The back cover's "AUDITION COPY" rubber stamp further indicates this particular copy was distributed as a promotional pressing rather than a standard retail unit.
albums.fidelity: This is an original Rudy Van Gelder mono cut, mastered directly from the analog session tapes at his Englewood Cliffs studio, and pressed in the mid-to-late-1960s Blue Note/Liberty era plant with the characteristic dense, punchy Van Gelder sound collectors prize. Collectors on the forums generally rate these mid-60s Van Gelder-stamped Blue Note mono originals as sonically superior to the later United Artists and Liberty reissue pressings, and to the 1985 Toshiba-EMI Japanese reissue, which is competent but noticeably softer. Modern audiophile reissues (Music Matters 45rpm, Analogue Productions, Blue Note Classic Vinyl/Tone Poet series) offer quieter surfaces and often wider dynamic range from remastered tapes, but many Van Gelder-era purists still prefer the tonal immediacy of this original cut. Within Cornbread's own fidelity hierarchy, this Van Gelder-stamped "New York, USA" mono original sits at or near the top, surpassed sonically only by top-tier modern audiophile remasters where available.

The back-cover "AUDITION COPY" rubber stamp confirms this specific copy was a label promo sent to radio or press rather than a standard retail copy. No street address or Liberty corporate line appears on the labels, consistent with the brief transitional label window used just before Liberty's credit was added to later Blue Note pressings.

albums.albumStory: Delightfulee was assembled from two 1966 sessions that caught Lee Morgan working in contrasting settings: a tight quintet with Joe Henderson, McCoy Tyner, Bob Cranshaw and Billy Higgins, and a larger, more ambitious ensemble featuring Wayne Shorter, Phil Woods, Philly Joe Jones and unusual horn colors like French horn and bass clarinet. The record arrived after the huge crossover success of "The Sidewinder" had made Morgan Blue Note's most commercially valuable young trumpeter, and it finds him balancing that visibility with genuinely exploratory hard-bop writing rather than repeating a hit formula. Original pieces like "Ca-Lee-So" and "Zambia" sit beside a soulful reading of the Beatles' "Yesterday" and the Broadway standard "Sunrise, Sunset," reflecting jazz's growing appetite at the time for pop and show tunes. Morgan, a Philadelphia prodigy who had already passed through Dizzy Gillespie's band and the Jazz Messengers before his Blue Note stardom, plays with the fluid, blues-drenched brilliance and biting tone that made him one of the defining hard-bop trumpet voices of the 1960s. Liner notes by the noted critic Leonard Feather situate the record within Morgan's ongoing growth as composer and bandleader. Though somewhat overshadowed commercially by his earlier boogaloo hits, the album is valued by listeners as a showcase of Morgan's compositional range and his gift for pairing top-tier sidemen in adventurous small- and medium-group hard bop.

This white/blue design was used company-wide from 1966 through 1970 following Liberty's purchase of the label, and since this title was recorded in 1966 and not issued until late 1967, the whole release window falls inside that Liberty-ownership era, placing this pressing among the first Liberty-label copies of the catalogue number, ahead of the later United Artists-address and Manhattan-era labels. The pressing plant is not identified on the label, and it is a flat label with no deep groove visible around the spindle.

Collectors on the forums generally regard these Liberty-era Van Gelder-mastered pressings as sonically very close to the earliest lacquers, since Van Gelder continued cutting Blue Note stereo masters himself well after the change in label ownership. This pressing outranks the later United Artists-address and mid-1980s reissues, which used later stampers, and stands well above the digital CD reissue; no audiophile (Music Matters/Analogue Productions/Tone Poet) edition of this specific title currently exists.
