albums.albumStory: Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio on April 9 and 21, 1965, The Rumproller found Lee Morgan chasing the funky, boogaloo-inflected momentum of his massive 1964 hit "The Sidewinder," this time leaning on outside writers - including Andrew Hill for the loping title cut - rather than his own pen for the lead single. By this point Morgan was Blue Note's reigning young star, a former Jazz Messengers and Art Blakey alumnus whose trumpet combined dazzling technique with an unmistakably soulful, blues-rooted sensibility. Joining him is tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson, then emerging as one of the label's most vital voices, alongside a fresh rhythm section of pianist Ronnie Mathews, bassist Victor Sproles and drummer Billy Higgins. The record captures the mid-1960s hard-bop mainstream at its most commercially minded, pairing groove-oriented material with the harmonic sophistication that defined the era's Blue Note house style. Critical reception was mixed-to-positive at the time and has remained so since, with some critics viewing it as a somewhat formulaic attempt to replicate "The Sidewinder's" success, while others praise the strength of the individual performances, particularly Henderson's soloing and Higgins' propulsive drumming. Nonetheless, the album holds a solid place in Morgan's prolific mid-1960s Blue Note run and remains a favorite among soul-jazz and boogaloo collectors for its instantly catchy title track.

This NY USA mono pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title, ahead of the Liberty-era NY reissues (still Van Gelder-mastered but without the ear/Plastylite pressing), the 1970s United Artists-era blue label reissues, and later 1980s-90s EMI/Manhattan reissues, all of which use lesser-quality vinyl and mastering chains. albums.title: The Sidewinder
albums.musicians: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Joe Henderson (tenor sax), Barry Harris (piano), Bob Cranshaw (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)
sides:

albums.albumStory: Recorded on December 21, 1963 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio, The Sidewinder was cut as a fairly routine Blue Note date built entirely from five new Lee Morgan originals, with the loping title track added almost as an afterthought to round out the program. Morgan, a prodigy who had joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band as a teenager and later anchored Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, was rebuilding his career after a period of personal decline when this session became his unexpected comeback vehicle. Joining him were tenor saxophonist Joe Henderson, newly signed to Blue Note himself, pianist Barry Harris on loan from Riverside, bassist Bob Cranshaw, and drummer Billy Higgins, who together lock into a loose, blues-drenched boogaloo groove that leaves wide-open space for extended solos over simple harmonic vamps. The title track's easy backbeat and earworm bassline caught on unexpectedly with radio and jukebox audiences, turning what Blue Note had pressed in only a few thousand copies into the label's best-selling record and, according to producer Michael Cuscuna's account, a financial lifeline for the company. Its crossover success also proved influential and controversial in equal measure, spawning a wave of similarly groove-based "boogaloo" jazz-funk sides across the mid-1960s hard bop catalog and drawing some critical grumbling that commercial appeal was overtaking artistic ambition. Decades on, The Sidewinder is regarded as a cornerstone of the hard bop/soul-jazz idiom and a high point in Morgan's celebrated run of Blue Note leader dates, prized by critics and listeners alike for its irresistible groove and the quality of the blowing from Morgan and Henderson.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1964) - Blue Note "New York, USA" label; BNLP-4157 Van Gelder matrix prefix consistent with original stamper.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the plain blue-and-white two-tone Blue Note design with the arc reading "BLUE...NOTE", "33 1/3 MICROGROOVE LONG PLAYING" in the upper arc, and "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC • NEW YORK USA" printed flat beneath the title - with no street address and no "Division of Liberty Records" text. Neither side shows a deep groove. This "New York, USA" address format replaced the earlier street-address labels (767 Lexington Ave / 47 West 63rd St) around 1963 and remained in use until Liberty's 1966 buyout added "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" beneath it, so this label design places the pressing in the 1964-1966 window. Combined with the BNLP-4157 Van Gelder matrix format that is the original stamper prefix for this title (later pressings often show a plain "BLP 4157" or "BLN" style matrix), this is consistent with an early pressing in the "New York, USA" era, ranking it ahead of the Liberty-era and later United Artists/Manhattan reissues in the label hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: This is a Van Gelder mono cut, mastered directly by Rudy Van Gelder at his Englewood Cliffs studio and (if a true first stamper) pressed at Plastylite, the pressing plant collectors regard as producing the punchiest, most dynamic vintage Blue Note sound. Collectors on the forums consistently rank original Van Gelder-cut New York-label mono pressings of The Sidewinder above the 1966+ Liberty-era repressings and well above the Manhattan/Capitol CD-era reissues in warmth and impact. Among later options, the Music Matters 45rpm mono/stereo audiophile reissues and the Blue Note Classic Vinyl series are well regarded for tape-sourced clarity but are generally described by collectors as smoother/cleaner rather than possessing the raw punch of an original Van Gelder-Plastylite pressing. The deadwax does not identify whether this pressing carries the Plastylite ear; if it does, it sits at or near the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title, and if it does not, it still ranks above Liberty-era and reissue pressings but below a documented first stamper.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in August 1956 when Lee Morgan was barely eighteen, this session captures the young trumpeter already fluent in the Clifford Brown-influenced hard bop language after his stint with Dizzy Gillespie's big band. Arranger Benny Golson supplied three of the six compositions along with Philadelphia friend Owen Marshall, giving the date a cohesive, big-band-inflected writing sensibility despite the small sextet format. The frontline pairing of Morgan with Hank Mobley and little-known altoist Kenny Rodgers, backed by Horace Silver, Paul Chambers and Charlie Persip, produced a set balancing Golson's melodic, sophisticated charts with blowing room for the young leader. This was Morgan's second Blue Note leader date, arriving as he was quickly establishing himself as one of the label's brightest new voices and would soon join Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. The album stands as an early testament to Morgan's precocious talent and to Golson's emerging skill as a composer-arranger within the hard bop idiom. It was well received in its day, with liner notes from critic Leonard Feather praising Morgan's rapid maturation, and it remains valued by collectors and historians as a formative document in the trumpeter's brief but towering career.

albums.albumStory: "Pres" Is Blue documents Lester Young's working club band caught live at the Savoy Ballroom in New York in 1950, captured not by a record label but by an audience member with a portable tape recorder who happened to be present on several nights. Young, the tenor saxophonist whose light, floating tone and rhythmic innovation had reshaped jazz phrasing in the Count Basie band of the late 1930s, was by 1950 a few years past his wartime military ordeal and the personal decline that followed it, yet still capable of the melodic invention and behind-the-beat swing that made him one of the music's most influential stylists. The band here-trumpeter Jesse Drakes, pianist Kenny Drew, bassist Aaron Bell and drummer Jo Jones-was Young's regular working unit of the period, and the relaxed, dance-hall setting gives the performances an informality absent from his studio dates. The liner notes make clear the tapes were never intended for release: they were acquired years later from the fan who made them, then cleaned up and re-recorded at RCA Victor's New York studios in April 1962 before Charlie Parker Records issued them. Critically the album has always been valued less for fidelity than for content, prized by Young specialists and completists as a rare document of his in-person sound away from the recording studio, offering warm, spacious readings of standards like "Stardust" and "Pennies From Heaven" that reveal a side of his artistry the formal sessions rarely captured. It stands as a footnote but a cherished one in the Lester Young discography, evidence of a still-vital player working a dance floor rather than a control booth.

This is the only label design used for this title; Charlie Parker Records (run by Aubrey Mayhew after acquiring rights to the Parker/Young name and catalogue) used this exact label format for its early-1960s mono jazz reissue line, placing this pressing in that 1962-63 window rather than any later reissue era. Slight variations in pressing rings exist across copies, indicating two stamper generations from the same original run rather than a distinct later edition; no subsequent reissue, foreign or domestic, of this specific LP was made.
albums.fidelity: The source is a fan's portable-recorder aircheck of a 1950 Savoy Ballroom dance date, later cleaned up and re-dubbed at RCA Victor's New York studios in April 1962 before mastering; it is inherently a lo-fi, amateur-tape source rather than a proper studio recording, and period dealer descriptions note the sound is merely serviceable rather than hi-fi. No audiophile reissue, remaster, or alternate mastering of this LP is documented anywhere (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet, etc. have never touched it), so this original Charlie Parker Records pressing is by default the best and only vinyl fidelity option for the title; a listener's expectations should be set by the source recording, not the pressing.

albums.albumStory: Pres compiles small-group sides Lester Young cut for Norman Granz's labels in the early-to-mid 1950s, drawing on separate rhythm-section dates rather than one continuous recording, with Hank Jones, Ray Brown and Buddy Rich backing him on one session and John Lewis, Gene Ramey, Jo Jones, Joe Shulman and Bill Clark rotating through others. By this point Young, the tenor player whose light, floating tone and rhythmic daring had reshaped the instrument's vocabulary in the Basie band of the late 1930s, was well into his postwar Verve/Norgran period, revisiting standards and originals in intimate combo settings after years of big-band and jam-session work. The album leans on the popular songbook of the day alongside several Young originals, letting his lyrical, behind-the-beat phrasing carry tunes the liner notes single out for their literate lyrics. Coming after the war years and a difficult Army stint, the record captures a still-inventive but more world-weary Pres, an artist whose influence on later tenor players was already assured by the time of these sessions. Jazz historians have long treated the Norgran/Verve small-group dates as a mixed but valuable body of work, not as tightly conceived as Young's 1930s Basie or Kansas City Six recordings but essential for the singular sound of his later horn.

albums.albumStory: The Master's Touch anthologizes Lester Young's 1944 Savoy studio dates, drawing together alternate and master takes from the sessions that produced some of his most enduring small-group sides just before his induction into the Army disrupted his career. Young was already the defining tenor stylist to emerge from the Count Basie band, and these sessions capture him at the peak of his light, floating, harmonically advanced tenor conception, alongside fellow Basie-ites like Basie himself, Buddy Tate, Jo Jones, Freddie Green and Harry Edison, as well as swing contemporaries such as Roy Eldridge, Cozy Cole and Billy Butterfield. Compiling both issued masters and rejected alternate takes side by side, the set gave listeners an unusually intimate look at Young's improvisational process, letting them hear how a phrase or solo shifted from take to take. The album stands as a key document of the transition from big-band swing to the small-combo language that would feed directly into bebop, with Young's behind-the-beat phrasing and airy tone pointing the way for a generation of tenor players. Critically, it has long been prized by jazz historians and collectors as essential Lester Young, filling in the picture between his celebrated Basie-era work and his postwar Verve and Aladdin recordings. Its reputation rests on the sheer quality of the playing across these compact, blues-drenched performances, cementing Young's status as one of the most influential improvisers in jazz history.

albums.albumStory: Lester Young, the tenor saxophonist whose light, floating tone and behind-the-beat phrasing had already reshaped jazz saxophone during his years with Count Basie and on the classic Billie Holiday sides of the 1930s, spent much of the 1950s recording prolifically for Norman Granz's Norgran and Verve labels. This set gathers a group of small-combo studio sides, most cut with a rhythm section drawn from Oscar Peterson's working trio, pairing Young's famously relaxed, singing style against the crisp, driving support of Peterson, Barney Kessel and Ray Brown. The album takes its title from the Ellington-Mills standard that anchors the second side, a tune Young - who insisted a musician should always know a song's lyrics before improvising on it - treats with characteristic restraint rather than bravado. Alongside durable standards like "Somebody Loves Me" and "I'm in the Mood for Love," Young contributes three originals ("Another Mambo," "Kiss Me Again," "Big Top Blues") that show his writing hewing to the same understated, blues-tinged lyricism as his horn work. By this point Young was past his mid-1930s and Basie-era commercial peak but still deeply admired by a generation of tenor players who had absorbed his cooler, more melodic alternative to Coleman Hawkins's muscular approach. The record was received as a solid, unhurried entry in Young's extensive Granz discography, valued less for innovation than for the warmth and consistency of a mature stylist still very much in command of his voice. It remains a representative document of Young's Verve years and of the intimate, blowing-session format Granz favored for his stable of swing and bebop-adjacent veterans.

albums.albumStory: Blues Walk was recorded on July 28, 1958 at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack studio, coming right on the heels of Lou Donaldson's Lou Takes Off and cementing the blues-drenched, soul-jazz direction he'd been refining since the mid-1950s. Donaldson, a Charlie Parker-schooled alto saxophonist from Badin, North Carolina, had by this point built a reputation as one of the most accessible and groove-oriented voices to emerge from Blue Note's hard-bop stable, and this session - built around a stripped-down quintet with Herman Foster's bluesy piano and, crucially, Ray Barretto's conga - pushed that sensibility further toward the Latin-tinged, dance-floor-friendly sound that would define his later career. The title track became one of Donaldson's signature compositions, a deceptively simple blues line that swings hard and has since been covered widely and sampled repeatedly in hip-hop. Ballads like The Masquerade Is Over and Autumn Nocturne showcase Donaldson's warm, vocal-like tone, while Denzil Best's Move and the original Callin' All Cats keep the tempo brisk. The album is widely regarded as one of the high points of Donaldson's Blue Note run and a touchstone of the blues-based, groove-first strain of hard bop that would evolve into soul jazz through the 1960s. It remains a favorite among collectors and DJs alike for both its musical directness and its enduring influence on funk and hip-hop sampling culture.

NYC" address arced above the spindle and a small (R) trademark symbol at the bottom rim, matched by deep-groove rings on both sides - this is the fourth Blue Note label state used roughly 1959-1962, distinguished from the earlier "no INC/no (R)" third-state label that ran 1958-1959. Blue Note occupied the 47 West 63rd Street address from 1957 to 1966, and BST 1593 (the stereo counterpart to mono BLP 1593) entered Blue Note's stereo catalog around mid-1959, squarely inside this fourth-label production window. The presence of the (R) mark and "INC." therefore does not push this copy to a later pressing - it is the label design current at the time of Blues Walk's original stereo release, placing this copy at the head of the stereo pressing line rather than behind a still-earlier stereo variant.
albums.fidelity: This is an all-analog Rudy Van Gelder cut from the original session tapes, pressed at Plastylite (confirmed by the ear stamp) - the gold standard for Blue Note sonics and the top of this album's fidelity hierarchy alongside the mono first pressing. Collectors on the forums generally favor these deep-groove RVG/ear originals over any subsequent Liberty or United Artists era repress for both tonal warmth and dynamic punch. The 2019 Music Matters 33/45rpm audiophile reissues (mastered by Kevin Gray from the analog tapes) are well regarded and often preferred for surface noise and bass control, but the original RVG lacquer retains the historical and much of the sonic edge prized by purists. Modern 180g Blue Note Classic Vinyl Series reissues are digitally-sourced and rank well below both the original and the Music Matters pressing in critical esteem.

albums.albumStory: Recorded on July 28, 1958 for Alfred Lion's Blue Note label, Blues Walk arrived as alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson was sharpening the soulful, blues-drenched attack that would define his mature style. Donaldson had come up through the bebop ranks in the early 1950s, closely tied to the Charlie Parker lineage, but by the late 1950s he was steering his own quintet toward a rawer, groove-based sound built on riffs, congas and the blues form itself. The addition of Ray Barretto's conga to the standard piano-bass-drums quartet gave the date a Latin-tinged, dance-floor lift that distinguished it from the harder bebop dates on the label, and the title track became one of Donaldson's signature compositions. The album balances originals like the title cut, "Play Ray" and "Callin' All Cats" with warmly played standards such as "The Masquerade Is Over" and "Autumn Nocturne," showcasing Donaldson's vocal-like tone and his gift for melodic, blues-based improvisation. Blues Walk is widely regarded as a foundational text of the soul-jazz movement that would flourish on Blue Note through the 1960s, and it remains one of Donaldson's most celebrated and influential recordings, prefiguring the boogaloo and groove-jazz records he and others would make in the years that followed.

NYC" arced above the spindle, mono catalogue number BLP 1593, and the "33 1/3 MICROGROOVE LONG PLAYING" legend. This West 63rd Street address design was in use from 1956, when Blue Note moved from Lexington Ave, through the early 1960s. The runout carries the BN-LP-1593 etched matrix, the RVG stamp and the Plastylite "ear," placing the pressing in Blue Note's own-plant original-issue window rather than the later address-less Liberty-era labels (c.1963 onward) or the New York, USA labels used after 1965.
albums.fidelity: The dead wax carries Rudy Van Gelder's own RVG stamp and the Plastylite "ear," confirming this is a lacquer cut by Van Gelder himself and pressed at the Plastylite plant - the combination collectors on the Hoffman-forum regard as the gold standard for Blue Note's mono catalogue, with a warmth and immediacy that later Liberty- and United Artists-era repressings (cut from dubbed or EQ'd tapes) do not match. Within the album's own fidelity hierarchy this deep-groove West 63rd St. mono original sits at the top alongside the RVG-stamped stereo counterpart, ahead of the 1960s Liberty-era reissues, the more recent Classic Records QUIEX 200g reissue, and even the well-regarded 2019 Music Matters Jazz 33 1/3 RPM audiophile pressing, which most Hoffman-forum listeners rate as an excellent but still secondary alternative to a clean original. This particular copy's G+ vinyl means some of that original mastering's advantage is undercut by surface wear and groove damage.

albums.title: Cole Slaw
albums.musicians: Lou Donaldson (alto saxophone), Herman Foster (piano), Earl May (bass), Bruno Carr (drums), Ray Barretto (congas)
sides:

albums.albumStory: Cole Slaw was cut on June 19, 1964 at RCA's New York studios, one of a run of albums Lou Donaldson made for Argo/Cadet during the mid-1960s after leaving Blue Note for a few years. Donaldson had emerged in the late 1940s as a Charlie Parker-influenced altoist before steering toward a warmer, blues- and R&B-inflected "soul jazz" style that would define his best-known work. Here he leads a compact quartet plus Ray Barretto's congas, which lend a loping Latin-tinged pulse to standards like "Poinciana" and "There Is No Greater Love" alongside two Donaldson originals, "Li'l Miss Fine" and "Soul Gumbo." The album is emblematic of the mid-'60s crossover jazz-for-jukeboxes aesthetic - unpretentious, danceable, steeped in blues feeling - that helped keep Donaldson working steadily through a transitional period in jazz's commercial fortunes. It never achieved landmark status but is valued by soul-jazz collectors as a solid, groove-heavy example of Donaldson's mid-career sound, sitting between his classic Blue Note quartet sides and his later, funkier organ-combo work. Critical notice at the time was modest, but the record has endured as a minor favorite among rare-groove and mod-jazz diggers for its title cut and the Barretto-driven rhythm feel.
albums.lpNotes: Argo DJLP-747 promotional "Revue Copy" (mono, 1964) - cream Audio Odyssey label, deep groove, "NOT FOR SALE" stamp; a trade/press-service pressing contemporary with the commercial issue.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the cream "AUDIO ODYSSEY BY ARGO" label design with the ARGO block logo at left, a plain single black ring at the perimeter reading "ULTRA HIGH FIDELITY" and "LONG PLAYING 33 1/3 RPM ... MADE IN U.S.A.", deep-groove pressing, and the disc is stamped "NOT FOR SALE" with a promo number (#13514/#13515) and catalogue prefix "DJLP-747" plus a rubber-stamped "REVUE COPY" - all era markers Argo used on trade/press-service pressings distributed alongside the regular commercial black-label LP-747 in the early-to-mid 1960s. Argo's Chicago-based cream Audio-Odyssey labels date to the label's mid-1960s design window before the Cadet-era red/white/blue labels supplanted them around 1965-66. Because this is a service/promo pressing rather than the retail black-label LP, it sits alongside - not strictly before or after - the standard commercial mono pressing in the release's hierarchy; it was manufactured from the same plates/stampers at the same time as the trade release rather than representing a later reissue.
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Ray Hall at RCA's New York studio and produced by Esmond Edwards, this is a straightforward, well-recorded but not audiophile-grade mid-'60s jazz date; Argo/Chess pressings of this era are generally solid but not renowned for exceptional vinyl quality compared to contemporary Blue Note or Riverside pressings. There is no known audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Speakers Corner, etc.) of this title, so the fidelity hierarchy is simply original mono/stereo Argo pressings versus later Cadet-era pressings; this deep-groove mono promo, being an early trade pressing, likely predates any later Cadet stamper generations and should sound at least as good as, if not marginally better than, later commercial copies.

albums.albumStory: Recorded April 27, 1961 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio and released by Blue Note in July 1962, Gravy Train captured altoist Lou Donaldson's working quartet with pianist Herman Foster, bassist Ben Tucker and drummer Dave Bailey, augmented by Alec Dorsey's congas for extra rhythmic heat. Coming on the heels of Blues Walk and Here 'Tis, the album continued Donaldson's turn from straight bebop toward a bluesy, backbeat-driven "soul-jazz" sound built on jukebox-friendly standards and originals, straight-ahead jazz, bebop and blues done Donaldson's way. It stands as a solid, representative entry in Donaldson's prolific early-1960s Blue Note run rather than a landmark, valued more for its consistency and groove than for any single innovation.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1962) - New York, USA label, deep groove side 1, RVG stamp + Ear in the deadwax.

The matrix (BN-LP-4079-A/B) carries an RVG stamp and EAR/Plastylite mark etched in the deadwax, among the last Blue Notes to carry the RVG stamp before it was replaced later in 1961-62 by the full "VAN GELDER" etching. This combination of NY-address label, deep groove on side 1, RVG stamp and Ear places this copy in the earliest, first-pressing manufacturing run of BLP 4079, ahead of any later 1960s NY-label repress that dropped the deep groove and RVG stamp.
albums.fidelity: Van Gelder's original 1961 all-analog tape, cut to lacquer by RVG himself as shown by the RVG stamp in the runout; the Ear (Plastylite) mark confirms an original Plastylite-pressed disc rather than a later custom-pressed run. Collectors on the forums generally rate these early-1960s NY-label Van Gelder-cut Blue Notes very highly for warmth and presence, ranking them above the mid-60s Liberty-era NY/Div. of Liberty pressings and well above generic reissues; no audiophile remaster (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet) of this specific title exists, so this original pressing represents the top of the album's known fidelity hierarchy alongside other RVG/Ear first pressings.

albums.title: Here 'Tis
albums.musicians: Lou Donaldson (alto sax), Grant Green (guitar), John "Baby Face" Willette (organ), Dave Bailey (drums)
sides:
1. A Foggy Day (Gershwin)
2. Here 'Tis (Lou Donaldson)
3. Cool Blues (Charlie Parker)

1. Watusi Jump (Lou Donaldson)
2. Walk Wid Me (Donaldson)
albums.albumStory: Recorded for Blue Note in January 1961, Here 'Tis captures alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson at the moment he pivoted his hard-bop language toward the earthier, funkier feel that would define soul jazz, introducing New York audiences to two young sidemen he had discovered on tour, guitarist Grant Green and organist John "Baby Face" Willette. The set mixes originals steeped in gospel and blues vamping ("Here 'Tis," "Watusi Jump," "Walk Wid Me") with a bop-tinged reading of Charlie Parker's "Cool Blues" and a warm ballad treatment of "A Foggy Day," letting Donaldson show both his bebop pedigree and his growing commercial instincts. Green's clean, single-note guitar lines and Willette's churchy Hammond organ swing gave the date a groove-heavy, blues-drenched character that anticipated the organ-combo boom Blue Note would ride through the mid-1960s. Donaldson, a North Carolina-born altoist who came up through Charlie Parker's shadow before finding his own populist voice, used albums like this to bridge jazz's improvising rigor with dance-floor and jukebox appeal. The record helped launch Grant Green's own prolific Blue Note career and stands as a foundational document of the soul-jazz movement, still cited by critics and DJs as one of the genre's most durable and influential grooves.
albums.lpNotes: Mixed-label mono repress (mono, c.1962-65) - Side 1 "47 West 63rd" label, Side 2 address-less "New York, USA" label; RVG + Plastylite ear retained on both sides.
albums.labelNotes: Side 1 carries the "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC. \u00b7 47 WEST 63rd \u00b7 NYC" rim text used on Blue Note's true first-issue mono labels (1961-62), while Side 2 has already switched to the address-less "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC \u00b7 NEW YORK USA" rim text that Blue Note introduced as it phased out the street address, generally placed in the c.1962-66 window. Neither label shows a pressed-in deep groove, consistent with the flat-edge West 63rd-era stock rather than the earlier deep-groove Lexington Ave labels (1956-58). This side-to-side mismatch is a documented Blue Note phenomenon (plants exhausting old label stock on one side while drawing new stock for the other) and places this copy as a mono repress made from leftover early labels and new labels rather than the strict simultaneous-both-sides-63rd first pressing; it still carries the era-correct RVG/ear stampers, so it sits just behind the true firsts in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Cut by Rudy Van Gelder directly from the January 1961 session tapes and pressed at Blue Note's Plastylite plant (ear mark, "9M" etch), this mono pressing shares the same first-generation metalwork lineage as the strict first-issue copies, so its sonics are essentially indistinguishable from an original despite the mixed labels. Collectors on the forums generally rank any RVG/ear-stamped mono BLP 4066 well above the later stereo Liberty-era and Music Matters/United Artists reissues for warmth and presence, though slightly below a pristine simultaneous-both-sides-63rd copy in collector prestige (not necessarily sound). Modern audiophile remasters - the Analogue Productions 45rpm 2LP (Kevin Gray/Ron Rambach, mastered from tape) and the Blue Note Tone Poet mono LP (Kevin Gray) - are quieter and more resolved on modern equipment but are prized as separate, complementary listening options rather than replacements for the vintage RVG cut's tonal character.
albums.generalNotes: BLP 4066 mono, mixed-label pressing: Side 1 shows the "47 WEST 63rd" rim text used on true 1961-62 first-issue labels, but Side 2 has already moved to the address-less "NEW YORK, USA" text that Blue Note phased in through the early-to-mid 1960s. Both sides retain the era-correct RVG stamp and Plastylite ear (etched "9M"), confirming an authentic Van Gelder-cut, Plastylite-pressed mono disc rather than a later Liberty-era pressing. The side mismatch indicates a repress run using leftover early label stock alongside newer stock, placing this copy just after the strict simultaneous-both-sides-63rd first pressing in the hierarchy.

albums.title: Live: Fried Buzzard
albums.musicians: Lou Donaldson (alto sax, flute), Bill Hardman (trumpet), Billy Gardner (organ), Warren Stephens (guitar), Leo Morris (drums)
sides:

albums.albumStory: Lou Donaldson had already built a substantial reputation as a bebop-rooted alto saxophonist through his 1950s and early 1960s Blue Note work when this live set was captured over a weekend at the Bon Ton Club in Buffalo, New York, in August 1965. Cadet (the rebranded Argo, Chess Records' jazz imprint) shelved the tapes for several years, finally issuing them in 1970 as Donaldson's soul-jazz sound and reputation for crowd-pleasing, groove-driven playing had grown. The quintet, featuring the underrated trumpeter Bill Hardman, organist Billy Gardner, guitarist Warren Stephens and drummer Leo Morris (later known as Idris Muhammad), plays a mix of Donaldson originals like the title track and blues-drenched standards such as "Summertime" and "The Best Things in Life Are Free." The back cover's own liner notes frame the record as a deliberate rejection of over-produced studio jazz in favor of raw, spontaneous performance, complete with the crowd's reactions and Donaldson's between-song banter left intact. It captures Donaldson at a pivotal midpoint between his hard-bop roots and the funkier, boogaloo-inflected direction he would soon pursue on Blue Note albums like Alligator Bogaloo. While never as celebrated as his studio classics, the album is valued by soul-jazz collectors as an unvarnished document of a working club date and of Hardman's underappreciated horn work alongside Donaldson.

No deep groove or alternate address is present, and no later Cadet/Chess Records-era or GRT-era redesign is visible, so this is the standard and, so far as documented, only domestic label variant for this catalogue number. Its placement within that 1965-1970 block-letter window is consistent with the album's 1970 release date printed on the back cover credits.
albums.fidelity: This is a straightforward late-1960s Cadet (Chess) in-house production, mastered and mixed at Ter Mar Studios in Chicago rather than by an audiophile-grade engineer, and pressed via GRT-era Chess manufacturing; the recording itself is a single-microphone-era club live tape, so surface noise and modest tape hiss are part of the source rather than the pressing. No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Music Matters, Speakers Corner, etc.) of this title exists, so this original Cadet stereo pressing is, by default, the top of its own fidelity hierarchy alongside any later CD reissue, which collectors on the forums generally regard as sonically comparable rather than superior.

albums.musicians: Lou Donaldson (alto sax), Tommy Turrentine, Jr. (trumpet), Roy Montrell (guitar), John Patton (organ), Ben Dixon (drums)

albums.albumStory: Recorded on July 17, 1963 at A&R Recording Studio in New York, Signifyin' captures alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson at a pivotal turn in his career, as he moved decisively from his earlier Charlie Parker-indebted bebop toward the earthy, backbeat-driven soul jazz that would define his mid-1960s work. The session paired Donaldson with organist "Big" John Patton, whose Hammond work anchors the date's deep groove and gospel-blues feel, alongside trumpeter Tommy Turrentine, guitarist Roy Montrell and drummer Ben Dixon. It was Donaldson's debut recording for Chess's Argo subsidiary after years on Blue Note, produced under Esmond Edwards's supervision, and it leans on original blues-based compositions alongside a pair of standards, "Time After Time" and "Don't Get Around Much Anymore." The record is often cited as an early, fully-formed statement of the soul jazz/organ-combo sound Donaldson would refine on his celebrated Blue Note run later in the decade. Critics have retrospectively praised the band's tight, funky cohesion, with Donaldson's blues-rooted phrasing riding comfortably atop Patton's grooves. Within Donaldson's long career - which spanned Blakey-era hard bop through to acid-jazz-era boogaloo hits - Signifyin' stands as a transitional but assured document of the organ-combo direction that made him one of soul jazz's most enduring and commercially successful figures.

The matrix carries the LP-724 mono prefix with side numbers 12603/12604, matching the mono configuration rather than the LPS-724 stereo matrix (PR4S-...) found on the blue-label stereo copy. This places the copy at the mono first-issue stage of the release, ahead of the blue-label stereo pressing and well ahead of the later Cadet-era reissues of the same catalogue number.

No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Music Matters, Speakers Corner, etc.) of this title exists, and later reissues were routine Cadet-era commercial repressings rather than upgraded cuts, so this original mono pressing sits at the top of the album's practical fidelity hierarchy alongside its stereo LPS-724 sibling. Collector discussion on forums of this specific Argo soul jazz era is thin compared to Blue Note dates, reflecting the label's lower audiophile profile rather than any known sonic problem with the cut itself.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in December 1972 at A&R Recording Studio in New York, Sophisticated Lou found alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson - a hard-bop veteran whose 1950s and 60s Blue Note dates had defined soul-jazz - stepping into a lush, string-laden pop-jazz setting arranged and conducted by Wade Marcus. Producer George Butler paired Donaldson with a crossover repertoire of standards and contemporary pop songs, including a fresh take on his own signature composition Blues Walk alongside Stevie Wonder's You Are the Sunshine of My Life and film themes from The Happy Ending and The Long Goodbye. The move reflected the wider early-1970s push by major labels to soften jazz artists' sound for adult-contemporary radio, following a lineage of strings-backed dates by figures like Charlie Parker and Clifford Brown. Reviewers of the era noted the album's romantic, mellow surfaces contrasted with Donaldson's still-vigorous, blues-rooted alto phrasing, giving the record a warmer reception among soul-jazz collectors than among hard-bop purists. It arrived at a transitional point in Donaldson's catalogue, sandwiched between his grittier funk-jazz sides for Blue Note and the fully commercial soul outings that would follow. While not considered among his most influential work, the album remains valued by collectors as a document of Blue Note's early-1970s pivot toward a smoother, string-backed sound and as a showcase for Donaldson's ability to retain his identity within an orchestral frame.

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio across two February 1960 sessions, Sunny Side Up captures alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson at the peak of his classic run for his label, leading a quintet built around trumpeter Bill Hardman and pianist Horace Parlan. Donaldson had emerged as one of the era's most reliably soulful alto voices, a Charlie Parker disciple who favored gutbucket blues phrasing and R&B-tinged swagger over harmonic experimentation. The program balances blues-drenched originals like the earthy, boogaloo-adjacent 'Goose Grease' and 'The Truth' with warmly rendered standards such as 'The Man I Love' and 'Softly As In A Morning Sunrise,' giving the date the relaxed, jukebox-friendly feel typical of Donaldson's late-1950s and early-1960s work. Parlan, arriving fresh from a stint with Charles Mingus, brings a percussive, blues-rooted comping style that dovetails naturally with Donaldson's attack, while Hardman's brassy trumpet sharpens the front line. The session arrived at a pivotal moment as the label pushed further into the hard bop and soul-jazz idiom that would define much of its 1960s catalog. Critics and collectors have long viewed the album as a satisfying, unpretentious entry in Donaldson's discography, valued more for its groove and stellar sidemen than for any single standout composition. Its lasting appeal rests on exactly that unfussy consistency, a hallmark of a saxophonist whose decades-long career remained one of jazz's most durable and danceable.
albums.lpNotes: 2008 Classic Records test pressing of the mono 200g reissue of this Blue Note title - blank die-cut jacket, one printed Test Pressing label, hand-dated 4/24/2008.
albums.labelNotes: The Side 1 label is the generic blue-banner 'Classic Records / (remember the sound...)' logo with blue rim text arcing 'CLASSIC RECORDS' over 'TEST PRESSING' and a hand-inked date and catalogue number, a stock design used across that company's test runs beginning in the early 2000s rather than a finished period Blue Note label. No deep-groove ring or period address text appears on this label style. Side 2 carries no printed information at all, only light handling marks, typical of a one-sided test stamper. This label design places the copy in Classic Records' pre-release quality-control stage, ahead of the finished retail mono reissue's own numbered labels.
albums.fidelity: The mono reissue this test pressing previews was remastered and cut by Bernie Grundman from the analog master tapes onto 200-gram Quiex SV-P vinyl, pressed by a custom pressing facility; collectors on the forums rate this Grundman cut very highly, generally ranking just behind an excellent original first-pressing cut but ahead of later stereo-only reissues of this mono-only title. As a test pressing struck from the same lacquers and stampers as the commercial run, it should sound identical to a standard-issue copy of that pressing, with any difference limited to quality-control variance rather than mastering. It is a distinct, earlier remaster from the more recent 180-gram Blue Note reissue of this title.
albums.generalNotes: This is a 2008 Classic Records test pressing of their Bernie Grundman-mastered mono 200-gram reissue, not an original pressing or a numbered retail copy. The blank white die-cut jacket with a typed identification sticker, the single one-sided printed Test Pressing label matching the hand-written date, and the completely blank second label are all hallmarks of a pre-release quality-control pressing. The etched runouts match the reissue's mastering codes, confirming it as the same cut used for the commercial run rather than a distinct mastering. It stands outside the standard issue/reissue hierarchy for this title as a pre-release artifact rather than a numbered commercial pressing.

albums.albumStory: Recorded May 9, 1962 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio and issued in 1963, The Natural Soul finds alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson deep into the soul-jazz groove he pioneered for Blue Note, pairing his blues-drenched, gospel-tinged alto with the young organ-guitar-drums combo of John Patton, Grant Green and Ben Dixon plus trumpeter Tommy Turrentine. Donaldson had already helped define the funky, backbeat-driven strain of hard bop that made jukeboxes and jazz clubs move, and this session - a direct follow-up to his earlier organ-combo dates - doubles down on that formula with original blues lines like "Funky Mama" and "Sow Belly Blues" alongside a warm, unhurried reading of the Gershwin standard "Love Walked In." The album crystallizes a period when Donaldson, criticized by some purists for playing to the room rather than the avant-garde, was quietly building one of the most influential bodies of accessible, blues-based jazz of the era. Its easy, danceable grooves and Patton's percolating organ work helped cement the organ-combo sound that would echo through soul jazz and later soul and funk records. Contemporary liner notes framed Donaldson as one of the music's most consistently satisfying and underrated players, a reputation the album's relaxed, groove-forward sequencing bears out. Decades on, The Natural Soul remains a touchstone of the Blue Note soul-jazz catalogue and a favorite among collectors and DJs drawn to its unpretentious, foot-tapping swing.
albums.lpNotes: Original 1963 mono pressing - Blue Note New York USA label, no deep groove, Van Gelder stamp and Plastylite ear in the deadwax.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show the classic white and blue Blue Note design with the arced "33 1/3 MICROGROOVE" legend, "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC · NEW YORK USA" beneath it, and BLP 4108 with no West 63rd Street or Liberty text - the plain "NEW YORK USA" address used from roughly 1957 into 1963/64, before Blue Note added the "A DIVISION OF LIBERTY RECORDS" line around 1966. This pressing's labels show no deep-groove ridge, corresponding to the no-deep-groove variant of this catalogue number (variant reference 3792268), unlike the deep-groove copies that represent the very earliest stamper runs. That places this copy in the second wave of the original 1963 mono pressing run - a genuine New York-label first edition, just not the earliest deep-groove lacquer.
albums.fidelity: Cut and pressed from Rudy Van Gelder's original analog masters, with his stamp and the Plastylite "ear" marking an original-era lacquer and pressing plant. Collectors on the forums consistently rate original Blue Note New York mono pressings of this era among the best-sounding versions of these sessions, prized for Van Gelder's punchy, immediate organ-combo sound. This no-deep-groove New York mono copy sits just behind the very earliest deep-groove stamper copies in the collector hierarchy, but well ahead of the later Liberty-era "Division of Liberty Records" pressings and any digital reissues, which soften the tape's original warmth and dynamics.

The runout carries BN-LP-4108-A/B, the Plastylite ear, and the Van Gelder stamp, marking an original-era pressing rather than a later Liberty-era reissue.

albums.albumStory: Recorded February 18, 1959 at Van Gelder Studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, LD+3 paired alto saxophonist Lou Donaldson with Gene Harris's newly formed piano trio The Three Sounds, who had only just debuted on Blue Note themselves. Donaldson, a Charlie Parker disciple with a tone leaner and more direct than Bird's, had already built a solid Blue Note career through the 1950s and was moving toward the peak commercial run that would culminate in Blues Walk later that same year. The blend of Donaldson's bop-rooted alto with the funky, blues-drenched piano trio proved a natural fit, since the Three Sounds' grounded, groove-based comping gave Donaldson's fluent, Parker-inflected lines a soulful undertow. The set mixes standards (Three Little Words, Just Friends, Blue Moon, Don't Take Your Love From Me) with a Bird contrafact (Confirmation) and two Donaldson originals (Smooth Groove, Jump Up), giving the record a program that swings between straight bebop and the loose, riff-based feel that would soon define soul-jazz. Critics have long ranked it among the strongest sessions in either artist's catalog, praised for Donaldson's full-bodied tone and unforced swing and for how assured the Three Sounds already sound as accompanists. The album stands as an important bridge session, helping cement Donaldson's reputation as a first-rate alto voice while showcasing the Three Sounds just as they began their own prolific run of Blue Note dates.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1959) - Blue Note deep-groove 47 West 63rd label with no "Inc"/no ® wording; RVG stamp + Plastylite ear in deadwax.
albums.labelNotes: The label is the white body/blue rim Blue Note design with the arc reading "BLUE NOTE RECORDS - 47 WEST 63rd - NYC," a single deep groove ring, and arc text showing no "Inc" alongside "Blue Note Records" - the earliest of the 47 West 63rd label states, used c.1957-early 1960s before Blue Note incorporated and added "Inc." and a ® registration mark to the same address labels around 1961. This design also exists in a near-identical later state with "Inc" and ® added, both still carrying RVG stamp and Plastylite ear in the deadwax. The absence of "Inc"/® on this label places the copy in the earlier of the two states. This positions the copy at or very near the top of the BLP 4012 mono pressing hierarchy, ahead of the later flat-edge/no-deep-groove NY labels and far ahead of the 1972 United Artists reissue.
albums.fidelity: Cut by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his own Hackensack session tape, this deep-groove 47 West 63rd pressing represents the original mono mastering generation, prized by collectors on the forums for the warmth and immediacy typical of vintage RVG Blue Note cuts. It ranks above later 1960s NY-USA label pressings, the 1972 United Artists reissue, and Japanese reissues (King/Toshiba-EMI), all of which derive from subsequent mastering generations or tape copies. Modern audiophile treatments - Classic Records' 200-gram LP and the Music Matters 2x45rpm reissue - use remastered cuts that often win praise for surface quietness and extended top end but are generally regarded by Blue Note collectors as sonically different companions to, rather than replacements for, an honest original Van Gelder pressing like this one.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Blue Note BLP 4012 mono - earliest 47 West 63rd deep-groove label state, lacking the "Inc" and ® wording that Blue Note added to the same address labels around 1961. Deadwax shows RVG stamp and the Plastylite ear on both sides, consistent with an original-era Blue Note NJ pressing rather than a later reissue. Deep groove appears on both sides, matching the early West 63rd label configuration rather than the flat-edge/no-groove transitional labels that followed.

albums.albumStory: Assembled by Columbia in the late 1960s, this compilation gathers recordings Louis Armstrong made for the label across roughly four decades, from his 1955-56 remakes of Hot Five staples like 'West End Blues' and 'Struttin' With Some Barbecue' to his mid-1960s All-Stars concert performances. Armstrong, who had already reshaped jazz as a soloist and vocalist in the 1920s with the Hot Five and Hot Seven, spent his later career as a globally beloved entertainer, and this set captures that later persona fronting his working small group, the All-Stars. The centerpiece is 'Mack the Knife,' the Kurt Weill/Bertolt Brecht theme from 'The Threepenny Opera' that Armstrong had turned into a hit a decade earlier and which remained one of his signature vocal numbers. 'Cabaret,' recorded in 1966, shows Armstrong still mining contemporary Broadway material for his songbook late in his career. The collection blends the trumpet virtuosity that made him the music's most influential soloist with the warm, gravelly singing that made him a household name far beyond jazz circles, and it stands as an accessible summary of why Armstrong is regarded as one of the central figures in American popular music. Critically, such Armstrong compilations were valued less as artistic statements than as durable, well-loved samplers of a titan's most enduring recordings.

albums.labelNotes: The labels on this copy are the red Columbia 'walking eye' (2-eye) design with the guarantee logo top and bottom and rim text reading '"COLUMBIA", MARCAS REG. PRINTED IN U.S.A.' - the standard late-1960s domestic Columbia stereo label used from roughly 1965 through the early 1970s, with no deep groove and a plain catalog-number layout (CS 9438, no 360 Sound banner, no orange label variant). This places the pressing in the original 1967 Columbia release window for this compilation rather than any later Columbia reissue (which would carry the orange label from the mid-1970s) or the modern Curb Records reissue (different catalog number and jacket). The front cover's 'Electronically Re-Channeled for Stereo' banner and matching XSM matrix prefixes confirm this is the true-stereo-rechannel pressing paired with the mono CL 2638 release noted on the back cover.
albums.fidelity: This is an electronically re-channeled 'fake stereo' pressing, explicitly labeled as such on the jacket, derived from mono session tapes rather than true multitrack stereo masters. Collectors on the forums generally regard Columbia's rechanneled stereo Armstrong LPs of this era as inferior to the original true mono pressings (CL 2638), which preserve the source fidelity without the phasey, artificially widened rechannel processing. Within this title's own history there is no audiophile reissue tier to compare against, so this stereo rechannel sits below the mono original but is the only stereo option Columbia issued for this specific compilation.
albums.generalNotes: 1967 Columbia CS 9438 stereo pressing, electronically re-channeled from mono sources as stated on the jacket. No later orange-label Columbia reissue markers or Curb Records reissue elements (different catalog number/jacket) are present, supporting an original-issue identification for this compilation.

albums.albumStory: Satchmo Sings gathered Louis Armstrong's vocal performances of contemporary pop, R&B, and country hits of the day, arranged for orchestra rather than his small combo, reflecting Decca's push to market Armstrong as a popular vocalist alongside his identity as a jazz trumpet giant. Armstrong had by the mid-1950s become one of the most beloved crossover entertainers in America, his gravelly voice as recognizable as his horn, and this collection - built from singles and studio dates rather than a single unified session - let Decca repackage his singing appeal for the LP market. The song choices, spanning Hank Williams' "Your Cheatin' Heart" to the doo-wop-era "Sincerely" and standards like "April In Portugal," show Armstrong's ability to make radically different material sound like his own through his phrasing and warmth. The album arrived amid a broader mid-1950s trend of jazz and swing-era stars cutting vocal pop albums for wider audiences, and it cemented Armstrong's commercial standing even as critics debated whether his singing sessions diluted his more serious jazz legacy. Its lasting importance lies less in any single arrangement than in documenting Armstrong the singer at the height of his popular fame, a persona that would culminate a few years later in his chart-topping vocal hits of the early 1960s.

albums.albumStory: Ambassador Satch documents Louis Armstrong and his All-Stars during their celebrated 1955 European tour, splicing live concert recordings from Amsterdam's Concertgebouw and a Milan theater with a handful of studio tracks cut in New York and Hollywood, all stitched together by producer George Avakian with dubbed audience noise to create the illusion of a single continuous concert. By the mid-1950s Armstrong had become one of America's most effective unofficial cultural emissaries abroad, and this album captures the personal warmth and instrumental command that made him beloved across the Continent even as his domestic image was sometimes reduced to that of a genial entertainer. The band heard here - Edmond Hall's clarinet, Trummy Young's trombone, Billy Kyle's piano, Arvell Shaw's bass and Barrett Deems' drums - was one of the most cohesive editions of the All-Stars, revisiting New Orleans-rooted repertoire like "Muskrat Ramble" and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band's "Tiger Rag" alongside standards such as "All of Me." The record stands as a touchstone of Armstrong's later career, reaffirming his stature as jazz's most charismatic ambassador at a moment when younger modernists were reshaping the music's direction. Critics have long praised the record's spirit and musicianship, and it remains regarded as one of the strongest documents of the touring All-Stars era.
albums.lpNotes: 1956 Columbia CL 840 mono, 6-eye deep-groove label with printed "NOT FOR SALE" promotional overprint - an original-era promotional pressing, not a later reissue.
albums.labelNotes: The labels photographed show the classic Columbia "6-eye" design: red print on white stock, six walking-eye Columbia logos ringing the perimeter, deep groove around the spindle, and "CL 840" printed at the bottom of each side beside the small "LP" trademark roundel. Both sides carry an overprinted "NOT FOR SALE" line above the side designation, in the same red ink and typeface as the rest of the label copy, indicating a Columbia promotional/DJ pressing rather than a stamped-over commercial label. This 6-eye design with deep groove was Columbia's standard label from the label's introduction (c. 1955) through the early 1960s, placing this pressing in the original mid-to-late-1950s manufacturing window rather than a later reissue; the printed (not stamped) NOT FOR SALE legend is consistent with a factory-run promotional variant of the same era, not a later re-set label.
albums.fidelity: This is a straightforward mono analog cut from Columbia's original 1956 masters, mixing live European concert tape (with dubbed audience sound) and 1956 studio sessions; there is no audiophile remaster of note for this specific mono LP beyond the later SACD/CD reissues. Collectors on the forums rate original 6-eye Columbia pressings of this era as solid if unspectacular sonically, dependent on shellac/vinyl quality of the era rather than any celebrated mastering engineer credit. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this deep-groove 6-eye promo pressing sits with the other original 1956 6-eye pressings at the top, ahead of later Columbia repress stampers, 1971 Hallmark UK reissue, and the modern digital CD/SACD remasters which offer improved clarity but lose the analog warmth of the original cut.

The matrix numbers (XLP37957-1A / XLP37958-1A) carry the earliest -1A stamper generation for this catalog number, consistent with an original-era pressing rather than a later Columbia repress.

albums.albumStory: In April 1961, producer Bob Thiele brought together two towering but rarely-paired giants of jazz - Louis Armstrong, the trumpet-and-vocal embodiment of New Orleans-rooted swing, and Duke Ellington, its most sophisticated composer-bandleader - for two days of recording at RCA's New York studio, with Ellington sitting in as pianist alongside Armstrong's working All-Stars (Trummy Young, Barney Bigard, Mort Herbert, Danny Barcelona). The pairing had been building since the two men's 1960 work together on the film and score of Paris Blues, and Thiele shepherded the idea past both men's famously overbooked managements into a brief, tightly-scheduled studio date. This first LP drew ten of the seventeen tracks recorded, virtually all Ellington compositions or co-compositions, letting Armstrong's warm horn and gravelly voice reinterpret staples such as "Mood Indigo," "Cotton Tail" and "Black And Tan Fantasy" as a tribute from one master to another. The record stands as the only studio meeting of these two founding fathers of jazz and has long been regarded by critics and historians as an essential, career-capping document for both men.
albums.lpNotes: Japanese Nippon Columbia-manufactured stereo pressing (SL-5120-RO), a later foreign license issue subordinate to the 1961 US Roulette original.
albums.labelNotes: The label seen here is a bright orange/yellow sunburst-ray design reading "ROULETTE / 33 1/3 RPM STEREO" at the top, catalogue number "SL-5120-RO" and matrix references "(RO-358-119)" / "(RO-358-120)" printed at left, with rim text stating the record was "MADE BY NIPPON COLUMBIA CO., LTD" and rights reserved to "ALBIEMA COLUMBIA CO., LTD" (a Japanese licensing credit). This sunburst design and Nippon Columbia manufacturing credit are consistent with the wave of Japanese-licensed reissues of American jazz catalogues (Blue Note, Roulette, etc.) that Nippon Columbia pressed and distributed domestically through the 1970s, well after the original 1961 US Roulette Birdland-series release (R/SR-52074, announced in Billboard 8/7/61) which used Roulette's own US label design. The ¥1,800 price sticker on the back cover confirms this is a Japanese domestic-market pressing rather than an export or US copy, and the SL-5120-RO catalogue prefix places it in a distinct Japanese numbering series unrelated to the US R/SR-52074 catalogue number, so it postdates and is subordinate to the American original in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: This is a Japanese Nippon Columbia stereo pressing rather than the original Roulette/RCA-cut American release; Nippon Columbia's jazz-reissue pressings of this era are generally clean and quiet but are cut from tape/dub sources rather than the original US mastering, so collectors on the forums typically rank the 1961 US Roulette stereo original above Japanese license pressings for openness and immediacy. Modern audiophile cuts - the Classic Records 200g LP and 45rpm box, and the Mobile Fidelity 2LP - are prized above both for mastering quality but are all now out of print. This copy sits below the US original and below the audiophile reissues in the fidelity hierarchy, valued mainly for its rarity as a Japanese-only variant.
albums.generalNotes: This is a Japanese pressing manufactured under license by Nippon Columbia (rim text "MADE BY NIPPON COLUMBIA CO., LTD"), catalogue SL-5120-RO with matrix references RO-358-119/RO-358-120, distinct from the original 1961 US Roulette Birdland-series release R/SR-52074. The sunburst-ray label design and Nippon Columbia credit place it as a later Japanese domestic license pressing rather than a first pressing; the ¥1,800 price sticker on the back cover corroborates a Japanese retail sale. No US "Printed in USA" or Roulette-house label elements are present, confirming this is not the American original.

albums.albumStory: Recorded for Roulette across two sessions on April 3 and 4, 1961 at RCA Victor's Studio A in New York, this material paired two of jazz's founding titans - Louis Armstrong, the trumpet virtuoso and singer who shaped the entire vocabulary of jazz improvisation, and Duke Ellington, the era's most consequential composer and bandleader - in a stripped-down small-group setting rather than Ellington's usual orchestra. Backing them were Armstrong's touring All Stars rhythm section, plus clarinetist Barney Bigard, a former longtime Ellingtonian who had since joined Armstrong's band, giving the date a genuine reunion flavor. The single marathon date yielded enough material for two LPs: 'Recording Together for the First Time' appeared first in 1961, and this second helping, 'The Great Reunion,' followed in 1963, built entirely around Ellington's own songbook - 'It Don't Mean A Thing,' 'Solitude,' 'I Got It Bad and That Ain't Good' and others - recast in Armstrong's husky, instantly recognizable phrasing. Critics and historians have long prized the encounter for its easy, unforced chemistry: Ellington's harmonic sophistication meeting Armstrong's blues-rooted swagger with neither artist compromising his own musical personality. The session stands as a late-career highlight for both men and remains one of the most beloved intergenerational summit meetings in jazz history, still cited today as a model of two giants meeting as equals.
albums.lpNotes: 1974 EMUS budget reissue (Roulette-family label) of the 1963 Roulette SR-52103 program - Bell Sound-mastered stereo pressing, not a first pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The label seen here is plain yellow with black text, the word 'EMUS' set in bold block capitals at the top, the title and artist credits below it, 'Produced by Bob Thiele' underneath, and 'STEREO / ES-12014' at lower left with speed and side at lower right - a simple, unadorned budget-label design with no deep groove and no Roulette branding. EMUS was founded in 1974 by Morris Levy as one of Roulette's budget reissue imprints, recycling masters from Roulette's catalog; ES-12014 reissues the 1963 Roulette SR-52103 program. The Bell Sound 'SE' etching in the runout points to a Bell Sound Studios (NYC) custom mastering job done for this reissue rather than a carry-over of the original Roulette lacquers, consistent with a mid-1970s repress rather than a first pressing.
albums.fidelity: The 'SE' etching after Bell Sound in the runout points to a Bell Sound Studios (NYC) custom mastering job commissioned for this EMUS reissue rather than a reuse of the original 1963 Roulette lacquers, which is typical of Roulette-family budget lines of the era. As a mid-1970s cut-rate repress, this pressing is generally regarded by collectors as sonically serviceable but a step below the original Roulette stereo pressing, and well below the later audiophile remasters - Classic Records' 200g cut and Mobile Fidelity's 'Original Master' edition - both mastered with greater care from better-generation sources. Within the album's overall fidelity hierarchy this EMUS pressing sits near the bottom: original Roulette > Classic Records 200g / MFSL audiophile reissues > later 180g reissues > this EMUS budget cut.
albums.generalNotes: This is the 1974 EMUS ES-12014 stereo reissue of Armstrong & Ellington's 1963 Roulette album, not the original Roulette pressing. EMUS was Morris Levy's Roulette-family budget imprint, and the plain yellow, unadorned label design with no Roulette branding matches EMUS's known 1970s house style. The runout shows a Bell Sound 'SE' mastering stamp, indicating a fresh cut made for this reissue rather than the original 1963 Roulette lacquers. Cover and vinyl are NM- in shrink/NM, consistent with a well-kept, unopened later pressing rather than a rare first issue.

albums.albumStory: Captured live at the American Jazz Festival in Newport, Rhode Island on July 5 and 6, 1956, this album pairs Louis Armstrong's touring All-Stars with Eddie Condon's Chicago-style Dixieland ensemble on the same bill, though the two leaders never actually share a bandstand on record. By 1956 Armstrong's All-Stars, with Trummy Young, Edmond Hall and Billy Kyle, were a well-drilled unit whose Newport appearances had already become annual events for producer George Avakian's Columbia documentation of the festival. Condon, the guitarist-impresario who had been a fixture of small-group Chicago and New York jazz since the 1920s, brought a rotating cast of veteran swing and Dixieland players including Wild Bill Davison and Bud Freeman. The album captures the informal, good-natured competitive spirit that characterized the Newport festival's early years, with each group running through its own signature repertoire of standards and blues. albums.lpNotes: 1956 Columbia CL 931 mono - 6-eye deep-groove label, runout suffixes -1B/-1D place it within the original pressing generation but not the earliest -1A stamper.
albums.labelNotes: Both side labels are the classic red Columbia "6-eye" design: white "COLUMBIA" arc logo at top, six small "eye" logos in black side panels (three per side, matching the deep-groove/6-eye Columbia standard used c.1955-1962), red field, black rim bands, and "NONBREAKABLE"/"MADE IN U.S.A." rim text with no ring-band slogan. The vinyl has a deep groove, consistent with early-to-mid Columbia 6-eye pressings before Columbia phased out deep groove circa 1958-59. The runout suffixes here (-1B and -1D) are later stamper generations than the earliest -1A/1A copies, so this is an early but not the very first stamper pressing within the same 6-eye deep-groove first-issue label design.
albums.fidelity: This is a mono live recording from 1956, mastered for Columbia's standard 6-eye era LP cutting rather than any audiophile process; sound quality reflects the limitations of remote festival recording of the period, with reasonable balance but limited depth compared to studio Columbia jazz dates. Collectors on the forums generally regard the original 6-eye mono pressing as the most authentic and best-sounding version, since no audiophile reissue (Mobile Fidelity, Analogue Productions, Classic Records, etc.) of this specific title exists. The only later variant is the 1994 CD box on Sony/Legacy, which offers cleaner surfaces but a different, remastered sound signature rather than a vinyl-cutting improvement over this LP.
albums.generalNotes: 1956 Columbia CL 931 mono, first-issue 6-eye deep-groove red label design. albums.albumStory: Mississippi-born and church-trained, Margie Joseph arrived at Stax's Volt imprint in 1970 after early sessions cut with Muscle Shoals players while she was still based in New Orleans, and this debut LP became her definitive introduction to soul audiences. Producers Fred Briggs and Darryl Carter, working as the Colsoul team, built the record around a striking reinterpretation of the Supremes' "Stop! In the Name of Love," stretching it into an extended, dramatically monologue-prefaced centerpiece that showcased Joseph's gospel-trained phrasing and improvisational daring. The remaining material blended fresh Stax-Memphis originals with Muscle Shoals-cut sides, giving the album a hybrid Southern-soul sound that sat between the grit of Memphis funk and the polish of Alabama session musicianship. Joseph's voice - flexible, melodic, and more restrained than the era's belters - distinguished her from contemporaries and helped establish her as an underappreciated but critically respected deep-soul singer. The album arrived at a pivotal moment for Stax, newly independent from Atlantic and reshaping its Volt subsidiary's identity, and it helped signal the label's continued vitality in the early 1970s soul marketplace. Though never a major commercial blockbuster, it has grown in stature among soul collectors and critics as a showcase for both Joseph's artistry and the fertile Stax/Muscle Shoals creative exchange of the period.
albums.lpNotes: Original US press (stereo, c. 1970) - Monarch yellow-bolt-label plant-error variant; VS-0157/VS-0158, Mastercraft marks, Δ15323/Δ15323-X.
albums.labelNotes: Both side labels show a bright yellow field with the black "VOLT RECORDS" wordmark and a single large freestanding black double-zigzag/bolt device beneath it, followed by the artist name, quoted album title, catalog number VOS-6012, STEREO, and side/matrix data (VS-0157/VS-0158) at upper right - no ring text or arc band is present. This bold yellow-and-black bolt design is Volt's earlier/mid-1960s Atlantic-distribution-era house style; by the time this LP was actually issued in the newly-independent post-1970 Stax/Volt era, the era-correct VOS-6000-series design had shifted to the dark-blue label with red bolt seen on most copies of this catalog number, including Terre Haute and standard Monarch pressings. Monarch's pressing plant used leftover stock of this older yellow-bolt label in error on some VOS-6000-series titles, and the printed matrices (VS-0157/VS-0158) with Mastercraft/Monarch stampers on this copy are consistent with that recognized plant-error variant rather than the standard contemporary blue-label pressing.
albums.fidelity: This is the original-era analog US cut, with Mastercraft metalwork and Monarch pressing. The cutting engineer initials on this yellow-label variant are typically read as HC (Howard Craft) on standard blue-label pressings; the runout etching on this copy reads HL, so that attribution remains probable rather than certain. Monarch's work here is competent but not audiophile-grade, yielding a warm, dense midrange and the somewhat compressed presentation typical of early-1970s Stax/Volt product; clean vinyl is especially important through the extended eight-minute "Stop! In the Name of Love." No standalone modern audiophile LP reissue exists for this title, and collectors on the forums have not settled a fidelity consensus for it, so a clean original US pressing (blue or yellow label) remains the sonic reference point; the 1993 CD twofer reissue is not a fidelity competitor to a well-preserved original vinyl copy.
albums.generalNotes: Original US Volt VOS-6012 stereo, pressed by Monarch, bearing the scarce older-style yellow-and-black double-bolt Volt label rather than the era-correct dark-blue/red-bolt design used on most copies of this title. This is identified by the yellow label design itself, the printed side matrices VS-0157 (Side One) and VS-0158 (Side Two), and the Mastercraft marks with Monarch Δ15323/Δ15323-X. The standard issue carries blue labels on both Terre Haute and Monarch pressings, confirming that this yellow-label copy is the deviant plant-error pressing. The album was first advertised/released in late 1970, though its chart run has led some to date it to 1971; it is not the 1972 "Phase II" follow-up, VOS-6016.

albums.albumStory: Recorded across three sessions in Hollywood in the summer of 1959, this is arranger-pianist Marty Paich's tribute to swing-era standards refracted through the tightly voiced, mid-sized big-band sound he had pioneered on his celebrated Mel Torme collaborations. Paich assembled a crack roster of West Coast studio and jazz players for the date, most notably altoist Art Pepper, on loan from another label, and vibraphonist Victor Feldman, also on loan, alongside trumpeter Jack Sheldon, pianist Russ Freeman and drummer Mel Lewis, giving the session an unusually strong solo bench for what was billed as a swing repertory record. The book leans heavily on Ellington, four of the eight tunes including a swinging instrumental take on the vocalese classic "Moanin'" and the Ellington-Strayhorn staples "Warm Valley" and "Cottontail", plus Cole Porter's "Love For Sale" and other standards, each reworked with Paich's harmonically adventurous, contrapuntal charts rather than played as straight repertory. The record arrived at the height of Paich's run as one of the era's most in-demand jazz arrangers, and it stands as a prime example of the West Coast cool school's application of modern arranging technique to older material. Critically it has endured as a favorite among cool-jazz collectors less for chart innovation alone than for the quality of the blowing Paich drew out of his soloists, with Pepper's turns singled out by later listeners as some of his best studio work outside his own leader dates. It remains a benchmark of late-1950s West Coast big-band jazz and a key entry in both Paich's and Pepper's discographies.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (stereo, 1959) - Warner Bros. gold shield deep-groove label, matrix S 38427/S 38428 R2.
albums.labelNotes: The labels on this pressing carry the gold/champagne Warner Bros. shield design: a single black-outlined, red-filled WB shield at 12 o'clock, no additional arc or color band beyond the plain WARNER BROS RECORDS / VITAPHONIC ... STEREO ... LONG PLAY rim wording, with the catalogue number WS 1349 and the matrix reference S 38427/S 38428 printed directly beneath it, and a deep groove ring on both sides. This gold-shield label was Warner's design from the label's 1958 launch through the early-to-mid 1960s, before it was reset to the later black corporate WB shield with color banding. That label design, the deep groove, and the early R2 matrix suffix place this pressing at the front of the WS 1349 stereo run, ahead of the later black-label stereo repress and well ahead of any Discovery/Trend or Japanese reissue, none of which share this label art or matrix.
albums.fidelity: This is an all-analog late-1950s Warner Bros. Hollywood cut, sourced directly from the original 1959 session tapes with no digital step in the chain; the deep-groove gold-label stamping and R2 matrix suffix indicate an early stamper generation rather than a worn late repress. Collectors on the forums rate original Warner Bros. jazz stereo pressings of this vintage as solid and punchy, if occasionally hard-edged in the trumpets typical of early Warner stereo engineering, with the mono pressing sometimes preferred by purists for a smoother blend of the horn section. There is no audiophile reissue of this title from the major reissue houses to compare against; the later Discovery reissue and Japanese pressings are several generations removed from the original lacquer and rank below this early-stamper stereo original in the fidelity hierarchy.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Warner Bros. WS 1349 stereo original first pressing. The gold/champagne shield label, deep groove on both sides, and the S 38427/S 38428 R2 matrix pair beneath the catalogue number place this within Warner's earliest stereo run for the title, ahead of the later black-label repress and well ahead of the Discovery/Trend and Japanese reissues, which carry entirely different matrices. No promo or club markings are present; this is a standard commercial stereo first issue.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in October 1976 at London's Palladium during a triumphant European tour, this live document caught Marvin Gaye newly free of the stage fright that had kept him largely off the road for years, performing with renewed confidence and showmanship. Three sides survey his career in revue form: recent material, then two extended medleys spanning his 1960s Motown hits and his early-70s message-music era, and a third medley of his classic duets with guest vocalist Florence Lyles standing in for Tammi Terrell and Diana Ross. The fourth side breaks format entirely with a new studio recording, "Got To Give It Up," a sparse, extended party jam Gaye built after Motown pushed him toward the disco era; it became one of the biggest hits of his career, topping pop, R&B and dance charts. Released in March 1977, the double album arrived at the commercial peak of Gaye's career, bridging the sensuality of Let's Get It On and I Want You with the raw confession of the forthcoming Here, My Dear, and it went on to double-platinum sales. Critics were unusually receptive to a live album of this scale, praising both the concert sides' polish and the audacity of closing out a live record with a full studio side. Decades later its legacy took an unexpected turn when "Got To Give It Up" became the centerpiece of the landmark "Blurred Lines" copyright litigation, reasserting the song's cultural footprint.
albums.lpNotes: Original US press (1977) - Tamla T7-352R2 brown/gold globe label; 'W' deadwax etch identifies a Wakefield Manufacturing (Phoenix) pressing.
albums.labelNotes: This copy shows the mid-to-late-1970s Tamla design: a brown upper panel with the gold Tamla globe logo in a cream box, a yellow lower field, and rim text reading "A Product of Motown Record Corp." This design superseded the earlier black "globe on map" Tamla label around 1975 and remained in use until Motown began folding artists onto the plain Motown label in the early 1980s. The mixed 1976/1977 copyright lines across the four sides track the October 1976 concert taping versus the later-finished studio side, and the T7-352R2 number with job numbers 2697-S through 2700-S matches the March 1977 first-issue run. This title was pressed concurrently by several contract plants (Monarch, Wakefield, Columbia/CTH, PRC) distinguished by runout suffixes; the etched 'W' on this copy points to Wakefield Manufacturing (Phoenix), one of the original-pressing plants rather than a later reissue.
albums.fidelity: Mastering is uncredited on the jacket and labels, as is typical for late-70s Motown product of this scale; this copy was pressed by Wakefield Manufacturing in Phoenix, a competent but not top-tier Motown contract plant compared with Columbia's or RCA's better facilities. The album is a heavily produced, sweetened live document overall, with the stripped-down studio cut of "Got To Give It Up" standing out as the sonic highlight of the set. No audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, Tone Poet or similar) has ever tackled this title, so original US pressings like this one remain the reference cut; the 2013 UMe/Motown reissue, sourced digitally, sits below any well-preserved original vinyl pressing regardless of plant.

albums.albumStory: Marvin Gaye Live! documents Gaye's return to the stage after years of self-imposed exile triggered by Tammi Terrell's 1967 onstage collapse and her subsequent death, an ordeal that left him gripped by stage fright and reluctant to tour. By the time of this concert he had reinvented himself as a studio auteur with What's Going On, Trouble Man and Let's Get It On, the latter becoming his biggest-selling album and making him Motown's top-selling artist during his lifetime, success that helped push him back onto a stage. He performed before more than 14,000 fans at the Oakland Coliseum Arena on January 4, 1974, reportedly sending his brother out first to gauge the crowd's reception. The set leaned into his 1970s persona with Trouble Man, Inner City Blues, Distant Lover, Let's Get It On and What's Going On, while his 1960s Motown hits were compressed into a self-deprecatingly titled, up-tempo "Fossil Medley", and he premiered the new song "Jan", written for his girlfriend Janis Hunter. The slowed, smoldering rendition of "Distant Lover" became the night's breakout moment and a hit single, remaining his onstage signature for years afterward. Backed by a 40-piece orchestra of Los Angeles studio musicians under arranger/conductor Gene Page, the performance translated his intimate, studio-crafted 1970s sound into a large-scale arena seduction, and the resulting album stands as a defining artifact of 1970s live soul and a beloved chapter in Gaye's career.
