albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the mid-1970s Tamla design: cream/tan field, maroon upper band, boxed Motown globe logo over the TAMLA wordmark, "© 1974 MOTOWN RECORD CORPORATION / TRADEMARK MOTOWN RECORD CORPORATION" printed above the title, and "A PRODUCT OF MOTOWN RECORD CORP." on the bottom rim - the standard Tamla design used from the early 1970s through mid-decade, matching the June 1974 first issue. The runouts (T6-333S1-D5RS-7651-1 O3B / -7652-2 O3B) correspond to a US original stamper configuration; a separate pressing of this same release was run at the RCA Indianapolis plant and carries an explicit "I" stamp. The exact plant for this copy (Hollywood-area vs. RCA Indianapolis) is not identified from the runout etching alone. Either way, the die-cut inner gatefold and 1974 Motown copyright text on the jacket firmly place this copy within the original first-issue print run rather than any later Motown reissue.
albums.fidelity: This is a Motown in-house cut of a Wally Heider live remote recording, mixed at Motown's Hitsville U.S.A. studios and lacquer-cut at RCA Studios Hollywood; the sound is typical mid-70s Motown - warm and midrange-forward, with horns and strings somewhat congested and arena ambience compressed, so the ceiling is set by the tape and mix rather than by any particular stamper. The O3B stampers on this copy are mid-run rather than the very first lacquers, but original 1974 US Tamla pressings are generally quiet and well-manufactured, and collectors on the forums favor these originals over the thinner 1980s Motown represses. There is no dedicated audiophile reissue program (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) for this title comparable to treatments given What's Going On or Let's Get It On, so a clean original US Tamla pressing like this one sits at or near the top of the album's realistic fidelity hierarchy.

albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York in June 1958, Legrand Jazz paired the young French composer-arranger Michel Legrand with an all-star cast of American jazzmen - including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Bill Evans, Ben Webster and Art Farmer - to reinterpret jazz standards spanning Fats Waller, Django Reinhardt, Dizzy Gillespie, Jelly Roll Morton, Duke Ellington and Bix Beiderbecke. Legrand, already an established pop arranger in France, had fallen in love with American jazz and used the sessions to fuse his European harmonic sophistication with the swing and blues vocabulary of his heroes, assembling several different large-ensemble lineups across the dates to suit each arrangement's mood. The album is something of an anomaly in Miles Davis's discography, a sideman appearance on someone else's date during the same period he was shaping Milestones and preparing for Kind of Blue, and it captures Coltrane and Evans together on record months before their more celebrated pairing on Kind of Blue. For Legrand the record stands as a rare mainstream American jazz statement before he turned decisively toward the film-scoring career that would make him internationally famous. Critics have long praised the record's inventive, occasionally dense big-band charts and its unusual blending of European classical color with hot American jazz repertoire, and it remains a valued curiosity for the rare glimpse it offers of Davis, Coltrane and Evans as sidemen in someone else's ambitious arranging vision.
albums.lpNotes: 1958 US Columbia six-eye mono promo pressing - white/red "Demonstration - Not For Sale" label, deep groove, matrix XLP 44188-1F/44189-1D.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the white-field, red-print six-eye Columbia label with "DEMONSTRATION" and "NOT FOR SALE" printed directly into the label design, plus a flat deep-groove ring on both sides - hallmarks of a genuine 1958 Columbia promotional pressing rather than a later stock or reissue copy. Columbia's six-eye label design ran roughly 1955 into the early 1960s before being replaced by the black "Guaranteed High Fidelity" label and later the orange label, so the six-eye placement alone dates this pressing to the 1958-61 window. The deep groove and matrix suffixes (XLP 44188-1F / 44189-1D) are consistent with an early stamper generation cut close to the original lacquers, placing this copy at or very near the front of the CL 1250 mono pressing hierarchy - ahead of the later "CBS"-logo six-eye reissue (1961-62) which reused the same stampers, and well ahead of the black-label and orange-label reissues that followed.
albums.fidelity: Mono mix cut directly from the 1958 Columbia 30th Street Studio session tapes; Columbia's uncredited in-house engineering team of the period is generally well regarded for natural, warm big-band sound on six-eye era pressings. Collectors on the forums debate whether some Legrand Jazz mono copies are true mono or fold-downs, but original six-eye mono pressings like this one are considered the most authentic and best-sounding version, ahead of any later stereo remix or reissue. No audiophile reissue (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) of this specific title exists; modern colored-vinyl European reissues (c. 2017-2022) are widely regarded as sonically inferior to an original six-eye pressing.
albums.generalNotes: 1958 Columbia CL 1250 mono - a genuine promotional first pressing. The white-field six-eye label reads "DEMONSTRATION" and "NOT FOR SALE" as part of the printed label design (not a stamp), and both sides show the flat deep-groove ring, consistent with Columbia's 1958-era mono promo stock. Matrix suffixes 1F/1D indicate an early-to-mid stamper generation cut from the original lacquers rather than a later reissue. This is not the later "CBS"-logo six-eye repress (1961-62), which reused the same stampers but added CBS branding to the label.

albums.title: A Tribute To Jack Johnson
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Herbie Hancock (keyboards/organ, courtesy of Warner Bros. Records), John McLaughlin (guitar), Steve Grossman (soprano saxophone), Billy Cobham (drums), Michael Henderson (Fender bass); additional session personnel compiled into the LP include Chick Corea (electric piano), Dave Holland (electric bass), Jack DeJohnette (drums), Sonny Sharrock (guitar) and Bennie Maupin (bass clarinet), with Brock Peters as the voice of Jack Johnson.
sides: 1. Right Off
1. Yesternow
albums.albumStory: Recorded in early 1970 as the soundtrack to William Cayton's documentary about heavyweight boxing champion Jack Johnson, this album finds Miles Davis pushing the electric, rock-inflected direction he had opened on Bitches Brew even further toward raw, riff-based jamming. The centerpiece, 'Right Off', reportedly grew out of an impromptu studio warm-up: guitarist John McLaughlin began vamping while waiting for Davis, and was quickly joined by bassist Michael Henderson and drummer Billy Cobham, prompting Davis to walk in and improvise trumpet lines over the groove that producer Teo Macero then edited into a side-long piece. 'Yesternow' was assembled by Macero from multiple sessions and musicians, splicing together a slow-burning, bass-riff-driven mood piece that closes with dialogue from the film. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, following his full turn to electric jazz-rock fusion, and it stands as one of the most focused and rock-influenced statements of that period, prized by many listeners for its visceral, funk-driven energy. Though a modest commercial performer on release, it has since come to be regarded by critics and musicians as a high point of the jazz-fusion era and an essential entry in Davis's 1970s electric catalog, admired for the interplay of McLaughlin's guitar with Henderson and Cobham's rhythm section.
albums.lpNotes: Early US pressing (stereo, c.1971) - Columbia red label, KC 30455 catalog, Pitman NJ plant stamp in the matrix.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the plain red Columbia label with orange 'COLUMBIA' logotype repeating around the rim and the small two-eye logo box, with no white '360 Sound Stereo' overprint - a design Columbia used circa 1970-72 immediately before that wording was added to the same red livery. The catalog number is printed as KC 30455 on both labels and jacket (spine/back), the original Columbia numbering used before the company's mid-1970s renumbering to the PC prefix. Later copies carry a PC sticker over the printed KC number or a '360 Sound Stereo' white-text label, both markers of a later print run. The matrix suffixes (MAL-30455-1A, MBL-30455-1F) with the 'P' code point to Columbia's Pitman, NJ plant, consistent with early-1970s US manufacturing for this catalog block. Taken together (KC prefix, plain red/orange label lacking 360 Sound text, Pitman stamp, low lacquer-cut letter suffixes) this sits at or very near the front of the domestic US pressing run rather than a mid-70s PC-era repress or Canadian pressing.
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Stan Tonkel and produced/edited by Teo Macero from the original 1970 Columbia studio masters; this US Pitman pressing represents Columbia's standard early-1970s cutting rather than an audiophile mastering, with quality generally solid but variable by copy, as was typical of Columbia's high-volume plants of the era. Collectors on the forums generally regard original Columbia pressings of this title as punchy but not particularly quiet or deep-bass extended compared to modern remasters. The 2016 Mobile Fidelity MFSL 1-440 180g reissue is widely considered the sonic high-water mark for the album, offering greater clarity, quieter surfaces and tighter bass than any vintage Columbia pressing, including this one. Within the vintage-pressing tier, an early KC-prefix red-label copy like this one is regarded as among the more desirable original variants, ranking above later PC-era reissues and Canadian pressings but below the MFSL and other modern audiophile cuts.
albums.generalNotes: This is an early domestic US Columbia pressing rather than a later PC-era repress. The KC 30455 catalog prefix (versus the later PC 30455 renumbering used from roughly 1973 onward, sometimes applied via sticker over the original KC print) and the plain orange-on-red Columbia label without the '360 Sound Stereo' overprint both point to a 1971-72 manufacturing window. The matrix codes (MAL-30455-1A, MBL-30455-1F) with the 'P' suffix indicate Columbia's Pitman, New Jersey pressing plant, consistent with early US stock for this title.

albums.title: Bags' Groove
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Sonny Rollins (tenor sax, side 2), Milt Jackson (vibraphone, side 1), Thelonious Monk (piano, side 1), Horace Silver (piano, side 2), Percy Heath (bass), Kenny Clarke (drums)
sides:
1. Bags' Groove (take 1)
2. Bags' Groove (take 2)

1. Airegin
2. Oleo
3. But Not for Me (take 2)
4. Doxy
5. But Not for Me (take 1)
albums.albumStory: Bags' Groove compiles two Miles Davis sessions from 1954: a December 24 date with vibraphonist Milt Jackson, pianist Thelonious Monk, Percy Heath and Kenny Clarke, and an earlier June 29 session featuring Sonny Rollins on tenor and Horace Silver on piano. The December date has become one of the most mythologized sessions in jazz history, fueled by later, partly embellished accounts of friction between Davis and Monk over how the pianist should comp behind the trumpeter's solos. Whatever the truth of that tension, the two contrasting takes of Jackson's title tune capture the loose, blues-drenched interplay that defined small-group jazz of the era. The June session, essentially an early Rollins showcase, produced enduring Rollins originals including Oleo, Airegin and Doxy alongside two takes of the Gershwins' But Not for Me. The album arrives at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, just before he assembled his classic quintet with John Coltrane and signed with Columbia, and it stands as a landmark documenting both Davis's maturing conception and Rollins's emergence as a major composer-improviser. It is widely regarded as one of the essential hard bop recordings of the 1950s, prized for its blend of blues feeling, harmonic sophistication, and unresolved creative tension that has fascinated critics and musicians for decades.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1957) - Prestige yellow/black label, 446 W. 50th St. NYC address, deep groove, hand-etched RVG in the runout.
albums.labelNotes: The label design is the classic Prestige yellow-and-black design with the swirl and star graphics, reading "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. • 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." around the rim, with pronounced deep groove on both sides. This 446 W. 50th St. NYC address was used from the label's founding through the 1958 relocation to Bergenfield, New Jersey, after which the address text and deep groove disappeared from the labels. The hand-etched "RVG" plus "AB" (Abbey Record Manufacturing) suffix in the runouts is consistent with Prestige's earliest custom-pressed runs of this catalog number. This combination of address, deep groove and runout etching places this copy squarely as a first-pressing example, ahead of the Bergenfield-address second pressing and all later reissues in the hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Mastered from Rudy Van Gelder's original Hackensack tapes and lacquers, with his hand-etched RVG stamp confirming a Van Gelder-cut original rather than a later re-cut. Collectors on the forums generally regard these mid-1950s Prestige/Van Gelder mono originals as warm but narrow-band by modern standards, a function of the era's mastering chain rather than pressing quality, with Abbey's pressings considered solid if unspectacular. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this RVG/deep-groove 446 W. 50th St. original sits at the top for vintage collectors, ahead of the later Bergenfield-address repress, the 1960s-70s blue-label reissues, and the OJC reissue. The more recent Analogue Productions/Craft audiophile remaster from the original tapes is generally rated the most refined-sounding cut but is prized for surface quiet and extended top end rather than vintage authenticity.
albums.generalNotes: 1957 Prestige PRLP 7109 mono - original first pressing. The 446 W. 50th St. NYC label address (pre-1958 Bergenfield move) combined with deep-groove labels and hand-etched RVG runouts (PRLP-7109-A/B RVG A AB) is the canonical marker of this variant. The "AB" suffix confirms Abbey Record Manufacturing as the pressing plant, consistent with Prestige's own custom pressing arrangement of the period. VG+ vinyl grade with deep groove intact supports the first-pressing attribution.

albums.albumStory: Birth of the Cool compiles twelve sides Miles Davis recorded with a specially assembled nine-piece band across three 1949-1950 New York sessions, growing out of a brief but pivotal engagement the group had played at the Royal Roost in 1948. Davis conceived the project with close collaborators Gil Evans and Gerry Mulligan, drawing on writing contributions from John Lewis, John Carisi and George Wallington, and on the unusual instrumentation of French horn and tuba to create softer, more arranged ensemble textures than the prevailing bebop idiom. Coming immediately after Davis stepped out from Charlie Parker's quintet, the sessions announced him as a bandleader and conceptual arranger rather than simply a virtuoso soloist, a role he would return to repeatedly across his career. Though the original singles sold modestly on release, the music's restrained tempos, chamber-like counterpoint and unusual voicings anticipated the cool and West Coast jazz movements that flourished in the years before Capitol finally compiled the sides as this LP. The record is now regarded as one of the most influential documents in jazz history, foundational to cool jazz and an early example of "third stream" thinking that blended jazz with classical arranging sensibilities. Its collaborative writing and unusual sonic palette shaped generations of arrangers and small-group composers, and it remains central to Miles Davis's legacy as an artist whose impact often came as much through concept, personnel and arranging as through his trumpet playing.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1957) - Capitol turquoise dome-logo label, plain 'Long Playing' text, no anvil stamper mark, matrix T1-762-B2 #2 / T2-762-D1.
albums.labelNotes: This copy shows the early turquoise Capitol label with the large white "dome" (Capitol building) logo centered at top and the plain "LONG PLAYING" legend at bottom of both side labels, with no "High Fidelity" suffix text and rim text reading "MANUFACTURED BY CAPITOL RECORDS, INC. \u2022 HOLLYWOOD, CALIFORNIA \u2022 U.S.A." This large dome-logo turquoise design with plain "Long Playing" wording (rather than "Long Playing * High Fidelity") and no Scranton anvil symbol in the runout is the first-pressing configuration for T-762, made shortly after the album's original 1957 release; the near-identical label but with "Long Playing * High Fidelity" and a Scranton anvil stamper mark constitutes the second pressing. The plain wording, the absence of the anvil mark, and the Hollywood, California manufacturing text place this as a first-issue-window US pressing rather than a Scranton, export, or later colorband/reissue copy.
albums.fidelity: Mono mastering drawn from the original 1949-50 session tapes, cut for Capitol's 1957 LP compilation; the sound is inherently limited by the vintage 10-inch-era source rather than by this cutting itself. Collectors on the forums generally rate the early no-anvil turquoise-label Capitol pressings as warmer and more natural than the later black-colorband reissues or the 1971 expanded 'Complete Birth of the Cool' compilation, which some find brighter and thinner sounding. This early turquoise, plain-'Long Playing', no-anvil pressing sits at or near the top of the vintage mono fidelity hierarchy for T-762, ranking above the Scranton-anvil second pressing, the colorband reissue, Pathe Marconi European pressings, and the expanded Capitol Jazz Classics/Complete compilations, while modern audiophile reissues (where they exist) trade some of this vintage warmth for quieter surfaces.

albums.title: Bitches Brew
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Wayne Shorter (soprano sax), Bennie Maupin (bass clarinet), Joe Zawinul (electric piano), Chick Corea (electric piano), Larry Young (electric piano), John McLaughlin (electric guitar), Dave Holland (bass), Harvey Brooks (electric bass guitar), Jack DeJohnette (drums), Lenny White (drums), Don Alias (drums, congas), Jim Riley aka Jumma Santos (percussion, shaker)
sides: 1. Pharaoh's Dance - J. Zawinul
1. Bitches Brew - M. Davis

1. Spanish Key - M. Davis
2. John McLaughlin - M. Davis

1. Miles Runs the Voodoo Down - M. Davis
2. Sanctuary - W. Shorter
albums.albumStory: Recorded over three days in August 1969 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio, Bitches Brew marked Miles Davis's decisive commitment to electric, rock- and funk-inflected jazz after the tentative steps of In a Silent Way. Davis assembled a sprawling ensemble of overlapping electric keyboards, electric bass and guitar, multiple drummers and percussionists, and Bennie Maupin's bass clarinet, then worked with producer Teo Macero to splice, loop, and layer the freewheeling studio jams into the album's dense, hypnotic long-form pieces. Arriving as Davis, already a towering figure across bebop, cool, hard bop, and modal jazz, sought to reach a younger rock audience, the record's uncompromising sound alienated segments of the traditional jazz establishment even as it became a commercial breakthrough unprecedented for a Davis jazz release. Anchored by the sprawling, cyclical groove of the title track, it is now regarded as the founding document of jazz-fusion, reshaping the genre's possibilities for the following decade. Critically divisive on release, its influence proved lasting and profound, paving the way for Davis's own subsequent electric period and for a generation of fusion musicians who followed in its wake.
albums.lpNotes: 1970 US Columbia PG26 stereo, red label with repeating orange rim text (post two-eye design), Shorter-only Sanctuary credit, mixed Santa Maria/Terre Haute pressing - a second-wave 1970 pressing, not the original two-eye first press.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show Columbia's continuous repeating rim design - 'COLUMBIA' text alternating with a small diamond-framed eye icon runs all the way around the red field, rather than the earlier design with only two large CBS eye logos fixed at 9 and 3 o'clock. Columbia introduced this repeating-rim-text red label around July 1970, superseding the original two-eye label used on the true first-pressing run from March-June 1970, and it was itself later replaced by a plain solid-orange label around 1972. Side 4 credits 'Sanctuary' to W. Shorter alone; the initial dual Davis/Shorter mis-credit found on early two-eye copies was corrected before this label design appeared. This places the pressing in Columbia's second major 1970 label-design wave - a genuine 1970 US pressing, but not the more collectible earliest two-eye first press.
albums.fidelity: Original 1970 Columbia pressings were assembled under Teo Macero's supervision without a separate mastering-engineer credit on the disc; quality varies by plant, and Santa Maria and Terre Haute pressings of this era are rated by collectors on the forums as solid, warm, dynamic vintage cuts, though somewhat less consistently quiet than the best Pitman copies. This mixed Santa Maria/Terre Haute, rim-text-label example sits below the rarer two-eye first pressings in the collector hierarchy but above later 1970s solid-orange-label represses in punch and perceived dynamics. Modern audiophile reissues (Mobile Fidelity, Music On Vinyl, and other 180g remasters) offer quieter surfaces and extended low end but are valued by some collectors more for consistency than for matching the analog immediacy of a good original pressing.
albums.generalNotes: This is not a two-eye pressing: the label carries the continuous repeating orange 'COLUMBIA' rim text with small eye icons that Columbia adopted from around July 1970 onward, replacing the original two-eye (two large CBS logos at 9/3 o'clock) design used on the true first pressings. Sanctuary is already correctly credited to W. Shorter alone, consistent with this later label state. Runout etchings show Santa Maria (S) plant markings on sides 1-3 and Terre Haute (T) on side 4, a normal mixed-plant setup for Columbia's high-volume 1970 manufacturing of this title. Net verdict: a genuine 1970 US original release, but from the second label-design generation rather than the more collectible two-eye first pressing.

sides:

albums.albumStory: Blue Haze compiles three separate Prestige sessions Miles Davis led in 1953-54, a period when heroin addiction had made him, in Ira Gitler's contemporaneous phrase, close to jazz's "forgotten man of 1955." The earliest material, a May 1953 quartet date with John Lewis, Percy Heath and Max Roach, is joined by a March 1954 session featuring Horace Silver and Art Blakey and an April 1954 quintet date with alto saxophonist Davey Schildkraut that produced the album's most celebrated track, "I'll Remember April." Musically the record captures Davis honing the lyrical, harmonically searching trumpet voice that would soon anchor hard bop, moving through standards like "That Ole Devil Moon" and "When Lights Are Low" alongside originals such as "Tune Up," "Miles Ahead," and the brooding title cut "Blue Haze," co-credited to bassist-composer Charles Mingus. The sessions predate Davis's galvanizing comeback appearance at the 1955 Newport Jazz Festival, so the album effectively documents raw talent critics had begun to overlook amid his personal struggles. It is prized less as a unified artistic statement than as an essential window into Davis's early-to-mid-1950s Prestige period, pairing him with musicians - Silver and Blakey, Lewis and Roach - who would become architects of the emerging hard-bop idiom. Decades on, Blue Haze remains a steady fixture in critical surveys of Davis's formative Prestige years, valued for capturing the trumpeter mid-transformation, not long before his move to Columbia Records would redefine modern jazz.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1956) - Prestige yellow/black fireworks label, 446 W. 50th St. NYC address, "HI FI" text, deep groove; hand-etched RVG in the deadwax with AB/1 stamper codes.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the yellow-and-black "fireworks" Prestige label with the "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. \u2022 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." address and abbreviated "HI FI" legend, with a deep groove stamped into the label field - the earliest 12-inch Prestige label design, used while the company's office was on West 50th Street in Manhattan. Prestige relocated to Bergenfield, New Jersey in 1958, after which the same fireworks artwork was reprinted in a slightly different "egg-yolk" yellow with the Bergenfield address and fuller "HIGH FIDELITY" wording, marking the second-pressing label; that later label also generally lacks the deep groove. The NYC address, "HI FI" abbreviation, and deep groove together place this copy in the first Prestige pressing run following the LP's 1956 release, itself a repackaging of the 1954 10-inch Prestige 161. The hand-etched "RVG" plus machine-stamped "AB"/"1" stamper codes in the deadwax are consistent with Van Gelder-cut lacquers from this earliest pressing era.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his Hackensack studio tapes, this deep-groove NYC-label pressing represents the earliest and most sought-after cut of Blue Haze, made when Van Gelder's lacquers were pressed close to the source without intervening tape generations. Collectors on the forums generally regard these mid-1950s Van Gelder-mastered Prestige originals as warmer and more immediate than later Bergenfield-era repressings, though the mono masters can sound somewhat boxy by modern standards, reflecting 1953-54 tape and small-room recording limitations rather than the cutting itself. There is no audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Music Matters, etc.) specifically for Blue Haze, so within its own reissue lineage this NYC first pressing sits at the top, followed by the 1958 Bergenfield second pressing, and further below by 1960s Prestige/Fantasy reprints and later OJC reissues, which use further-generation tape masters and are generally considered sonically inferior.
albums.generalNotes: This is the original 1956 Prestige PRLP 7054 mono first pressing. The yellow/black fireworks label reads "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." with "HI FI" (not the later "HIGH FIDELITY"), and the vinyl carries a deep groove, distinguishing this NYC-era issue from the 1958 Bergenfield, NJ second pressing. The deadwax bears a hand-etched RVG with AB and 1 machine-stamped codes, marking Van Gelder-cut lacquers from this first-pressing run; the record was pressed by Abbey Record Manufacturing Co. for Prestige. None of the later label variant elements - Bergenfield address, egg-yolk yellow, non-deep-groove pressing - appear on this copy.

albums.title: Blue Moods
albums.countryOfOrigin: Denmark (licensed pressing of the US Debut master, distributed by Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S)
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Britt Woodman (trombone), Teddy Charles (vibraphone, credited on label as "percussion"), Charles Mingus (bass), Elvin Jones (drums)
sides:
1. Nature Boy (Eden Ahbez)
2. Alone Together (Dietz - Schwartz)

3. There's No You (Adair - Hopper - Durgom)
4. Easy Living (Robin - Rainger)
albums.albumStory: Blue Moods was recorded on July 9, 1955, at Van Gelder Studio in Hackensack, New Jersey, for Charles Mingus and Max Roach's fiercely independent, artist-owned Debut Records, cut as Miles Davis was climbing back from the personal low point of his heroin years toward the triumphant Prestige and Columbia periods that followed within months. Rather than assembling a conventional hard-bop unit, Mingus paired Davis with an unusual chamber-jazz lineup built around Teddy Charles's vibraphone and Britt Woodman's trombone, with Mingus himself on bass and a young Elvin Jones on drums, producing a spare, unhurried session built on standards plus Mingus's own arrangement of "Alone Together" (the remaining tracks were arranged by Charles). The album's brevity - just four tunes across a lean twenty-seven minutes - and its moody, unhurried restraint anticipated the cool, spacious aesthetic Davis would refine within a few years on Kind of Blue, making it a small but telling document of Davis mid-transformation. Davis reportedly resented the unconventional instrumentation Mingus assigned him, and the resulting session captures an uneasy but fruitful tension between a leader eager to move forward and a co-op label pursuing its own experimental agenda. Blue Moods has long been regarded by historians less as a commercial landmark than as a fascinating way-station in Davis's stylistic evolution, and it remains a significant artifact of the short-lived but historically important Mingus-Roach Debut label. Critical assessment has generally been favorable if modest, with the album prized chiefly by collectors of Davis's complete discography and of the Debut catalogue rather than ranked among his major statements.
albums.lpNotes: Danish Debut pressing (c. 1957-early 1960s) - grey "debut" label with "MADE IN DENMARK" rim text, licensed by Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S/Brande Boghandel; stamped DEB-120-A/DEB-120-B matrices, not the 1955 US first pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The grey Debut label carries the star-topped script "debut" logo and small "33 1/3 rpm LONGPLAY" banner, with "MADE IN DENMARK" arced at the top rim in place of the New York street address printed on the 1955 US original grey label. In 1957 the Brande Boghandel bookshop, working with Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S, secured rights to press the American Debut catalogue for the Scandinavian market, retaining the original US catalogue number (DEB 120) and cover artwork. That places this copy in the post-1957 Danish licensed pressing run - later than the true 1955 US first pressing but predating Debut's absorption into the Fantasy reissue program (1962) and the later French and OJC reissue generations. The stamped (rather than etched) DEB-120-A/DEB-120-B matrix format is consistent with an early-generation Danish plate rather than a later re-cut.
albums.fidelity: The back cover documents the original 1955 mastering approach: cut at 160 lines per inch instead of the usual 210-260, deliberately widening and deepening the grooves to allow greater bass extension and level - a hallmark of the Debut/Mingus-supervised Van Gelder cutting rather than a later remaster. This Danish pressing reproduces that mastering philosophy via a European-cut lacquer derived from the US plates/tape rather than the original US metal parts, so fidelity is generally regarded by collectors as respectable but a step below a clean US first pressing pressed directly from Van Gelder's original masters. Collectors on the forums favor the original 1955 US Debut pressing or the 1962 Fantasy red-vinyl reissue for the most faithful, full-bodied transfer, with the Danish pressing occupying a middle tier and the later French fake-stereo and OJC reissues ranked lowest in the overall fidelity hierarchy. Surface quality on Danish Debut pressings varies by copy.
albums.generalNotes: This is a Danish licensed Debut pressing of DEB-120, not the 1955 US first pressing, produced under the Brande Boghandel/Skandinavisk Grammofon A/S arrangement that began in 1957. The "MADE IN DENMARK" rim text on an otherwise US-style grey Debut label, paired with stamped (not later fake-stereo etched) DEB-120-A/B matrices, places this within the early Danish run rather than the 1960s French or US reissue lines. Cover and label copy reproduce the original 1955 back-cover text and mastering notes verbatim, indicating the Danish pressing used plates derived from the US artwork and liner notes rather than a redesigned Scandinavian issue. No runout photo was supplied, so stamper/plant-level confirmation beyond the label design itself is not possible.

albums.title: Decoy
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, synthesizer), John Scofield (guitar), Branford Marsalis (soprano saxophone), Bill Evans (soprano/tenor sax, flute, electric piano), Robert Irving III (synthesizer, electric drum programming), Darryl 'The Munch' Jones (electric bass), Al Foster (drums), Mino Cinelu (percussion), Gil Evans (arranger on 'That's Right')
sides:
1. Decoy
2. Robot 415
3. Code M.D.
4. Freaky Deaky

1. What It Is
2. That's Right
3. That's What Happened
albums.albumStory: Decoy, released in June 1984, captures Miles Davis deep into his 1980s electric comeback following his return from retirement with The Man with the Horn and We Want Miles. The album blends dense, moody electro-funk grooves largely shaped with young keyboardist Robert Irving III alongside more open, guitar-driven material co-written with John Scofield, who was becoming an increasingly important foil in Davis's working band. Two tracks were captured live at the 1983 Montreal jazz festival, giving the record a mix of tightly produced studio funk and looser stage improvisation, while 'That's Right' features an arrangement by longtime collaborator Gil Evans, tying the record back to one of Davis's most significant artistic partnerships. Branford Marsalis and Bill Evans trade soprano saxophone duties on the album, underlining Davis's continued interest in showcasing new talent even as he leaned harder into synthesizers and programmed drums. Sitting between the more polished Star People and the pop-facing You're Under Arrest, Decoy is often viewed by critics as a transitional, moodier entry in Davis's 1980s catalog, and it earned a Grammy nomination for Best Jazz Fusion Performance. Its cool, brooding atmosphere and rhythm-forward writing helped cement the template Davis continued exploring through the rest of the decade, making it a key document of his evolution from acoustic hard bop pioneer to electric innovator.
albums.lpNotes: 1984 US Columbia FC 38991 original pressing - red 'walking eye' label, Masterdisk-cut AL/BL-38991-1B lacquers, gatefold jacket.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the standard 1984 red Columbia 'walking eye' label with catalog number FC 38991 and AL/BL-38991 matrix prefixes typical of Columbia's early-1980s in-house pressing scheme, under which titles were simultaneously stamped from Masterdisk lacquers at multiple CBS-owned plants (Pitman NJ, Terre Haute IN, Carrollton GA, Santa Maria CA) with differing stamper suffix letters. The -1B suffix on both sides places this among the earlier stamper generations cut shortly after the album's June 1984 release, though the multi-plant simultaneous release model makes precise plant identification from the matrix alone unreliable without a visible etched plant symbol. Columbia's 'walking eye' red label design was standard for the label throughout the late 1970s into the mid-1980s, so the label art itself only confirms the general era, not a specific pressing run. There is no meaningful first-pressing premium structure for this title as with rarer jazz LPs - all early-80s domestic Columbia pressings of Decoy trade in a narrow, low price band regardless of exact stamper letter.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Bob Ludwig at Masterdisk from the original 1984 mix; this era of Columbia pressings is generally well regarded for a clean, punchy cut of Davis's synth-heavy 1980s productions, though the studio mix itself (dense synths, programmed drums) limits ultimate sonic transparency compared to his acoustic-era Columbia LPs. Collectors on the forums generally treat the various early-80s domestic Columbia stampers (-1A through -1E) as sonically similar, with no consensus 'best' stamper commanding a premium. There is no audiophile reissue series (Analogue Productions, Mobile Fidelity, etc.) for Decoy, so this original Masterdisk-cut Columbia pressing remains the best commercially available vinyl fidelity reference for the album, ahead of later Sony/Legacy CD remasters for tonal warmth if not ultimate noise floor.
albums.generalNotes: 1984 Columbia FC 38991 - standard domestic US first-issue pressing. Red 'walking eye' Columbia labels with matching AL-38991-1B / BL-38991-1B Masterdisk matrix numbers on both sides confirm an early-stamper US pressing from Columbia's multi-plant simultaneous release run for this title. No club-edition text, promo markings, or foreign rim text are present, indicating a standard retail US copy rather than a Columbia House or export pressing. Barcode and copyright date (1984 CBS Inc.) on the jacket are consistent with a first-year pressing.

albums.title: E.S.P.
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Wayne Shorter (tenor sax), Herbie Hancock (piano), Ron Carter (bass), Tony Williams (drums)
sides:
1. E.S.P.
2. Eighty-One
3. Little One
4. R.J.

1. Agitation
2. Iris
3. Mood
albums.albumStory: Recorded in Los Angeles in January 1965, E.S.P. documents the studio debut of Miles Davis's celebrated "Second Great Quintet" - Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, and Tony Williams - the first time this exact lineup appeared together on record following Shorter's arrival to complete the group. Almost the entire program consists of new originals contributed by the bandmembers themselves rather than standards, signaling a deliberate turn toward a freer, more abstract compositional and harmonic language. The album arrived at a pivotal juncture in Davis's career, following his mid-1960s live work and preceding the increasingly exploratory studio albums (Miles Smiles, Nefertiti, Sorcerer) that would follow through 1968. Its loosened rhythmic interplay and open harmonic frameworks, especially from Williams and Hancock, proved enormously influential on the development of post-bop and would help set the template for the
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing era (mono, 1965) - Columbia CL 2350; red 2-eye label with "Nonbreakable" text, Pitman plant etch in runout.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the classic red Columbia "2-eye" mono label - twin oval "eye" logos at 9 and 3 o'clock, "360 Sound" arced in white at the bottom, "MONO" and "Nonbreakable" text beneath the catalog number - the design Columbia used circa 1963-1966 before phasing out mono LPs around 1967-68. The catalog number CL 2350 with matrix XLP 79816-1B / XLP 79817-1A and a "P" etch confirms pressing at Columbia's Records Pressing Plant in Pitman, New Jersey, one of the East Coast plants used for early runs of this title. The rim reads "Printed in U.S.A." with no later orange-rim or 1-eye era text, and the presence of "Nonbreakable" (dropped from slightly later 2-eye pressings) supports placing this squarely in the earliest 1965 pressing run rather than the circa-1967 2-eye reissue that dropped that text.
albums.fidelity: This mono mix was mastered from the original 1965 Columbia session tapes; 2-eye era Columbia mono pressings of E.S.P. are well-regarded by collectors for their punchy, immediate sound typical of mid-60s Columbia jazz mono cuts, though quality can vary somewhat between the Pitman and Terre Haute plants used for this title. This Pitman 2-eye mono pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for E.S.P., ahead of the circa-1967 2-eye stereo-only reissue and the later 1-eye orange-rim stereo reissues; dedicated audiophile reissues of this specific title are scarce, so a clean vintage 2-eye mono copy like this remains the benchmark for collectors chasing the original sound.
albums.generalNotes: 1965 Columbia CL 2350 mono pressing in the red 2-eye label era (used c.1963-1966), consistent with an original first-pressing-run copy. Matrix XLP 79816-1B / XLP 79817-1A with a "P" etch confirms Pitman, New Jersey plant manufacture, one of the plants used for early East Coast pressings of this title. The label retains "Nonbreakable" text and the back cover keeps the original mono-era Columbia disclaimer, both dropped from the circa-1967 2-eye reissue and absent entirely from later orange-rim 1-eye pressings, reinforcing the early dating.

albums.title: Friday Night In Person At The Blackhawk, San Francisco - Volume I
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Hank Mobley (tenor saxophone), Wynton Kelly (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums)
sides:
1. Walkin'
2. Bye Bye Blackbird

1. All Of You
2. No Blues
3. Bye Bye (Theme)
4. Love, I've Found You (piano solo by Wynton Kelly)
albums.albumStory: Recorded live over a Friday and Saturday night residency in April 1961 at the Blackhawk club in San Francisco, this album captures Miles Davis's working quintet with Hank Mobley on tenor in place of the departed John Coltrane, backed by the redoubtable rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers and Jimmy Cobb. Columbia split the sprawling club tapes into two companion LPs, "Friday Night" (Volume I) and "Saturday Night" (Volume II), giving listeners an unusually intimate, in-the-room document of Davis on the bandstand rather than in the studio. The set leans on staples from his repertoire - "Walkin'," "Bye Bye Blackbird," "All Of You" - alongside the originals "No Blues" and the closing theme "Bye Bye," played with the loose, extended-solo freedom of a working club date. Mobley's presence has often been overshadowed by Coltrane's tenure, but the Blackhawk tapes are among the best surviving evidence of his stint with Davis and of a quintet quietly transitioning toward the more exploratory band Davis would assemble later in the decade. Critically, the album has long been regarded as a solid if secondary entry in Davis's vast Columbia discography - valued less for innovation than for its relaxed documentation of a great small group at work. It remains a touchstone for collectors of Davis's early-1960s Columbia period and of live hard-bop recording in general.
albums.lpNotes: 1st-era pressing (mono, 1961) - Columbia six-eye red label, CL 1669, flat "ledge" label with no deep groove, consistent with the late-1961 six-eye die changeover rather than the earlier deep-groove run.
albums.labelNotes: The label area has no deep groove - it is a flat ("ledge") six-eye label. Columbia's pressing plants phased out the deep-groove die in favor of a shallow "ledge" beginning in late 1961, with old and new dies sometimes used side by side while stock was used up; CL 1669 was first issued in August/September 1961, squarely inside that changeover window, so a flat-label six-eye copy is fully consistent with an original-era six-eye pressing rather than proof of a later pressing. This places the copy within the same six-eye, pre-"CBS"-overprint production era as a deep-groove copy of the same catalogue number, but from the later side of the 1961 die changeover rather than the earliest deep-groove run.
albums.fidelity: The original 1961 Columbia mono cut was mastered from the Blackhawk club tapes recorded under producer Irving Townsend; as a live nightclub recording it has inherent room noise, imperfect balance and a warmer but narrower dynamic range than a studio date. Collectors on the forums generally favor the mono mix for cohesion on this title, though the stereo CS 8469 spreads the horns and rhythm section more distinctly. Six-eye era Columbia pressings are typically well-cut and reasonably quiet for the period, but this title has since been surpassed in fidelity by the expanded, newly-mastered 2003 Columbia/Legacy "Complete" box (engineered by Mark Wilder from the original tapes) and by the audiophile-grade 2021 Mosaic/Craft vinyl box of the complete Blackhawk sessions, both of which offer cleaner transfers and fuller unedited performances than the original single LP.
albums.generalNotes: 1961 Columbia CL 1669 mono - six-eye red label places this copy inside Columbia's 1955-62 label design window, consistent with an original-era pressing rather than the later two-eye or 360 Sound reissue labels. Mono CL-prefix catalog number and "NONBREAKABLE" text (no STEREO banner) confirm this is the mono edition, distinct from the parallel CS 8469 stereo issue. Matrix suffixes (1C/1A) indicate stamper-generation codes rather than a re-mastered cut; the label does not indicate deep-groove presence.

albums.title: Jazz Track
albums.genre: Jazz - Hard Bop / Cool / Film Soundtrack
albums.producer: George Avakian (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud sessions, supervising), Cal Lampley (May 26, 1958 sextet session)
albums.composer: Miles Davis (Side 1, film score); Bronisław Kaper/Ned Washington, Victor Young/Ned Washington (Side 2 standards)
albums.performerOrchestra: The Miles Davis Quintet (Side 1); The Miles Davis Sextet (Side 2)
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet); Side 1 - Barney Wilen (tenor sax), René Urtreger (piano), Pierre Michelot (bass), Kenny Clarke (drums); Side 2 - Julian "Cannonball" Adderley (alto sax), John Coltrane (tenor sax), Bill Evans (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums)
sides:
1. Générique
2. L'Assassinat De Carala
3. Sur L'Autoroute
4. Julien Dans L'Ascenseur
5. Florence Sur Les Champs Elysées
6. Diner Au Motel
7. Évasion De Julien
8. Visite Du Vigile
9. Au Bar Du Petit Bac
10. Chez Le Photographe Du Motel

1. On Green Dolphin Street
2. Fran-Dance
3. Stella By Starlight
albums.albumStory: Jazz Track brings together two pivotal but very different Miles Davis dates: the improvised score he recorded in Paris on December 4-5, 1957 for Louis Malle's "Ascenseur pour l'échafaud," and three standards cut in New York on May 26, 1958 with the sextet that would soon record Kind of Blue. The Paris session is one of jazz's most celebrated instances of scoring to picture on the spot, with Davis and a mostly French pickup band reportedly improvising while watching projected footage, yielding a spare, atmospheric music that helped define the vocabulary of jazz film scoring. The New York side documents the first studio pairing of Davis with Bill Evans alongside Cannonball Adderley, John Coltrane, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, the same lineup that would shortly make Kind of Blue, and its reading of "Stella By Starlight" is widely regarded by musicians and critics as among the finest on record. Arriving at the hinge between Davis's hard-bop years on Prestige and his modal breakthroughs of 1959, the album shows him working in two starkly different contexts within months of each other. Assembling a European film score alongside a domestic studio date made for an unusual pairing, but it preserved both performances for American audiences before the film's own soundtrack saw domestic release. Critically the record has often stood in the shadow of Davis's more unified statements, yet the Evans-Adderley-Coltrane tracks are prized as essential precursors to Kind of Blue and the Paris material remains a touchstone of jazz-and-film history.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1959) - Columbia 6-eye deep-groove label; runout stampers XLP44601-2AE III/XLP44602-2G with no plant-suffix letter indicate an original New York-plant pressing.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show Columbia's classic red/black "6-eye" design with deep groove and the pre-1958 rim-text ordering (walking-eye logo between the circled "Lp" mark and "Marcas Reg."), the mono flagship format dating to roughly 1956-1961. The runout stampers XLP44601-2AE III and XLP44602-2G carry no plant-suffix letter, distinguishing them from the later Terre Haute ("TA"), Pitman ("P"), and Hollywood ("H") regional repressings of this same title that used descendant stamper generations. That absence of a plant code, combined with the deep-groove 6-eye label, places this copy among Columbia's original New York-plant pressings, essentially contemporaneous with the album's initial late-1958/early-1959 release and ahead of every subsequent regional or later-label variant in the CL 1268 hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: Mastered from the original Columbia tapes for the December 1957 Paris score and May 1958 New York sextet date, this 6-eye mono pressing represents Columbia's original NY-plant mastering of CL 1268. Columbia's late-1950s New York pressings are generally well regarded by collectors for quiet surfaces and warm, present mono sound, though the Paris film-session tapes are inherently more modest in fidelity than Columbia's own 30th Street studio dates. Collectors on the forums rate these original 6-eye mono pressings above the later 360 Sound red-label and Half-Speed/Mastersound-era reissues, and this early no-plant-suffix stamper places the copy at the top of that mono hierarchy; no widely recognized audiophile remaster (Mobile Fidelity, Analogue Productions, etc.) of this specific title exists to supersede it.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Columbia CL 1268 mono - original first pressing. Red/black 6-eye deep-groove labels with the correct 1956-61 rim-text order, and runout codes XLP44601-2AE III (side 1) and XLP44602-2G (side 2) lack the TA/P/H plant-suffix letters seen on later Terre Haute, Pitman, and Hollywood repressings of this title, placing this among the earliest NY-plant stampers cut for the release. Deep groove present on both sides per collector grading, consistent with the 1956-61 Columbia 6-eye era. No promo or club markings are present.

albums.title: Kind of Blue
albums.composer: Miles Davis (as credited on label; Bill Evans later given co-writing credit for "Blue in Green" on some reissues)
albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, leader), John Coltrane (tenor saxophone), Julian "Cannonball" Adderley (alto saxophone, courtesy of Riverside Records; lays out on "Blue in Green"), Bill Evans (piano; plays on all tracks except "Freddie Freeloader"), Wynton Kelly (piano on "Freddie Freeloader" only, courtesy of Riverside Records), Paul Chambers (bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums, misprinted as "James Cobb" on this jacket)
sides:
1. So What
2. Freddie Freeloader
3. Blue in Green

1. Flamenco Sketches
2. All Blues
albums.albumStory: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York across two sessions in March and April 1959, Kind of Blue grew out of Miles Davis's growing interest in modal composition, an approach he had begun testing on "Milestones" the year before, trading dense chord changes for simple scalar frameworks that opened up space for improvisation. Davis reportedly brought the band only brief sketches rather than fully written charts, asking his sidemen to improvise around scales and moods encountered largely for the first time in the studio, a method the original liner notes by pianist Bill Evans compared to the direct, unrevisable brushwork of Japanese ink painting. The sextet assembled for the date - Davis, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, with Wynton Kelly sitting in for "Freddie Freeloader" - represented an extraordinary concentration of talent, several of whom would soon lead their own historically important groups. The album arrived at a pivotal juncture in Davis's career, following his hard-bop and cool-toned work for Prestige and early Columbia, and it redirected jazz improvisation toward modality just as Ornette Coleman and others pushed the music toward free forms by a different route. Kind of Blue is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever made, cited by generations of musicians across jazz, rock, and classical music as a foundational listening experience, and it remains a fixture of best-albums lists and jazz history curricula. Its restrained, spacious lyricism - epitomized by "So What" and "Blue in Green" - demonstrated that jazz improvisation could be harmonically simple and emotionally profound at once, cementing the album's legacy as a touchstone of twentieth-century American music.
albums.lpNotes: Early six-eye mono pressing (Columbia CL 1355) - deep groove label, XLP47324-1B / XLP47325-1C runout stampers, an early but not the absolute first (-1A/-1A) stamper generation.
albums.labelNotes: The label design is Columbia's red "six-eye" style (six small "eye" logos around the rim, "Guaranteed High Fidelity" text at the top of the label field, deep groove visible around the spindle hole, and "NONBREAKABLE" printed under the catalog number) on both sides - a design Columbia used roughly 1958 into the early 1960s before switching to flat-edge (non-deep-groove) six-eye labels and, later, the 1968+ "360 Sound" text. The runout stampers, XLP47324-1B (Side 1) and XLP47325-1C (Side 2), are among the earliest lacquer generations used on the commercial mono release, with 1A/1B/1C being the earliest letters found, placing this copy just behind the true first -1A/-1A pairing. Combined, the deep-groove six-eye label and low-letter stampers place this copy firmly in the 1959-1961 first-issue manufacturing window, ahead of the later flat-edge six-eye pressings and far ahead of the 360 Sound reissues.
albums.fidelity: The mono mix of Kind of Blue is generally preferred by collectors and engineers over the original stereo master, since the stereo reels were affected by a tape machine running slightly fast/slow during the sessions, a flaw largely sidestepped on the mono tape; this six-eye mono pressing sits near the top of the album's fidelity hierarchy for that reason. Early six-eye Columbia pressings from this era used relatively high-quality lacquers and pressings by Columbia's own plants, and collectors on the forums generally rate original six-eye mono copies (especially early-stamper ones like -1B/-1C) as warmer and more three-dimensional than later reissues. Later benchmarks include the 1997 Mark Wilder Columbia/Legacy remaster, the 2009 Sony Legacy 50th-anniversary mono LP reissue (cut from analog tape), and the Analogue Productions/Classic Records audiophile stereo reissues; most listeners still rank an early six-eye mono original like this one above those later cuts for tonal warmth, even though the later audiophile stereo pressings offer superior surface noise and channel separation.
albums.generalNotes: This is an early Columbia six-eye mono first-issue pressing of CL 1355, not a later reissue. Deep groove labels, the "Guaranteed High Fidelity" six-eye design, and the "NONBREAKABLE" rim text all point to manufacture in the 1959-1961 window, before Columbia dropped the deep groove and years before the 1968 switch to "360 Sound" labels. The runout stampers, -1B on Side 1 and -1C on Side 2, indicate an early stamper generation close to (but one or two removed from) the true first -1A/-1A pairing prized by specialists. The jacket's misspelling of "Cannonball" Adderley's surname as "Adderly" and drummer Jimmy Cobb's name as "James Cobb" are consistent with the original-issue back cover text used on early copies of this title.

albums.albumStory: Miles Davis and Horns splices together two formative Prestige sessions: a January 17, 1951 date, Davis's first for the label and his first time recording alongside Sonny Rollins, and a February 19, 1953 session built entirely around compositions and arrangements by tenor saxophonist Al Cohn. The 1951 session paired Davis's trumpet with trombonist Bennie Green and pianist John Lewis in a three-horn front line, producing originals like Davis's own "Down" and Lewis's "Morpheus" alongside standards such as "Blue Room" and "Whispering." The 1953 date brought together Cohn and Zoot Sims, two tenor players closely associated with the Woody Herman "Four Brothers" sound, with trombonist Sonny Truitt and a rhythm section anchored by Lewis and Kenny Clarke, yielding tightly arranged pieces like "Tasty Pudding" and "Willie The Wailer." Together the sessions capture Davis moving beyond his bebop apprenticeship and the Birth of the Cool dates toward the leaner, more blues-rooted voice that would soon define hard bop. Prestige compiled the material into this 12-inch LP in 1956, just as Davis's first great quintet was establishing him as a major bandleader, making the record a valuable document of his pre-stardom collaborations with Rollins, Cohn, Sims, and Lewis.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1956) - Prestige 446 W. 50th St. deep-groove fireworks labels; etched RVG dead-wax markings.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels show the classic yellow-background, black-rim Prestige "fireworks" design (arrows, stars, spiral logo scattered around the rim), with "PRESTIGE RECORDS INC. \u2022 446 W. 50th ST., N.Y.C." printed just inside the rim and "Remastered by Van Gelder" credited at three o'clock - both labels show a visible deep groove near the rim. That 446 W. 50th Street NYC address is the address Prestige used before its August 1958 relocation to Bergenfield, New Jersey, after which the same fireworks design was reprinted with the 203 South Washington Ave., Bergenfield address instead. The back cover repeats the 446 West 50th Street address, matching the labels and confirming jacket and disc belong together. This places the copy squarely in the original 1956 New York pressing run, ahead of the Bergenfield second pressing and well ahead of the retitled Early Miles reissues.
albums.fidelity: The labels credit Rudy Van Gelder's remastering and the dead wax carries his etched RVG stamp, marking this as an early New York pressing cut from his mastering work. Because the underlying 1951 and 1953 sessions predate Prestige's regular contemporary Van Gelder engineering, the sound has somewhat limited dynamic range and added period reverberation compared to a full mid-1950s Van Gelder session tape, but this remains the most immediate and collectible cut of the material. Later Bergenfield-era fireworks pressings can still draw on related Van Gelder metal and sound respectable, while the 1980s OJC reissue is a serviceable but lower-fidelity budget alternative; there is no dedicated Tone Poet, Music Matters, or Analogue Productions audiophile edition of this specific title.

The dead wax carries etched PRLP-7025-A RVG and PRLP-7025-B RVG. Prestige's move to Bergenfield, NJ in August 1958 places this 446 W. 50th labeling and jacket as the earliest New York pressing rather than a later fireworks repress.

albums.title: Miles Davis At Carnegie Hall
albums.performerOrchestra: Gil Evans and His 21-Piece Orchestra

albums.albumStory: Recorded live on the evening of May 19, 1961, this album documents a benefit concert at Carnegie Hall that marked a unique convergence in Miles Davis's career: his working quintet, featuring Hank Mobley on tenor sax alongside the rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers, and Jimmy Cobb, performing both standalone and backed by a 21-piece orchestra arranged and conducted by Gil Evans, Davis's most important large-ensemble collaborator. The program mixed hard-bop quintet vehicles like "So What" and "No Blues" with orchestral reworkings drawn from the Miles Ahead/Sketches of Spain vein, including Ahmad Jamal's "New Rhumba" and "The Meaning of the Blues," giving listeners a rare live document of the Evans-Davis orchestral sound performed in concert rather than assembled in the studio. Coming at a transitional moment for Davis - between the classic quintet years and his later shift toward Wayne Shorter and a more modal, exploratory direction - the record captures him at a peak of technical and expressive command, with contemporary critics singling out the trumpet's tone and the drama of the evening. Critical reaction at the time, excerpted on the original jacket from the New York Times, New York Herald Tribune, and Down Beat, was enthusiastic, with reviewers noting Davis's shift from restraint to an impassioned, brassy exuberance over the course of the performance. The album stands as an important entry in the Davis-Evans discography, valued both as a rare live big-band jazz recording and as a document of Davis's showmanship and interpretive range mid-career, and it remains a touchstone for listeners tracing the arc from Miles Ahead and Sketches of Spain through his live performance practice of the early 1960s.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing era (mono, 1962) - Columbia 6-eye label, promotional "Demonstration Record - Not For Sale" overprint, matrix XLP-56271-1A/56272-1B.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the red-and-black 6-eye Columbia label with the "Nonbreakable" notation under the catalog number and the diagonal pink "DEMONSTRATION RECORD / NOT FOR SALE" overprint, identifying it as a Columbia promotional pressing rather than a commercial stock copy. The 6-eye label design was Columbia's standard from the mid-1950s through mid-1962, when it began transitioning to the 2-eye design, a change that took place around June-July 1962, right around this album's release; the presence of the 6-eye label here places this copy squarely in that first pressing window rather than the later 2-eye reissue. Because promotional copies were drawn from the same early pressing runs sent to press and radio ahead of/at general release, the 6-eye demo label indicates this is a first-pressing-era pressing, distinguished from a general commercial 6-eye copy only by its promotional overprint and lack of a for-sale designation.
albums.fidelity: This is a mono pressing from Columbia's 6-eye era, mastered from the original 1961 concert tapes under producer Teo Macero; mono Columbia jazz pressings of this vintage are generally well regarded by collectors on the forums for their warmth and presence compared to the era's "electronically re-channeled for stereo" counterpart, which purists consider inferior since it is a fake-stereo derivative rather than a true stereo recording. As a promotional pressing drawn from early stampers, sound quality should be comparable to a standard 6-eye commercial mono copy of similar vintage, i.e., among the better-sounding versions of this title. No audiophile remaster (Mobile Fidelity, Analogue Productions, Music Matters, etc.) of this specific live album is known to exist, so within the album's fidelity hierarchy this 6-eye mono pressing sits at or near the top, well above the electronically re-channeled stereo pressings and later 2-eye/orange-label reissues.
albums.generalNotes: 1962 Columbia CL 1812 mono - original 6-eye label pressing issued as a promotional demonstration copy, not general retail stock. The 6-eye Columbia label with "Nonbreakable" text dates to the label's pre-mid-1962 design, before the changeover to the 2-eye label, which took place around June-July 1962, placing this pressing in the first-issue window. The diagonal pink "DEMONSTRATION RECORD/NOT FOR SALE" overprint and white promo sticker on the front cover mark this as a radio/press service copy rather than a commercial stock pressing, though it was drawn from the same early pressing run.

albums.albumStory: Porgy and Bess was the second full orchestral collaboration between Miles Davis and arranger-conductor Gil Evans, recorded over four sessions at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in July and August 1958, with Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn taking the vocal roles of George and Ira Gershwin's 1935 folk opera, whose book and lyrics were co-written by DuBose Heyward. Evans reworked the opera's songs into dense, brooding voicings for a large ensemble of brass, reeds and French horns built specifically around the color and phrasing of Davis's horn rather than a conventional big-band chart, pushing jazz orchestration into new territory. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the hard-bop small-group work of his mid-1950s quintet and sextet and the modal breakthroughs of Kind of Blue, recorded only months later, and its spacious, harmonically open writing is widely heard as a direct precursor to that watershed album. Alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley appears on the sessions though he went uncredited on the original jacket, a detail that has fed decades of critical and fan discussion. Porgy and Bess has been consistently ranked among the finest Davis-Evans collaborations and among the great orchestral jazz albums of its era, prized for its emotional depth on a program built entirely of other composers' material, and it remains a cornerstone in assessments of both Davis's interpretive genius and Evans's arranging artistry.
albums.lpNotes: 1959 promo pressing (mono) - Columbia six-eye deep-groove label overprinted "DEMONSTRATION"/"NOT FOR SALE," placing it in the same early manufacturing window as the standard first retail issue.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Columbia's red-and-black six-eye center label with a pronounced deep groove, the same design used across the company's catalogue from about 1958 into the early 1960s before the plain "Guaranteed High Fidelity" two-eye label replaced it around 1963-65. In place of the standard commercial text the label reads "DEMONSTRATION" above the title and "NOT FOR SALE" beneath the side/ASCAP line, marking this as a promotional pressing rather than a retail copy. Both the deep groove and the six-eye design place manufacture firmly within the album's first few years on the market, and the promo overprint identifies it as the demonstration issue struck alongside the standard first retail pressing rather than a later repress.
albums.fidelity: This is an original-era Columbia six-eye mono pressing, mastered from the 1958 session tapes cut at Columbia's 30th Street Studio; collectors on the forums generally rate the original mono six-eye Columbia pressings of this album as the most natural and best-balanced versions, ahead of the original stereo mix and well ahead of later CBS-era reissues. As a deep-groove six-eye pressing this sits at or very near the top of the vintage fidelity hierarchy for this catalogue number, since promotional copies were cut and pressed from the same early metalwork as initial retail runs. A later audiophile 45RPM reissue exists and is praised for openness and detail, but it derives from later-generation tape sources rather than the original mono cut, so mono purists still favor a clean original six-eye pressing like this one.

albums.albumStory: Round About Midnight was Miles Davis's debut for Columbia Records, cut at Columbia's New York studios in sessions spanning October 1955 and June and September 1956 while Davis was still technically finishing out his Prestige contract. It introduced his first great quintet - John Coltrane, Red Garland, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe Jones - a working band whose telepathic interplay reshaped small-group jazz and set Coltrane on the path to his own landmark career. Anchored by a moody reworking of Thelonious Monk's title tune, the program mixes standards ('All of You,' 'Bye Bye Blackbird') with bebop repertoire (Charlie Parker's 'Ah-Leu-Cha,' Tadd Dameron's 'Tadd's Delight'), spotlighting Davis's newly matured, harmon-muted lyricism against Coltrane's harder-edged tenor attack. The record marked Davis's leap from Prestige's hard-bop scene to a major label's resources and promotional reach, opening the decade of landmark Columbia albums that followed. It is widely regarded as a cornerstone of hard bop and one of the defining quintet statements of the mid-1950s, later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Its blend of restraint, harmonic sophistication and controlled intensity has kept it a fixture on best-jazz-album lists and an essential document of Davis's transformation from bebop sideman to major bandleader.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1957) - Columbia 6-eye deep-groove label, earliest documented XLP39109-1A/XLP39110-1A stampers.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Columbia's deep-groove 6-eye mono label (red field, black perimeter wedges each containing a small circled 'eye' logo, six in total, 'NONBREAKABLE' text, and the 'Lp' trademark ring at bottom) - the design used for CL 949 from its March 1957 release through the early 1960s before the deep groove and 6-eye rim graphic were retired in favor of the 2-eye 'Guaranteed High Fidelity' label circa 1962-63. This 6-eye deep-groove issue exists in several sub-variants distinguished mainly by stamper suffix (1A through 1K observed on side A) rather than by a differently laid-out label; this copy's stamped runout (XLP39109-1A / XLP39110-1A) is the lowest, earliest stamper pair for the catalog number. That places this disc at or very near the front of the six-eye deep-groove pressing run for CL 949, ahead of copies stamped 1C, 1G, 1H or 1K. Columbia pressed this title at its Hollywood, Bridgeport/NY, and Terre Haute plants, but the specific plant for this copy is not identified on the label.
albums.fidelity: This is an original 1957 Columbia mono cut sourced from Frank Laico's session tapes, not a later remaster; six-eye deep-groove Columbia pressings of this era are generally well-regarded among collectors for their warm, direct mono presentation, with early low-number stampers like this 1A/1A pair theoretically representing the freshest metal parts, though most listeners find plant-to-plant differences among Columbia's Hollywood, Bridgeport/NY, and Terre Haute pressing plants, and stamper-generation differences, subtle. Within the album's overall fidelity hierarchy this early six-eye deep-groove mono sits at or near the top, ranked above the later 2-eye 'Guaranteed High Fidelity' mono, the 1970s orange-label reissue, and the stereo/rechanneled CS 8649 pressings. It is generally considered comparable to, and by some vintage-mono purists preferred over, the 2013 Sony Legacy/Kevin Gray-mastered 180g mono reissue and the Mobile Fidelity SACD, which are praised for added clarity but not universally judged to surpass the original six-eye pressing's tonal character.

No stereo, budget, or record-club markings are present, consistent with a standard first-run mono original rather than a reissue.

albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet), Victor Feldman (piano, Hollywood sessions), Herbie Hancock (piano, New York sessions), George Coleman (tenor sax), Frank Butler (drums, Hollywood), Anthony 'Tony' Williams (drums, New York), Ron Carter (bass)

albums.albumStory: Recorded across two sessions in Hollywood and New York in the spring of 1963, Seven Steps To Heaven captures Miles Davis at a pivotal transitional moment, moving away from the classic quintet sound of the late 1950s toward the more exploratory group that would soon feature Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams alongside Wayne Shorter. The Hollywood tracks feature a short-lived West Coast lineup with Victor Feldman and Frank Butler, while the New York sessions introduced the teenage Tony Williams and a young Herbie Hancock, both of whom would become central to Davis's mid-1960s quintet. The album blends standards like 'Basin Street Blues' and 'I Fall in Love Too Easily' with the original title track, co-written by Feldman and Davis, which became a modern jazz standard in its own right. Critically, the record is viewed as a bridge album, less unified than the classic quintets that preceded and followed it, but historically important as the first appearance on record of the rhythm section that would soon revolutionize jazz. Its significance lies less in stylistic innovation on this particular record and more in personnel: it is the recorded birth certificate of the Hancock-Carter-Williams rhythm section under Davis's leadership. The album has remained a respected, if sometimes overlooked, entry in Davis's vast catalog, valued by historians for its transitional role between the hard-bop era and the more abstract, interactive small-group jazz Davis would pioneer through the mid-1960s.
albums.lpNotes: 1963 mono first pressing - Columbia CL 2051, red 2-eye 'Guaranteed High Fidelity' label, Pitman (P) plant stamper.
albums.labelNotes: The label is a red Columbia design with a two-eye logo (one 'eye' block at 9 o'clock, one at 3 o'clock), 'GUARANTEED HIGH FIDELITY' arcing along the bottom rim, 'NONBREAKABLE' printed near the spindle, and 'PRINTED IN U.S.A.' with the Columbia trademark notice — no '360 SOUND' arc or gold/six-eye elements appear. This two-eye red mono design was standard for Columbia from roughly 1961 through 1965, before the label shifted to the 'CBS/360 Sound' and later red/gold six-eye designs beginning c.1965-66. The catalog number CL 2051 (mono), as opposed to CS 8851 (stereo, printed on the jacket), places this copy within the album's original 1963 release window. The matrix suffixes XLP-59702-1D and XLP-59703-1F carry a 'P' plant stamp, indicating a Columbia Pitman, NJ pressing, one of several plants (also Terre Haute, Carrollton) used interchangeably for this high-demand title; shared lacquers were run across plants simultaneously, so the plant does not diminish first-pressing status. The label design and catalog configuration together place this disc within the first-issue mono pressing run.
albums.fidelity: This is a mono cut from the original 1963 Columbia analog masters; Columbia's early-1960s in-house mastering for Davis titles is generally well regarded by collectors on the forums, though not in the audiophile-legend tier of some Blue Note or Van Gelder jazz cuts. Pitman pressings from this era are generally solid, flat, quiet vinyl, comparable to Columbia's other major plants (Terre Haute, Carrollton) of the period. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy, this 2-eye mono original sits above later 1965+ six-eye/360 Sound reissues and generic budget reissues, but below modern audiophile treatments such as the Analogue Productions 45 RPM 2xLP stereo reissue, generally considered the sonic reference for this title. Mono collectors specifically prize the original CL 2051 pressing for its focused, punchy horn presence compared to the wider but sometimes thinner-sounding stereo mix of the era.

Back cover correctly lists both CS 8851 (stereo) and CL 2051 (mono) numbers, standard for Columbia jackets of this period. No 360 Sound or six-eye red/gold label elements are present, ruling out the later 1965+ reissue label designs.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain grew out of Miles Davis's fascination with Spanish and Andalusian folk and classical music, sparked in part by hearing Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez and by flamenco encountered around the time of his marriage to Frances Taylor. Recorded across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960, it was the third and most ambitious of Davis's large-scale orchestral collaborations with arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess. Rather than a conventional jazz combo date, the album places Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn as a singular, vocal-like voice floating over Evans's dense, classically inflected orchestrations for woodwinds, brass, and percussion, with almost no traditional swing rhythm section driving the music. The adagio movement from the Concierto became one of the most recognized themes in the jazz repertoire. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the modal breakthroughs of Kind of Blue and his subsequent quintet work, and it cemented his reputation as an artist unafraid to reshape jazz's boundaries. Critically it was hailed on release as a bold, atmospheric triumph and has remained one of the most acclaimed and influential orchestral jazz albums ever made, frequently cited alongside Kind of Blue and Miles Ahead as a high-water mark of the Davis-Evans partnership.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1960) - Columbia 6-eye deep-groove label, no CBS text, matrix XLP 49956/49957-1A.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Columbia's earliest "6-eye" red label design: "COLUMBIA" arched across the top in white, six small eye-in-triangle logos ringing the label (three per side), a circled "LP" logo at bottom center, no "CBS" branding anywhere, and the abbreviated credit "Orch. arranged and conducted by Gil Evans." This design, paired with a deep-groove ring pressed near the label edge, was Columbia's standard label from the mid-1950s until it was phased out for the two-eye and later "Guaranteed High Fidelity" black-label styles around 1961-62. CL 1480 was pressed from numerous stamper variants across its run, from the earliest 1A generation through later reground stampers into the 1AK+ range, with Hollywood "H" and Terre Haute "T" plant suffixes appearing on later pressings; the -1A suffix on both sides here places this pressing among the earliest stamper generations run at the outset of production, near the front of the original mono pressing run rather than a later reground stamper. No plant letter (H/T) appears in the runout, so the pressing plant is not identified.
albums.fidelity: This is an original 1960 Columbia mono cut, mastered from the analog session tapes at the dawn of Columbia's in-house mastering era; 6-eye deep-groove pressings are widely regarded by collectors on forums as the most natural, warm, and dynamically alive versions of this recording, especially in mono, which best represents Gil Evans's dense orchestration without the phasing artifacts of the era's stereo mixdowns. Later 2-eye and black-label Columbia reissues (mid-1960s onward) are generally considered a step down in vinyl quality and mastering freshness. Modern audiophile reissues - Mobile Fidelity's 2013 MFSL 1-375 (mono/stereo) and the more recent MoFi UHQR/standard 2025 pressing - are praised for quietness and clarity but some listeners find them slightly more polite or bass-heavy than the vintage 6-eye cut; among vintage and modern options, a clean original 6-eye mono like this one remains the benchmark reference pressing for many collectors, with the best modern reissues competing closely but not universally preferred.
albums.generalNotes: 1960 Columbia CL 1480 mono - original first pressing. The 6-eye maroon/silver Columbia label with deep groove and no CBS branding is Columbia's earliest LP label design, used through the early 1960s, and the -1A matrix suffix on both sides indicates an early stamper generation, among the earliest pressed for this catalog number. Released July 1960, shortly after recording wrapped in March 1960. No plant letter (Hollywood "H" vs Terre Haute "T") appears alongside the -1A suffix in the runout, so the pressing plant is not identified.

albums.musicians: Miles Davis (trumpet, flugelhorn), Gil Evans (arranger, conductor), Elvin Jones (drums, percussion), Jimmy Cobb (drums), Paul Chambers (bass), Janet Putnam (harp), Bernie Glow, Ernie Royal, Louis Mucci, Ray Triscari (trumpets), Jimmy Buffington, Earl Chapin, Tony Miranda, Bob Swisshelm (French horns), Frank Rehak, Dick Hixon (trombones), Bill Barber (tuba), Romeo Penque, Eddie Caine, Al Block, Danny Bank (woodwinds/reeds)
