albums.albumStory: Recorded April 29, 1966 at Rudy Van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio, Got a Good Thing Goin' captures organist Big John Patton at the height of his mid-1960s soul-jazz run for Blue Note, reunited once more with guitarist Grant Green in what proved to be their final recorded collaboration. The program pairs two extended Patton-Green originals, "The Yodel" and "Soul Woman," with three contemporary R&B covers - Marvin Gaye's "Ain't That Peculiar," Sam Cooke's "The Shake," and Duke Pearson's "Amanda" - reflecting Blue Note's mid-60s push toward a groovier, jukebox-friendly soul-jazz sound. Patton, a Kansas City-raised organist who cut his teeth in R&B bands before joining Lou Donaldson and later leading his own Blue Note dates, was among the most rhythmically direct and unpretentious organists in the label's stable, and this session is frequently cited as a high point of his catalog. Drummer Hugh Walker and conguero Richard Landrum push the record into a percussive, dance-oriented groove that helped define mid-60s organ-combo soul jazz alongside contemporaries like Grant Green's own leader dates and Lou Donaldson's records of the era. AllMusic's retrospective review awarded the album four and a half stars, and it remains a favorite among soul-jazz collectors for its hot, unfussy grooves, even as some listeners find the material simpler than Patton's more exploratory work. The session stands as a snapshot of Blue Note on the eve of its sale to Liberty Records, closing out a fruitful and influential chapter in both Patton's and Green's careers.
albums.lpNotes: 1966 stereo first pressing - Blue Note NY USA label (BST 84229), Van Gelder-stamped runout, catalog number falls inside the NY USA design window that closed later that year.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are the light-blue and white design reading "BLUE NOTE RECORDS INC · NEW YORK, USA" with no Liberty Records credit, the fifth Blue Note label style used roughly 1962-1966 across the BLP/BST 4081-4247 catalog run. Blue Note was sold to Liberty Records in mid-1966, after which remaining NY USA-labeled stock was used briefly before the imprint was updated to read "A Division of Liberty Records, Inc." Because BST 84229 falls within the NY USA catalog window and this copy retains the unmodified New York address text, it represents the label's last independent-era design for this title, pre-dating the Liberty-credited pressings that followed later in 1966. The runout reads BNST 84229 A/B with a Van Gelder stamp and matrix number 114; no Plastylite ear appears in the runout, which does not itself rule out a first-pressing plant.
albums.fidelity: Engineered by Rudy Van Gelder direct to the original stereo masters, this NY USA pressing sits at or near the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title, ahead of the thinner-sounding Liberty and United Artists-era pressings from roughly 1967-1973. Collectors on the forums generally favor these mid-60s Van Gelder-cut Blue Note stereo pressings for their warmth and immediacy over later reissues. No audiophile remaster (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet, etc.) of this specific title exists, so this original pressing represents the best commonly available sonic option; a 2000s CD reissue exists but is a digital, not vinyl, alternative.
albums.generalNotes: 1966 Blue Note BST 84229 stereo - original first pressing. Label reads "Blue Note Records Inc, New York, USA" with no Liberty Records text, placing it before the mid-1966 ownership-change relabeling; runout shows the BNST 84229 A/B etchings with matrix number 114 and a Van Gelder stamp. No Plastylite ear appears in the runout, which does not by itself rule out a first-pressing plant. Reid Miles cover design and back-cover ad art for contemporaneous Patton titles (Along Came John, Blue John, The Way I Feel, Oh Baby!) support a mid-1966 release window.

albums.musicians: Clifford Brown (trumpet), Maynard Ferguson (trumpet), Clark Terry (trumpet), Harold Land (tenor sax), Herb Geller (alto sax), Richie Powell (piano), Junior Mance (piano), Keter Betts (bass), George Morrow (bass), Max Roach (drums), Dinah Washington (vocal on "Darn That Dream")

albums.albumStory: On August 14, 1954, EmArcy A&R chief Bob Shad staged a public jam-session concert in Hollywood, drawing on musicians already in town for a Clifford Brown/Max Roach recording date, and rolled tape on an ad-hoc all-star band for a free-admission crowd. Three of the era's most exciting trumpeters - the meteoric young Clifford Brown, high-note specialist Maynard Ferguson, and the soon-to-be Ellington sideman Clark Terry - traded extended choruses over a rhythm section led by Max Roach, joined by reedmen Harold Land and Herb Geller; Dinah Washington, whose own portion of the concert became the companion LP "Dinah Jams," contributes a luminous guest vocal on "Darn That Dream." The record captures Brown at the very start of his ascent, only two years before he would be recognized as the most influential trumpet voice since Dizzy Gillespie, and less than two years before his death at 25 in a car accident in June 1956 cut short a career already reshaping the instrument. "Move" stands as one of the great trumpet-battle performances in the jam-session idiom, while the closing ballad medley shows Brown, Terry, Geller and pianist Richie Powell at their most lyrical and unguarded. The album was praised on release in early 1955 as a showcase for its trumpet section, and it has since been championed by critics as an essential and unusually well-realized document of the informal jam-session format. It remains a landmark in Brown's brief discography and a touchstone recording of 1950s West Coast-adjacent hard bop.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (mono, 1955) - US EmArcy MG 36002, blue drummer label, deep groove, blue-printed back cover; YMG36002A/B hand-etched matrix with stamped letters.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the original 'blue EmArcy type A' label: bright royal-blue field, one white oval 'EmArcy' script logo top-left, one drummer-boy illustration top-right, 'LONG PLAYING HIGH FIDELITY' curving around the rim, and 'Mercury Record Corporation / Made in U.S.A.' at the bottom, all sitting over a visible deep groove. The back jacket is printed in blue ink rather than black. Per EmArcy pressing chronology, this founding drummer-boy design and blue-ink back cover mark the label's earliest 36000-series issues (1954-c.1956), before Mercury switched the back-cover printing to black around 1956-57 for second issues and later moved to the double-oval EmArcy design. The blue label, deep groove, and blue back cover together place this copy firmly in the original February 1955 first-issue pressing window, ahead of any subsequent black-back or reissue pressing.
albums.fidelity: Recorded live-to-mono in Hollywood in 1954 under Mercury/EmArcy's 'Fine-Fairchild Margin Control' process and mastered/pressed through Mercury's Chicago operation; original deep-groove blue-label pressings like this one are considered the sonic benchmark for the title, with vivid, upfront brass and audible room ambience typical of a well-run live-to-tape jazz date. The 1975 Trip Jazz reissue is a thin, budget-grade cut, and the 1980s EmArcy/Polygram reissue series, while competently mastered, sounds noticeably cooler and more compressed than the original. No modern audiophile remaster (Tone Poet/Analogue Productions/Music Matters-class) of this title exists, so a clean original mono deep-groove pressing such as this one remains the best-sounding option available to collectors.
albums.generalNotes: 1955 EmArcy MG 36002 mono is the original US first pressing of this title. The blue 'drummer' EmArcy labels with deep groove, paired with the blue-printed back cover (which switched to black on c. 1956-57 second issues), place this copy in the earliest pressing window. The runouts read YMG 36002A / YMG 36002B 2, M1, hand-etched with stamped letters, consistent with the original matrix style for this catalog number. Released February 1955, drawn from the August 14, 1954 Hollywood concert, with Dinah Washington's guest vocal on "Darn That Dream."

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Fine Recording in New York between February and August 1959, this album was built around Dinah Washington's breakthrough crossover single, a dramatically retitled reworking of María Grever's 'Cuando vuelva a tu lado' with English lyrics by Stanley Adams. Producer Clyde Otis and arranger-conductor Belford Hendricks framed Washington's blues-rooted phrasing and gospel-tinged diction within lush, pop-oriented string and rhythm settings, a deliberate step away from her earlier straight blues and jazz sides. The title performance climbed into the pop Top 5 and won Best Rhythm & Blues Performance at the second Grammy Awards, later entering the Grammy Hall of Fame. Surrounding the hit are standards like 'I Remember You,' 'Cry Me a River,' 'Manhattan,' and 'A Sunday Kind of Love,' showcasing Washington's equal command of torch balladry and up-tempo swing. Arriving after fifteen years as a top blues and R&B star billed as 'Queen of the Blues,' the record marked the pivotal pop crossover of her career, paving the way for 'Unforgettable' and her celebrated duets with Brook Benton. Critics and historians regard it as a landmark of late-1950s vocal jazz/pop-R&B fusion and among the definitive statements of Washington's artistry.
albums.lpNotes: Original US mono issue (1959) - black/silver Mercury A2 deep-groove labels; MG 20479A MS1/MG 20479B MS2 Richmond-style matrices.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries Mercury's early black/silver mono 'A2' label design: arched MERCURY logo, LONG PLAYING/MICROGROOVE rim text, catalog number and 'Side' at left, 'A Custom High Fidelity Recording' at right, no oval logo above the spindle hole, and a pronounced deep groove on both sides. This plain-arch, no-oval-logo A2 style is the earliest Mercury mono MG-20000 configuration, used circa 1958-59, before the label added the three-stroke 'A3' variant and later the oval-logo 'B' design used into the early 1960s, and well before the red 'Mercury head in black banner' reissue label used by the mid-1960s. The runouts read MG 20479A MS1 (side 1) and MG 20479B MS2 (side 2), sitting within Mercury's original Richmond-era mono matrix run - a distinct, slightly later-lacquered stamper pairing for side 2 within the same first-issue label design, rather than the earliest-possible both-sides-MS1 stamper combination. This places the copy solidly in the 1959 original mono first-issue window, just not the earliest-possible both-sides-MS1 stamper combination.
albums.fidelity: George Piros engineered the New York sessions at Fine Recording, with separate mono and stereo masters cut; this disc carries the original mono tape via an MS1/MS2 Richmond-style lacquer pairing. No cutting-engineer initial appears in the matrix, so it cannot be credited as a Fine Recording 'FF' cut. Deep-groove manufacture ties it to Mercury's late-1950s National Record Pressing-era plants, generally a step above routine 1960s black-label and later red-label reissues. Collectors often prize the companion stereo SR-60158 for its wide, if unusually hard-panned, soundstage, while this mono pressing gives the more centered, focused vocal image typical of era mono cuts. The 2026 Verve Vault all-analog reissue (Ryan K. Smith, Optimal) is the modern benchmark for clean transfer quality, but this original mono pressing remains the reference vintage mono listening choice.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Mercury MG-20479 mono - original US first-issue pressing. The black/silver A2 label design (no oval logo, arched MERCURY, deep groove) matches Mercury's earliest MG-20000 mono configuration, predating the A3 and oval-logo B designs. The runouts MG 20479A MS1/MG 20479B MS2 place it in the original Richmond-era mono matrix sequence, with side 2's MS2 indicating a second lacquer rather than the earliest-possible both-sides-MS1 stamper pairing found on some copies. The pressing plant is not identified beyond the likely Mercury/National Record Pressing operation.

albums.musicians: Dizzy Gillespie (trumpet, vocals on track 1), Sonny Rollins (tenor saxophone), Sonny Stitt (tenor saxophone), Ray Bryant (piano), Tommy Bryant (bass, credited as "Tom Bryant" on this jacket), Charlie Persip (drums)

albums.albumStory: Sonny Side Up was recorded on December 19, 1957 at Nola Penthouse Sound Studios in New York, uniting trumpet giant Dizzy Gillespie with tenor saxophonists Sonny Rollins and Sonny Stitt for a single, high-stakes session under Norman Granz's Verve banner. The pairing was conceived as a study in contrasting modern jazz sensibilities: Stitt's driving, Parker-descended intensity set against Rollins's more exploratory, thematically-minded improvising. The album's centerpiece, Stitt's original "The Eternal Triangle," became an enduring jam-session vehicle and a signature cutting-contest tune for both saxophonists, trading increasingly heated choruses over a relentless tempo. Gillespie, already a titan of bebop's founding generation, anchors the session and even takes a rare vocal turn on the opener, while pianist Ray Bryant, bassist Tommy Bryant, and drummer Charlie Persip supply a tight, propulsive rhythm section. Released in January 1959, the record arrived as both Rollins and Stitt were consolidating reputations as premier tenor stylists, and the session has since become one of the most celebrated tenor-battle records in jazz history. It remains prized as a hard-bop touchstone for its head-to-head improvisational fireworks and its enduring influence on jazz musicians as a jam-session standard.
albums.lpNotes: 1st pressing (mono, 1959) - Verve MG V-8262 gray trumpeter label, deep groove; matrix MGV-8262-A/B 50564/50565.
albums.labelNotes: Both side labels show the gray Verve "trumpeter" design: a single trumpet-playing silhouette logo at left, "VERVE RECORDS" script logo at top, "CLEF SERIES" catalog line, "Under the personal supervision of Norman Granz" credit, and "MADE IN U.S.A." rim text, with deep groove construction visible on the pressing. This design was Verve's house label from the company's 1956 founding through roughly 1960-61, before Norman Granz sold Verve to MGM in 1961 and the trumpeter graphic was dropped for a plain black label. The runout matrix numbers stamped on this copy (MGV-8262-A 50564 / MGV-8262-B 50565) are the first-issue stampers, placing this copy at the top of the pressing hierarchy as the true January 1959 first issue rather than a later MGM-era black-label repress.
albums.fidelity: No mastering engineer is credited on the jacket, typical of Verve's late-1950s Clef/Norgran-descended releases produced under Norman Granz's direct supervision; the original US pressing plant work is generally solid though period-typical surface noise can occur. Collectors on the forums regard these early deep-groove trumpeter-label Verves as full-bodied and dynamic compared to the flatter, more compressed later 1960s MGM-era black-label pressings and 1990s/2000s European CD-era reissues. A 2025 Verve Vault Audiophile Series 180g reissue, mastered by Ryan K. Smith from the analog tapes and pressed at Optimal, is now the best modern audiophile option, but this original trumpeter pressing remains the vintage reference cut for the title.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Verve MG V-8262 mono - original first pressing. Gray "trumpeter" Verve labels with deep groove and Clef Series text on both sides match the earliest Verve house design used before the 1961 MGM buyout dropped the trumpeter logo. Runout matrix numbers (50564/50565) are the first-issue stampers. Side 1 grades NM, Side 2 VG+, jacket VG+; no later black-label or MGM-era markings are present.

albums.musicians: Gerry Mulligan (baritone sax), Zoot Sims (tenor sax), Bob Brookmeyer (valve trombone; piano on "Everything Happens To Me", uncredited on the jacket), Jon Eardley (trumpet), Dave Bailey (drums), Peck Morrison (bass)

albums.albumStory: Recorded in New York during September and October 1955, this was the first album by Mulligan's short-lived sextet and his first session as a leader for EmArcy. Mulligan formed the group after dissolving his celebrated pianoless quartet and taking several months away to reassess his musical direction. The new band expanded the quartet's spare, contrapuntal language into a four-horn ensemble while retaining an unusually open rhythmic foundation. Mulligan originals such as "Apple Core" and "Nights Of The Turntable" sit beside radically reworked standards, while "Broadway" and "Bernie's Tune" give the musicians room for extended collective interplay. Mulligan was already a central figure in modern jazz through his writing for Miles Davis's Birth of the Cool sessions, his big-band arrangements, and his success in bringing the baritone saxophone forward as a nimble lead voice. Contemporary reviewers praised the sextet's organic interplay, swing, and taste, with Whitney Balliett calling it perhaps the best modern small band then working. The group's brief existence and the overshadowing fame of Mulligan's earlier quartet long kept the album underrated, but it remains an important bridge between his pianoless small groups and his later Concert Jazz Band.
albums.lpNotes: 2nd US press (mono, c. 1956-57) - black-back cover; blue small-drummer deep-groove labels; MF2/etched MS Indianapolis metal.
albums.labelNotes: This copy has the blue EmArcy Type B small-drummer deep-groove label, curved "LONG PLAYING HIGH FIDELITY" rim text, and "MERCURY RECORD CORPORATION / MADE IN U.S.A." at the bottom. EmArcy, Mercury's jazz subsidiary launched in 1954, used blue-printed back covers through MG-36056; MG-36056 was the last title known in that form, with black-back jackets indicating a second issue from approximately 1956-57. This copy's black-printed back and typed MF2/MSII and MF2/MS markings place it behind the blue-back MF1/MI/A1/I first issue, with the matrix combination matching the RCA Indianapolis variant for this pressing, even though the small-drummer blue label itself also appears on the earliest copies.
albums.fidelity: This is a contemporary all-analog mono pressing from stamped MF2 metal with etched MS markings, made at RCA Indianapolis; no cutting engineer is independently documented. It sits behind the MF1/MI/A1/I first-cut copies but remains an early EmArcy pressing, with warm, naturally balanced mono well suited to the largely pianoless four-horn arrangements. RCA's Indianapolis work for Mercury is generally well regarded, though specific commentary on this title is sparse. The 1958 US repress is a lower vintage alternative, the 1979/1982 Japanese pressings offer quieter surfaces, and the 2016 Mosaic EmArcy Sextet Recordings box, mastered from the original mono tapes by Kevin Reeves and Ryan Smith, is the reference modern source.
albums.generalNotes: US EmArcy MG 36056 mono, best identified as a c. 1956-57 RCA Indianapolis second pressing rather than the blue-back first issue. The decisive evidence is the black-printed back cover, blue small-drummer deep-groove labels, and typed MF2/etched MS runouts; documented earlier copies pair the blue-back jacket with MF1/MI/A1/I metal. The music was recorded in September and October 1955 and was being reviewed as a new LP by February 1956.

albums.albumStory: Jennifer Warnes spent much of the 1970s as a backing singer in Leonard Cohen's touring band, and Famous Blue Raincoat grew directly out of that long friendship and musical apprenticeship as a full-album tribute to his songwriting, released in November 1986. A key impetus was 'Song of Bernadette,' which began as Warnes' own composition sketch before Cohen helped shape it, and the album also premiered 'First We Take Manhattan' and 'Ain't No Cure for Love' before Cohen recorded his own versions. Co-produced by Warnes and bassist Roscoe Beck, the record surrounds her warm, precise readings with lush, cinematic arrangements from an elite bench of West Coast session players - a deliberate contrast to the spare textures of Cohen's originals - and Cohen himself duets with her on 'Joan of Arc,' taking the role of the fire to her Joan. Initial critical reaction was mixed, with some reviewers finding the production overblown next to Cohen's austerity, but the album became a slow-burning commercial phenomenon, introducing a wide pop audience to Cohen's catalog at a low point in his visibility. It stands as Warnes' best-known and most enduring solo statement, cementing her reputation as an interpretive singer of exceptional taste. Its standing has only grown with time: it is now routinely cited as one of the finest tribute albums in popular music and is credited with helping revive broad interest in Leonard Cohen's work during the late 1980s.
albums.lpNotes: 1st press (US stereo, 1986) - Cypress 661 111-1 tree label, PolyGram-distributed; '49' label code = Specialty (Olyphant PA) pressing, Grundman-mastered, matrix 661-111-1-A/B.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the original 1986 Cypress 'tree silhouette' stereo label: pink/black tree artwork, block CYPRESS RECORDS logo, ©1986 copyright line, 'Printed in U.S.A.' and 'Distributed by PolyGram Records, Inc.' rim text. Cypress was a short-lived Los Angeles boutique label (division of Cypress Entertainment, Corinth Street address on the jacket) whose entire 1986-87 catalog run was PolyGram-distributed, so this design is the sole first-issue US configuration. The '49' printed below the speed line on the Side 1 label is the Specialty Records (Olyphant, PA) plant code, distinguishing this copy from the '57' Columbia Carrollton plant sub-variant that shares the identical 661-111-1-A/B stamped matrix family. The two plant sub-variants are otherwise contemporaneous first issues and trade interchangeably.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Bernie Grundman (Bernie Grundman Mastering credit on the jacket); the album itself was digitally tracked (the original CD carries a DDD SPARS code), so the LP is a Grundman cut of the digital-era production rather than all-analog. The original Cypress LP has long been an audiophile reference disc, prized for pristine, close-miked vocal clarity and dynamic low end, with no meaningful sonic difference reported between the Specialty and Carrollton runs. In the album's fidelity hierarchy it remains the reference vintage cut - above the Private Music reissue and the various CD/gold-CD editions - but it now sits below the modern summit editions: the 2015 Impex 180g 33rpm (Grundman cut from Warnes' personal analog mixdown masters) and especially the 2023 Impex 35th Anniversary 1STEP 45rpm box, which reviewers rank as the ultimate presentation.
albums.generalNotes: Original 1986 US first pressing on Cypress Records 661 111-1, stereo, Specialty (Olyphant PA) plant. The printed '49' plant code under the speed line on the Side 1 label is the Specialty identifier (the companion '57' code marks the Columbia Carrollton sub-variant), the ©1986 tree label with 'Distributed by PolyGram Records, Inc.' and 'Printed in U.S.A.' is the sole first-issue US configuration, and the runouts carry the shared original-issue matrix 661-111-1-A/B. Released November 1986.

albums.albumStory: Despite the "Jazz 1960" banner splashed across the cover, every note here was recorded in Hollywood in 1956 at Radio Recorders, during one of the most poignant stretches of Art Pepper's life: he had just been released from his first prison term in mid-1956 and cut these sides with pianist-arranger Marty Paich only weeks later, months before his career-defining "Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section" session. Five tracks feature Pepper's alto in a quartet with Paich, first issued on the rare Tampa LP pairing the two, including Pepper's own composition "Art's Opus"; the other five are Paich-led sides with Larry Bunker's vibes and Howard Roberts' guitar, drawn from an earlier Tampa 10-inch. By the time these masters resurfaced on Interlude with a glossy, bachelor-pad cover and a fabricated later release date, Pepper himself was once again behind bars, making the album an odd, bittersweet placeholder for an absent star. Paich, meanwhile, was emerging as one of the most important arrangers on the West Coast scene, later responsible for the charts on "Art Pepper + Eleven" and numerous Mel Torme sessions. Pepper's playing throughout is light, buoyant and melodically generous - the sound of a newly free man breezing through standards and originals - and the set is valued today as an important, if commercially obscure, early document of his mature alto voice.
albums.lpNotes: Original and only documented US pressing (mono, 1960) - Interlude MO-514 gray deep-groove Hollywood label; a recompilation of 1956 Tampa masters.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the gray-silver deep-groove label with the large white lowercase "i" Interlude logo and "INTERLUDE RECORDS INC - HOLLYWOOD" rim text, catalog MO-514 with printed "int 134-A/B" matrix numbers - the sole documented US pressing configuration for this title. Interlude Records Inc. was a short-lived Hollywood independent (c. 1959-62) run by Robert Scherman, and its catalog leaned heavily on earlier Tampa Records masters (TP series, 1956-57) that Scherman also controlled; MO-514 is a recompilation of that Tampa material rather than a new 1960 recording. The deep-groove pressing and single mono MO-500 series number place this firmly within the label's original 1960 issue window, with no second pressing or label-design change documented for the title.
albums.fidelity: The source tapes were engineered at Radio Recorders in 1956 by Val Valentin, later Verve's house engineer, which accounts for the unusually warm, present mono sound on this LP. Collectors on the forums rate this Interlude pressing highly for the material, describing it as sonically superior to the rarer, reportedly rougher-sounding original Tampa 10-inch/LP issues. In the overall fidelity hierarchy for this material, this Interlude mono pressing sits at or near the top: the Tampa originals are scarcer collector objects but not better sounding, later reissues on Charlie Parker Records (as "Chile Pepper") and V.S.O.P. are a tape generation removed and more variable, and no audiophile reissue of this specific compilation exists.

albums.albumStory: Kind of Blue was recorded by the Miles Davis Sextet at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York across two sessions in March and April 1959, with the group reading Bill Evans's sketched modal frameworks for the first time at the session rather than rehearsing beforehand, a working method Evans himself described in his own liner-note essay printed on the back cover. Davis had been moving away from dense chord-change improvisation toward modal composition, and this album became the definitive statement of that shift, built on scales rather than chord changes across all five performances. The sextet united Davis with Cannonball Adderley and John Coltrane on saxophones, Paul Chambers on bass, Jimmy Cobb on drums, and both Bill Evans and Wynton Kelly sharing the piano chair, an unusually stacked lineup of musicians who were each already, or would soon become, major bandleaders in their own right. The record arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, following his hard-bop and orchestral collaborations with Gil Evans, and it redirected jazz improvisation toward modal harmony for the following decade. It is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever made, cited as the entry point to jazz for generations of listeners and a foundational document of modal jazz. Critical reception was immediate and has only grown over the decades, with the album consistently ranked among the greatest recordings in American music.
albums.lpNotes: Original six-eye mono pressing (Columbia CL 1355, c. 1959-60) - flat label with no deep-groove ridge (confirmed on the Side 1/Side 2 label photographs), late-run stamper pair (1BH/1AL); ranks below the collection's other copy, which is a deep-groove pressing with earlier 1B/1C stampers.
albums.labelNotes: This copy has a flat label surface around the spindle hole - no deep-groove ridge - meaning this is not a deep-groove pressing. Columbia's six-eye red/black label design (arched COLUMBIA logo, six perimeter eye-logos in black wedge panels) was used circa 1958-1961 for mono Columbia releases; deep-groove stamping was gradually phased out at Columbia's plants during 1959-1960 as press hardware was updated, so a flat (non-deep-groove) six-eye label of this type dates to the later part of that six-eye window rather than the earliest lacquers. Combined with this copy's late-alphabet runout suffixes (XLP47324-1BH / XLP47325-1AL), the flat label places this as a later six-eye mono pressing generation, below the collection's other copy, which is deep-groove with earlier 1B/1C stampers, in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: This is an original 1959-era Columbia mono cutting, mastered from Fred Plaut's session tape by Columbia's in-house mastering staff rather than an outside engineer; the mono mix is generally regarded by collectors on the forums as the most faithful rendering of the album's original session balance, since the commonly circulated stereo mix has channel and speed anomalies from the master tape. Within the six-eye mono pressing run, sound quality varies by stamper generation, and this copy's later mother/stamper pair (1BH/1AL) places it below the handful of prized first-stamper (1A/1B/1C) copies that collectors on the forums single out as sonically superior, though it remains a legitimate vintage flat, non-remastered six-eye cut. Later audiophile mono reissues, notably Classic Records' 1997 200-gram mono LP and Mobile Fidelity/Music Matters stereo cuts, are prized for quieter surfaces and modern mastering but are generally regarded by mono purists as less essential than an authentic six-eye original for hearing the record as first issued.
albums.generalNotes: This is a genuine Columbia six-eye mono first-issue-era pressing of CL 1355, identified by the red/black six-eye label design used circa 1958-1961 before Columbia moved to the plain 2-eye label. However, the runout suffixes XLP47324-1BH and XLP47325-1AL are well down the documented mother/stamper alphabet sequence for this title, meaning this is a later six-eye pressing rather than a first-stamper (1A/1B/1C) copy. The side 2 label here lists "All Blues" before "Flamenco Sketches" in the corrected order, consistent with post-earliest-run six-eye copies. No deep-groove or dead-wax photo was available to confirm the deep-groove ridge; that detail would help further narrow the exact stamper generation.

albums.albumStory: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York on March 2 and April 22, 1959, Kind of Blue grew out of Miles Davis's turn toward modal composition, developed in dialogue with pianist Bill Evans, with the band given only skeletal scales and melodic sketches rather than fully written charts. The septet paired Davis with John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley on saxophones, Bill Evans on piano (with Wynton Kelly sitting in for "Freddie Freeloader"), Paul Chambers on bass, and Jimmy Cobb on drums, letting contrasting horn voices and two pianists explore the same modal frameworks from different angles. The album arrived at the peak of Davis's late-1950s creative run and marked a decisive break from bebop's harmonic density toward a spacious, scale-based improvisational language. Its relaxed tempos, blues-inflected melodies, and largely first-take performances captured a spontaneity that Evans, in his own liner note, likened to a painter working directly onto parchment without revision. Kind of Blue is widely regarded as the best-selling and most influential jazz album ever recorded, routinely cited as the genre's essential entry point and a fixture on best-album lists across all styles of music. Its introduction of modal improvisation reshaped jazz soloing vocabulary for generations of musicians who followed.
albums.lpNotes: 1997 RTI white-label TEST PRESSING for the Classic Records CS 8163 audiophile reissue - stamped 'APR 2 1997', matrix CS 8163 A1/B1 with BG (Bernie Grundman) lacquer suffix, sitting above the retail 200g run in the pressing hierarchy.
albums.labelNotes: The side labels are plain white RTI (Record Technology Incorporated) stock printed only with the RTI logo, the words "TEST PRESSING," and blank DATE/MATRIX NUMBER fields that have been hand-stamped "APR 2 1997" and "CS 8163 A1/B1" - there is no Columbia or Classic Records branding, deep groove, or track information printed on the label itself. This identifies the disc as a pre-release quality-control pressing struck at RTI for Classic Records' licensed audiophile reissue of Columbia's CS 8163, not a retail copy; Classic Records began issuing CS 8163 on 200g Quiex SV-P vinyl in the mid-1990s with Bernie Grundman recutting lacquers from the original three-track masters (the "BG" suffix in the runout confirms this cutting engineer). The jacket paired with this copy is the eventual 2001-copyright Classic Records/Sony licensed sleeve, but the stamped test-pressing date shows this specific BG lacquer/stamper pair was approved in April 1997, well ahead of that later retail print run. As an approval-stage RTI test pressing, this sits at the top of the Classic Records CS 8163 hierarchy, above the routine 200g retail copies that used the same or a subsequent stamper generation.
albums.fidelity: The lacquers were cut by Bernie Grundman directly from the original three-track analog session masters with no additional EQ, using Classic Records' all-tube cutting chain, then pressed at RTI on audiophile-grade vinyl; this test pressing captures that same Grundman cut at its earliest, pre-approval stage. Collectors on the forums rate the Classic Records Kind of Blue highly among tape-sourced reissues for openness and low-level detail versus standard CBS/Columbia pressings, though some prefer the later Analogue Productions/QRP 45rpm cut for outright resolution. Within the album's fidelity hierarchy this sits below the original 1959 six-eye Columbia lacquers (prized for tape freshness) and below the 2020s Analogue Productions 'Corrected Speed' 45rpm QRP pressing, but above routine 1970s-80s Columbia reissues and most CD/digital editions; as a test pressing it also offers an unusually clean, low-wear playback surface from that stamper pair.

The generic RTI 'TEST PRESSING' labels, rubber-stamped 'APR 2 1997' with matrix 'CS 8163 A1/B1,' identify the lacquer/stamper pair used for quality-control approval ahead of the commercial run. The 'BG' suffix ties the cut to Bernie Grundman's mastering from the original three-track analog masters, distinguishing this from both the vintage Columbia originals and the later retail 200g Quiex pressings. The plain white jacket-adjacent insert matches a test configuration rather than a packaged consumer product, confirming pre-release status.

albums.albumStory: Miles Davis and Horns compiles two early Prestige sessions from opposite ends of Davis's formative post-Parker period: a January 17, 1951 sextet date with Sonny Rollins (their first-ever studio pairing) and Bennie Green, and a February 19, 1953 septet session built around Al Cohn's compositions and arrangements, featuring the contrasting tenors of Cohn and Zoot Sims. Both dates capture Davis still finding his voice after leaving Charlie Parker's group, working in a harmonically rich, horn-heavy format that let him experiment with ensemble textures beyond the standard quartet or quintet. The Cohn-associated material, including "Tasty Pudding" and "Willie The Wailer," showcases a warmer, more relaxed strand of early-1950s bop-adjacent jazz, with Zoot Sims's soloing singled out by critics as a highlight of the session. The 1951 date, meanwhile, is historically important as the first recorded meeting of Davis and Rollins, two musicians who would go on to shape the language of modern jazz. Coming before Davis's mid-1950s quintet breakthroughs, this album offers a glimpse of a still-developing artist testing group concepts that would later inform his more celebrated Prestige and Columbia work. It remains a minor but valued entry in the Davis and Prestige catalogs, prized by collectors more for its personnel and historical placement than for landmark musical innovation, though the Davis-Rollins pairing gives it lasting documentary importance.
albums.lpNotes: 1983 Original Jazz Classics reissue (mono) - OJC-053, etched "OJC-053 A/B" runout confirms this is the Fantasy-era flat reissue, not the 1956 Prestige NYC original.
albums.labelNotes: The side-label photos show a yellow center label with a black outer rim, "PRESTIGE" arched in yellow-on-black at the top, "LONG PLAYING MICROGROOVE" arched at the bottom, and the characteristic OJC-era decorative motifs (a spiral/comma logo at upper left, a star logo and directional arrows scattered around the rim); the catalog is printed as "OJC-053 (P-7025)" with no deep groove and no 446 W. 50th St. or Bergenfield NJ Prestige address visible. This yellow/black spiral-and-star design (not the earlier Prestige "fireworks" art, and not a blue/cream design as an earlier note mistakenly stated) is the standard Original Jazz Classics label introduced by Fantasy Records in 1982-83 to reissue out-of-print Prestige, Riverside, and Milestone titles, replacing the original PRLP catalog numbers with new OJC-prefixed numbers. Placement of this design, combined with the etched "OJC 053 A/RE1 P" and "OJC 053 B/RE2 P (AP)" runout codes, firmly dates this copy to the 1983 Fantasy-era flat reissue rather than any vintage 1950s-70s Prestige pressing, putting it near the bottom of the PRLP 7025 pressing hierarchy.
albums.fidelity: The 1983 OJC-053 reissue was mastered flat from tape by George Horn's team at Fantasy Studios (Berkeley), not cut from Rudy Van Gelder's original lacquers, though it still derives from the same 1951/1953 Van Gelder-engineered Prestige sessions. Collectors on the forums generally rate early-1980s OJC flat transfers as accurate and listenable but noticeably less punchy and dynamic than a genuine 1956 Prestige NYC "fireworks" mono original. Within the album's full fidelity hierarchy, this OJC-053 pressing sits in the middle-to-lower tier: above later Fantasy/ABC-era commercial reissues in transfer fidelity, but well below an original NYC first pressing, and there is no audiophile-grade reissue (Music Matters, Analogue Productions, Tone Poet, etc.) of this particular title to compare against.
albums.generalNotes: This copy is the 1983 Original Jazz Classics reissue, catalog OJC-053, identifiable by its yellow label with black rim, spiral/star motifs, and "PRESTIGE" arched banner - the standard early-1980s OJC design, not a vintage Prestige NYC or Bergenfield label. The etched runout reading "OJC 053 A RE1 P" / "OJC 053 B RE2 P (AP)" is decisive dead-wax evidence confirming the Fantasy-era flat reissue rather than an original pressing. OJC-053 replaced the original PRLP 7025 catalog number as part of Fantasy's early-1980s reissue program, mastered flat from tape by George Horn's team rather than cut from original Van Gelder metal. This places the disc in the mid/lower tier of the PRLP 7025 pressing hierarchy.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain was the third and final large-scale orchestral collaboration between Miles Davis and arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead (1957) and Porgy and Bess (1959). Davis became fixated on Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez after hearing it, and Evans reimagined its adagio movement as the album's centerpiece, recording across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio. Evans built an unconventional ensemble around Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn - French horns, tuba, harp, bassoon, and flamenco-inflected percussion - blending Spanish classical and folk sources with his own compositions, including "Saeta," drawn from Holy Week processional music, and the closing "Solea." The sessions were exacting and demanding, with Evans meticulously shaping every orchestral texture, and the resulting album is often held up as the fullest realization of the Third Stream fusion of jazz improvisation and classical form. Davis himself counted it among his favorite recordings, and it marks a creative peak in both his and Evans's careers. The album won a Grammy Award, became one of the best-selling jazz records of its era, was later inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, and remains a touchstone of orchestral jazz.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain grew out of the extraordinary partnership Miles Davis had already forged with arranger Gil Evans on Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess, pushing it furthest into orchestral, Spanish-tinged territory. The centerpiece, an adaptation of Joaquin Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, originated when Davis heard the concerto's adagio and asked Evans to rework it as a feature for his trumpet against a large studio orchestra rather than a working jazz combo. Recorded in New York across sessions in November 1959 and March 1960, the album folds flamenco-inflected themes, bullfight and Holy Week processional imagery, and material drawn from Manuel de Falla into Evans's dense, coloristic orchestration, with Davis's trumpet and flugelhorn functioning almost as a classical soloist floating over shifting textures rather than trading bebop lines. It arrived at a pivotal moment in Davis's career, sandwiched between the hard-bop and modal breakthroughs of Milestones and Kind of Blue and his later electric period, confirming Evans and Davis as jazz's foremost orchestral colorists outside the big-band tradition. The record was a critical and commercial success, widely praised for its atmosphere and for Davis's uniquely vocal, vibrato-laden trumpet tone, and it won a Grammy for Best Jazz Composition. It remains one of the most acclaimed "third stream" recordings in jazz history and a touchstone for orchestral jazz, cited by critics as a high point of both Davis's and Evans's catalogs and a work that expanded jazz's vocabulary.

The orchestra credit is spelled out in full ("Orchestra arranged and conducted by Gil Evans") and the side indicators use regular, equal-sized capitalization ("SIDE 1" with the numeral not enlarged), the textual markers of the earliest "six-eye" sub-variant of CL 1480, the "Terre Haute Pressing." This places the disc in the earliest issue window for CL 1480, shortly after the album's July 1960 release and ahead of later six-eye pressings with abbreviated credit/enlarged numerals, and well ahead of the mid-1960s two-eye/CBS and later reissue labels.
albums.fidelity: Original Columbia in-house engineering (uncredited on the jacket) captured Evans's dense orchestration with considerable depth for 1960; the six-eye mono cut is generally regarded by collectors on the forums as the most natural-sounding version, since the era's stereo mixdown involved more compromises and the mono fold gives a more cohesive orchestral blend. This deep-groove six-eye pressing sits at the top of the fidelity hierarchy for CL 1480, ahead of later 1960s two-eye/360 Sound reissues and electronically rechanneled stereo pressings; later audiophile reissues (Mobile Fidelity, Speakers Corner/Music on Vinyl) are respected for quiet surfaces but are generally regarded by mono purists as secondary to a clean original six-eye mono copy for tonal accuracy.

albums.albumStory: Sketches of Spain (1960) was the third of Miles Davis's landmark orchestral collaborations with arranger Gil Evans, following Miles Ahead and Porgy and Bess, pushing their partnership further into a hybrid of jazz improvisation and Spanish/flamenco idiom. Its centerpiece, an adaptation of the adagio from Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, became the emotional core of the record, with Evans's lush, cinematic orchestration framing Davis's spare, vocal-like trumpet lines. Recorded with a large ensemble of woodwinds, brass, and percussion rather than a conventional combo across sessions in late 1959 and spring 1960, the album found Davis functioning as a soloist within an orchestral tone poem rather than a small-group bandleader, a departure that divided critics between those who found it beautiful and those who missed jazz spontaneity. Arriving between the modal breakthrough of Kind of Blue and his later 1960s quintet work, it cemented Davis and Evans as one of the most important composer-soloist pairings in jazz history. Its fusion of European classical form, Spanish folk color, and jazz phrasing proved deeply influential on third-stream and later orchestral/exoticist jazz projects. The album remains one of the most acclaimed entries in both artists' discographies, prized for its haunting atmosphere and orchestral ambition.

albums.albumStory: Stage Fright is The Band's third album, recorded in spring 1970 at the Woodstock Playhouse near their adopted hometown of Woodstock, New York, following the acclaimed Music from Big Pink and The Band and an exhausting run of touring that had left the group famous but strained. With longtime mentor John Simon stepping back, the five members self-produced for the first time, bringing in the young Todd Rundgren to engineer via a remote truck and Glyn Johns to handle the mix. Robbie Robertson's songwriting turns inward here, confronting the anxieties of sudden fame: the title track dramatizes stage fright itself, "The Shape I'm In" channels Richard Manuel's personal unraveling, "Daniel and the Sacred Harp" ponders art versus commerce, and closer "The Rumor" ends the record on a note of paranoia. The album became The Band's highest-charting release, reaching the Billboard top five, and earned a gold certification within months. Critics recognized a darker, more troubled tone than the group's earlier sepia-toned work, and Stage Fright is now regarded as the closing chapter of the classic trilogy that established The Band as foundational figures of Americana and roots rock. Songs from the record, especially the title track and "The Shape I'm In," remained fixtures of the group's live sets through The Last Waltz, and its unflinching look at fame's cost has only deepened its critical standing over time.

albums.albumStory: Recorded live at London's Talk of the Town cabaret venue, this 1967 album captured Tom Jones at the moment he was moving from teen-idol pop hitmaker into a full-blown Vegas-style showman, backed by a tuxedoed orchestra under Johnny Harris. The set mixes Jones's own hits - "It's Not Unusual", "What's New Pussycat?", "Green, Green Grass of Home" and the Bond theme "Thunderball" - with soul and R&B staples by Sam Cooke ("Ain't That Good News", "Shake") and the Chris Kenner/Fats Domino classic "Land of a Thousand Dances", alongside show-tune and pop standards like "Hello Young Lovers" and "That Old Black Magic". Produced by Peter Sullivan, Jones's regular Decca producer through the decade, the record documents the powerful, theatrical baritone and stagecraft already making Jones one of Britain's biggest live draws, a persona that would soon carry him into a long, hugely successful Las Vegas residency career. It stands as a notable document of the mid-1960s British vocal-pop and blue-eyed-soul crossover, showing a UK pop star confidently working American R&B repertoire for a supper-club audience, and remains a well-regarded snapshot of peak-1960s Tom Jones as a live performer rather than a studio hitmaker.

albums.albumStory: Lady in Satin was recorded February 18-21, 1958 at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York, produced by Irving Townsend - Billie Holiday's last completed album for Columbia and the penultimate studio statement of her life, released little more than a year before her death in July 1959. Holiday herself pushed for the project, insisting she wanted to record with Ray Ellis's lush strings-and-voices arrangements, a deliberately un-jazzy setting she chose over the objections of purists; she called it the favorite record she ever made. Her voice, weathered by decades of hard living, had lost its youthful suppleness, and critics at the time were divided over pairing that frayed instrument with Ellis's satin-smooth orchestra. But the emotional directness of performances like 'I'm a Fool to Want You' (co-written by Sinatra, who reportedly left the studio in tears at the power of her rendition) and 'You've Changed' transformed frailty into devastating expressive force. The album reframed Holiday not as a swinger but as one of the great dramatic interpreters of American song. It has since been inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame and is widely regarded as one of the essential vocal albums in jazz - the late-career companion piece to her 1930s-40s prime.

The six-eye design ran from mid-1955 to about 1962; around 1961-62 a small CBS overprint was added beneath the Columbia name marking repressings, and the two-eye '360 Sound' label replaced the six-eye entirely after 1962. The label-printed matrices x'Lp'43015/43016 match the first-issue mono. albums.fidelity: Recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio with its famed natural reverb, the original six-eye mono is prized by collectors for a warm, close, emotionally immediate vocal presence that puts Holiday front and center; collectors on the forums consider it the definitive way to hear the album despite the limited bandwidth of 1958 mono. Six-eye-era Columbia pressings are generally quiet and well cut. The original stereo CS 8048 six-eye is the audiophile grail but spreads the voice in a more diffuse orchestral field. Among modern reissues, the Analogue Productions editions (stereo 33 and the 2023 Ryan Smith/Sterling-cut 45rpm 2xLP pressed at QRP) outresolve the original, while Speakers Corner's mono reissue is the closest modern stand-in for this pressing. This copy's G-grade vinyl, however, will heavily compromise any of these inherent sonic virtues.

albums.albumStory: Carole King spent the 1960s as half of the legendary Brill Building-era Goffin-King songwriting team, penning hits like 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow' and 'A Natural Woman' for others before stepping out as a performer. Recorded in January 1971 at A&M's Studio B in Hollywood - concurrently with James Taylor's 'Mud Slide Slim,' using essentially the same band and even the same piano - 'Tapestry' was produced by her manager Lou Adler and captured with a deliberate live-in-the-room intimacy. Released February 10, 1971, it topped the Billboard chart for 15 consecutive weeks, remained on the charts for over six years, and became one of the best-selling albums in history (14x platinum in the US). It swept the 1972 Grammys, winning Album of the Year, Record of the Year ('It's Too Late'), Song of the Year ('You've Got a Friend'), and Best Female Pop Vocal Performance - King was the first woman to take all the top categories. Blending new material with reclaimed versions of her 60s classics ('Will You Love Me Tomorrow,' 'A Natural Woman'), the album defined the 1970s singer-songwriter movement and established the template for the confessional female singer-pianist. Its influence runs through generations of artists from Carly Simon to Adele, and it remains a permanent fixture on all-time greatest-album lists, preserved in the Library of Congress National Recording Registry.

LA BREA, HOLLYWOOD, CALIFORNIA 90028.' Lou Adler founded Ode in 1967 after selling Dunhill; A&M took over distribution in 1970, the label was briefly renamed 'Ode 70' in late 1970, and reverted to plain 'Ode' around November 1972. A&M's 1416 N. La Brea headquarters address appears in the rim text only until roughly 1972-73, when it was replaced by the P.O. Box 782, Beverly Hills address. The combination of the Ode 70 logo plus the La Brea rim text therefore brackets this copy in the 1971-72 first-issue window, at the top of the pressing hierarchy for this title.
albums.fidelity: The original lacquers for Tapestry are generally credited to Bernie Grundman, then chief mastering engineer at A&M, cut from Hank Cicalo's warm, dry, live-in-the-room analog tapes. Original US Ode pressings show notable copy-to-copy stamper variation - collectors on the forums report that most copies are dull, murky, or edgy, while a better stamper yields a genuinely open, full-bodied pressing that draws positive feedback, sounding somewhat mid-forward and rolled-off at the extremes even at its best. In the wider hierarchy, the 2013 Mobile Fidelity remaster (Krieg Wunderlich/Rob LoVerde) is widely considered a clear sonic improvement over the average original, with Grundman's 1999 Classic Records recut and the 2012 ORG 45rpm (Grundman/Bellman) as the other key audiophile alternatives; a clean, top-tier original Ode with a better stamper still competes with all of them and beats the mediocre majority.

albums.albumStory: Recorded on December 21, 1958 at Rudy Van Gelder's Hackensack studio and released the following year, Off to the Races arrived as trumpeter Donald Byrd was establishing himself as one of the era's most in-demand hard bop leaders and sidemen after his Detroit upbringing and stints with Art Blakey and Max Roach. The session pairs Byrd with a young, fiery Jackie McLean on alto and the underrated baritone specialist Pepper Adams, backed by a crack rhythm section of Wynton Kelly, Sam Jones, and Art Taylor, giving the record a harder, more aggressive edge than some of Byrd's later, more soul-jazz-leaning work. The program mixes a standard ("Lover") and a Sonny Rollins tune ("Paul's Pal") with four Byrd originals, including the boppish title track and the German-tinged blues "Sudwest Funk," named for a Southwest German radio station. Critically, the album is remembered as a solid, unpretentious showcase of late-1950s hard bop craftsmanship rather than a genre-defining statement, valued for its consistently strong blowing and the chemistry between Byrd, McLean, and Adams. It occupies a respected but modest place in Byrd's extensive Blue Note discography, appreciated by hard bop collectors for its personnel and unfussy, swinging character rather than for any singular historical breakthrough.

A nearly identical label used slightly later added a ® to the 47 West 63rd text, which collectors treat as a second-state pressing; this copy lacks that mark, placing it ahead of that variant in the pressing sequence. The deep groove plus the RVG/Plastylite ear stamps in the runout confirm this is a true Van Gelder-cut, Plastylite-pressed New York original rather than the later Liberty-era reissues (Bert-Co labels, no ear) that followed from 1966 onward.
albums.fidelity: Mastered by Rudy Van Gelder directly from his December 1958 mono session tapes and pressed by Plastylite (ear stamp), this is the top of the fidelity hierarchy for this title - warm, present horns and a tight, punchy rhythm section typical of Van Gelder's late-50s Hackensack mono cuts. Collectors on the forums generally rate original ear/RVG Blue Note mono pressings well above the later Liberty-era reissues, which used different mastering and lack the ear stamp, and well above generic 1970s-80s reissues; no major audiophile remaster (Music Matters, Tone Poet, Classic Records) of this specific title exists, so the original RVG/ear pressing remains the reference standard. The G/G deep-groove vinyl grading on this particular copy, however, means actual playback surface noise will be well below what a clean example of this pressing can deliver.
albums.generalNotes: 1959 Blue Note BLP-4007 mono - earliest issue of this title. Deep-groove 47 West 63rd St. labels lacking the later-added ® trademark, combined with RVG and Plastylite ear stamps in the runout, place this among the first pressings before Liberty took over the catalog and issued Bert-Co labeled reissues from 1966 onward. No stereo mix of the original session exists, so mono is the only correct configuration for a period-authentic copy.

albums.albumStory: By 1973 Herbie Hancock - already a Blue Note star, Miles Davis alumnus, and composer of 'Watermelon Man' and 'Maiden Voyage' - had taken his sextet through the dense electric explorations of the Mwandishi trilogy on Warner Bros. Watching audiences walk out on that music while crowds erupted for funk acts like Sly Stone and the Pointer Sisters, Hancock made a deliberate turn toward groove, dissolving the septet and building a new band around retained reedman Bennie Maupin, Oakland bassist Paul Jackson, LA session drummer Harvey Mason, and New Orleans percussionist Bill Summers. Recorded in 1973 at Wally Heider Studios in San Francisco with producer David Rubinson and released October 26, 1973, Head Hunters delivered four long tracks: the anthemic 'Chameleon' built on Jackson's two-note bass line and Hancock's clavinet-as-bass-guitar; a reinvention of 'Watermelon Man' opened by Summers' hindewhu-and-beer-bottle imitation of Ba-Benzélé pygmy music; 'Sly,' a layered tribute to Sly Stone; and the brooding closer 'Vein Melter.' The album became a phenomenon - the first jazz LP certified platinum, reaching #13 pop, #2 R&B and #1 on the jazz chart, with an edited 'Chameleon' crossing over to radio and dance clubs. It effectively codified jazz-funk as a commercial language, and its grooves and textures have been sampled by generations of hip-hop producers, making it one of the most influential electric jazz records ever made.
albums.lpNotes: Sony-era reissue (c. 1998-2004) - red Columbia label with '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.', KC 32731 + AL/BL label matrix, 3A recut lacquers; not a 1973 original.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the salmon/red Columbia reissue label: white 'COLUMBIA' arch at top, maroon print, label matrix 'KC 32731 / AL 32731' (side 1) and 'KC 32731 / BL 32731' (side 2), and the rim credit '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.' CBS Records was renamed Sony Music Entertainment in January 1991, so any label with this credit postdates the CBS era (1973 originals and all 1970s-80s pressings read '© 1973 CBS, Inc.'); combined with the pre-Sony BMG branding, that fixes this copy to roughly 1998-2004. The runouts ('AL-32731-3A RJ 3' / 'BL32731-3A BT') are 3A recut lacquers rather than the 1A/1B first cuts found on 1973 pressings, confirming a reissue generation. The A1 composer credit on the label reads 'Herbie Hancock-A. Willis-D. Rubinson-J. Cohen,' an anomalous credit that never appears on original labels, which credit Chameleon to Hancock/Jackson/Mason/Maupin. Other copies of this same reissue carry runouts ending in 'RML' rather than this copy's 'RJ 3'/'BT', pointing to parallel pressing runs within the Sony-era generation.
albums.fidelity: The source recording - cut at Wally Heider Studios by Fred Catero and Jeremy Zatkin - is famously robust, with a huge, dry funk low end that flatters almost any pressing. This reissue uses uncredited 3A lacquers, almost certainly derived from Sony's 1990s remaster chain rather than a fresh all-analog cut, and collectors treat it as a serviceable but unexceptional modern pressing. The widely available 1973 US originals (Pitman/Terre Haute/Santa Maria, 1A/1B stampers) remain the value-for-sound benchmark: warm, punchy, and cheap. At the top of the fidelity hierarchy sit the all-analog Analogue Productions reissues mastered by Ryan K. Smith at Sterling from the original tapes (APJ 084 33rpm, 2015; APJ 084-45 2x45rpm, 2017, pressed at QRP), with the Speakers Corner 180g also well regarded; this Sony cut sits clearly below all of those.

Decisive evidence: label rim credit reads '© 1973 Sony Music Entertainment Inc.' - a company name that did not exist before January 1991, whereas originals and all 1970s-80s pressings read '© 1973 CBS, Inc.' - and the runouts are 3A recut lacquers rather than the 1A/1B first-generation cuts. The A1 writer credit on the side 1 label (A. Willis/D. Rubinson/J. Cohen) is an anomalous credit not found on original pressings. This copy's runouts end 'RJ 3'/'BT', while other copies of the same reissue end in 'RML', indicating more than one pressing run within this Sony-era generation.

Collectors on the forums rate most Columbia/Legacy CD remasters (1997 Mark Wilder, 2003) as overly compressed and "brickwalled," making a clean original vinyl pressing like this one the preferred way to hear the album's dynamics. albums.albumStory: The jacket dates these sessions to April 1966 at RCA Recording Studios in New York, with producer Esmond Edwards presenting Kenny Burrell in a compact quartet setting. The program divides evenly between five Burrell originals and five outside songs, moving from the blues workout Mother-In-Law and Hot Bossa to People, Girl Talk, Erroll Garner's La Petite Mambo, and I'm Confessin'. Despite the romantic title and cover concept, this is not simply mood music: it folds blues, hard bop, bossa nova, and ballad playing into concise three-to-five-minute performances. Burrell, a Detroit musician who arrived in New York in 1956, was already one of the defining post-Charlie Christian jazz guitarists through his Blue Note, Prestige, and Verve recordings and his important work with Jimmy Smith. Midnight Blue and Guitar Forms had recently demonstrated both his popular reach and his orchestral sophistication; The Tender Gender applies those strengths to a leaner small-group format. The album reached Billboard's Top LPs chart in December 1966, peaking at No. 146 during a two-week run, and AllMusic later awarded it three stars. Its lasting reputation is that of an underrated Burrell favorite: less canonical than Midnight Blue or Guitar Forms, but a concentrated display of his melodic economy, blues attack, groove, and stylistic range.

Chess renamed Argo as Cadet in 1965; the back cover's 2120 South Michigan Avenue address places production before Chess's 1968 move and well before the 1969 GRT sale and 1971 label consolidation. albums.fidelity: Ray Hall and Bob Simpson engineered the RCA Studios sessions; no separate LP mastering engineer is credited, but the TR4M codes are RCA's custom mono matrix series and this record was pressed at RCA Indianapolis. The 1966 US mono and stereo cuts occupy the top historical tier as the earliest analog LP presentations, although period Cadet/RCA sound is not usually ranked with Blue Note's Van Gelder pressings. Collector reports are mixed: one describes the US record as crystal clear, while another found both domestic vinyl and the 1983 Japanese reissue somewhat dull and compressed, with the Japanese copy possibly marginally better. The later US and Japanese reissues can provide quieter playing surfaces but have no established audiophile advantage. No dedicated Tone Poet, Analogue Productions, Music Matters, or Mobile Fidelity-style modern LP reissue is documented, leaving a clean original US pressing as the default benchmark; this G+ copy will be limited by groove wear regardless of the cut.

albums.albumStory: Pink Floyd developed The Dark Side Of The Moon as a complete live work during 1972 before recording it at Abbey Road between June 1972 and January 1973 with engineer Alan Parsons. Roger Waters deliberately moved the band away from a loose instrumental suite toward a unified song cycle about the pressures that distort human life: time, money, work, conflict, death and mental collapse. The breakdown of former member Syd Barrett shadowed the project, giving its examination of madness a personal rather than merely abstract dimension. Clocks, cash registers, tape loops, synthesizer sequences and interview fragments were integrated into the music as structural elements rather than decorative effects. Clare Torry improvised the celebrated vocal for The Great Gig In The Sky in only a few takes, initially believing that little of her performance would be usable. The album transformed Pink Floyd from a respected underground band into a global act and demonstrated that progressive rock could be conceptually ambitious while remaining concise and immediate. Its critical stature has continued to grow, and it remains a defining example of the album as an immersive, continuous artistic statement.

The matching back cover prints SMAS 11163 at top center with no barcode, consistent with third-issue packaging rather than the barcode-bearing fourth (c. 1980-81) or rainbow-label fifth (July 1983) issues. The runouts pair G-99 with G-79 ER cuts, placing the Winchester metal used to a later pressing assembled from old-stock third-issue labels and jacket. Winchester pressings of this era are generally quiet and serviceable, but collector consensus ranks later US Capitol cuts below the UK Harvest SHVL 804 original and the best early US pressings. In the broader fidelity hierarchy, the 1979 Mobile Fidelity Stan Ricker half-speed, the 2003 Doug Sax/Kevin Gray edition, the 2016 Bernie Grundman remaster and the 2023 Analogue Productions UHQR all sit well above this routine Capitol repress. This copy's G-grade surface wear will overwhelm subtler mastering differences, and if both faces contain Side One it cannot serve as a complete listening copy.

albums.albumStory: The Wall grew out of Roger Waters' alienation on Pink Floyd's 1977 In The Flesh tour, when he spat at a fan pressing against the stage barrier and afterwards imagined literally walling himself off from the audience. Written almost entirely by Waters as a semi-autobiographical rock opera about Pink, a rock star whose dead wartime father, smothering mother, brutal schoolmasters and failed marriage become the bricks of a psychological wall, it drew directly on Waters' own loss of his father at Anzio and his English postwar boyhood. Recorded through 1979 in France and Los Angeles amid the band's tax exile and near-terminal internal warfare, the sessions saw Richard Wright dismissed and co-producer Bob Ezrin brought in to shape the sprawl into a narrative, pushing the disco-inflected arrangement and children's choir that turned "Another Brick In The Wall Part 2" into an unlikely worldwide number one. David Gilmour's contributions - above all the two solos on "Comfortably Numb," written to a Waters lyric about being medicated before a show - supplied the album's emotional release against Waters' bleakness. It stands as the last Pink Floyd album made by the classic four-piece and the peak of Waters' authorial control, the point where the band's post-Dark Side ambitions became fully theatrical, later realized in the wall-building stadium shows and Alan Parker's film. Contemporary critics were split between admiration for its scale and unease at its self-pity, but the album's stature only grew: it remains one of the best-selling records ever made and the touchstone concept album of its era. Its themes of isolation, authoritarianism and the corrosion of celebrity gave rock a template for the album-length personal epic that artists still work from.
albums.lpNotes: 1st US press (stereo, Dec 1979) - Columbia PC2 36183, Terre Haute plant ('T1' runouts); TML (The Mastering Lab / Doug Sax) stamps on all four sides; no-barcode first-issue gatefold with abbreviated inner credits.
albums.labelNotes: The labels are the custom 1979 US Columbia picture design created for this album: a white brick-wall field with Gerald Scarfe's hand-lettered 'PINK FLOYD THE WALL' and handwritten-style track listings, a different Scarfe character vignette per side (marching hammer/teacher, flower, doll, judge), the Columbia 'walking eye' box logo and 'Marca Reg.' rim text with © 1979 Pink Floyd Music Ltd. / Pink Floyd Music Publishers Ltd. credits. In 1979 Columbia was the CBS flagship US label, and Pink Floyd had moved from Harvest/Capitol to Columbia in the US with Animals (1977), so The Wall appeared on Columbia from day one - there is no earlier US label incarnation of this title. The picture-label design with the abbreviated one-line CBS manufacturing credit and the no-barcode sleeve marks the November/December 1979 first-issue window; the 1982+ repress added a rear barcode and expanded gatefold credits. This places the copy squarely in the original first-issue hierarchy, which the Terre Haute 'T1' plant marks and TML metalwork in the runouts corroborate.
albums.fidelity: Cut by Doug Sax at The Mastering Lab from the Guthrie/Gilmour tapes; having TML stamps on all four sides is the best case for a US copy, as many Columbia sets mix TML lacquers with later in-house recuts. Collectors on the forums rate the all-TML US pressing among the best-sounding editions of the album - open, punchy, wide dynamics, less compressed than mid-1980s repressings - and some listeners prefer it even to the UK Harvest SHDW 411 first press. Terre Haute 1979 pressing quality was generally good, though surface noise is the usual lottery, so quiet all-TML copies command the premium. Hierarchy: the UK Harvest first press and this US all-TML cut head the vintage tier, ahead of Pitman/Santa Maria recut sides and well ahead of the 1982 barcode repress; among moderns the 2016 Bernie Grundman/Pink Floyd Records remaster is well regarded and can beat a noisy original, and no Analogue Productions/Classic Records-class all-analogue audiophile LP exists to displace this cut.
albums.generalNotes: 1979 Columbia PC2 36183 US stereo - original first pressing from Columbia's Terre Haute, Indiana plant ('T1' in all four runouts), the Terre Haute Press, First Sleeve variant. All four sides carry P-prefixed PAL/PBL lacquer numbers with TML stamps (S / X / S / M) - a complete set of Doug Sax Mastering Lab metalwork, the configuration collectors look for since many copies mix TML and later recut sides; the typed 'PAL-3184/3185' numbers read as PAL-36184/36185, matching the disc catalog numbers. The jacket is the first sleeve: no rear barcode, only the small Columbia logo box with the one-line manufacturing credit on the back cover. Labels are the correct 1979 brick/Scarfe-character picture design with no promo wording, so this is a retail copy. The handwritten name inside the gatefold reads as an owner inscription, not a band autograph.

albums.albumStory: Wish You Were Here was recorded at Abbey Road between January and July 1975, with the band exhausted and creatively becalmed in the wake of the runaway global success of The Dark Side Of The Moon. Roger Waters shaped the record around the twin themes of absence and the corrosion of the music business, anchoring it with 'Shine On You Crazy Diamond', an elegy for Syd Barrett built on David Gilmour's four-note guitar phrase; the most famous story of the sessions is Barrett's unannounced arrival at the studio in June 1975, overweight and unrecognisable, while the band mixed the very song written about him. 'Welcome To The Machine' and 'Have A Cigar' are direct satires of the record industry, the latter sung by folk singer Roy Harper - who was recording in an adjacent studio - after Waters and Gilmour both struggled with the vocal. The title track's acoustic lament, framed by a car radio and a fake AM-radio guitar intro, became one of rock's most quoted songs of loss. The album marks the point where Pink Floyd shifted from studio-conceptual spectacle toward Waters' increasingly personal, embittered writing, the path that would lead to Animals and The Wall. It topped the charts in both the US and UK on release and, after mixed initial reviews from critics who found it thin next to Dark Side, was steadily re-evaluated as the band's most emotionally direct statement. Gilmour and Wright both named it their favourite Pink Floyd album, and it remains a cornerstone of progressive rock and one of the great records about friendship, disappearance and disillusion.
albums.lpNotes: Early US first-issue pressing (stereo, 1975-77) - Columbia PC 33453 custom handshake labels, no-barcode jacket; A-side lacquer AL 33453-1C with HTM (Harry T. Moss) etched, B-side BL 33453-3C; metalwork matches the documented Santa Maria pressing family, no plant mark in the transcription.
albums.labelNotes: This copy carries the custom die-cut 'mechanical handshake' labels (robotic arms, Hipgnosis/George Hardie artwork) unique to this title, with the PC 33453 stereo catalog number, AL 33453 / BL 33453 matrix numbers, (P)/(C) 1975 Pink Floyd Music Limited credits and a 'Marcas Reg. Printed in U.S.A.' rim. Wish You Were Here was Pink Floyd's first US release on Columbia after leaving Harvest, and the 1975 first issue paired these custom labels with a no-barcode jacket sealed in black opaque shrink with a round sticker, plus a printed lyric inner and Hipgnosis postcard. Columbia moved to barcoded jackets on late-1970s represses and dropped the custom label entirely when the title shifted to the JC 33453 prefix on standard Columbia labels in the 1980s. This label/jacket combination therefore anchors the copy firmly in the original 1975-77 first-issue window, ahead of every subsequent US variant.
albums.fidelity: The 'HTM' etch is Harry T. Moss, EMI's mastering engineer at Abbey Road, who cut the original UK SHVL 814 lacquers - its presence on this US Columbia means the American metalwork derives from Moss's cut, and collectors on the forums rate early PC 33453 copies for warmth, weight and an easy top end versus the thinner late-'70s represses and 1980s JC/plain-label copies. Pressing quality on early Columbia stock is decent but variable, and the pressing plant is not identified on the label. In the album's fidelity hierarchy this sits just below the UK Harvest SHVL 814 first pressing (the vintage reference cut, from the same Moss lineage) and roughly level with the best US originals, ahead of all later standard US repressings. The 1981 CBS Mastersound half-speed and the 2016 Bernie Grundman-cut reissue offer quieter surfaces and more modern detail, but the Moss-derived cut remains the satisfying vintage analogue choice.
albums.generalNotes: 1975 Columbia PC 33453 stereo - early US first-issue pressing, not a later repress. Custom die-cut handshake labels with the PC prefix, a back cover with no barcode, and first-generation A-side metalwork AL 33453-1C etched 'HTM' (Harry T. Moss's EMI cut) with B-side BL 33453-3C from the same first-issue family place it among the earliest US pressings. Santa Maria is the likely plant for this metalwork combination, though no stamped plant mark appears in the runout. The printed lyric inner sleeve is present; the original black shrink and sticker are gone.
